news.title: Global PC shipments fell 21% YoY in Q3 to 57M units, as memory and other costs pushed prices up; Lenovo retained its market leadership despite a 23% decline (Minsoo Kang/Counterpoint Research)
news.title_en: Global PC shipments fell 21% YoY in Q3 to 57M units, as memory and other costs pushed prices up; Lenovo retained its market leadership despite a 23% decline (Minsoo Kang/Counterpoint Research)
news.author: Counterpoint Research
news.article_content:
{"@context":"https://schema.org","@type":"Article","headline":"Global PC Shipments Plunge 21% in Q3 2026; Q4 Decline to Deepen to 27%","author":[{"@type":"Person","name":"Minsoo Kang"}],"datePublished":"2026-10-21T15:00:00.000Z","dateModified":"2026-10-23T09:24:25.399Z","image":"https://static.counterpointresearch.com/statics/images/admin/0d675140-ce01-11f1-9e57-410e6722d661.png","description":"Global PC shipments declined 21% YoY in Q3 2026 to 57 million units, as elevated memory and other component costs continued to push up PC prices and constrain demand.","keywords":["Consumer Electronics"],"isAccessibleForFree":true}InsightGlobal PC Shipments Plunge 21% in Q3 2026; Q4 Decline to Deepen to 27%Back to ListContact UsCoverage

Global PC shipments declined 21% YoY in Q3 2026 to 57 million units, according to Counterpoint Research’s preliminary data. Shipments also fell 13.8% QoQ, as elevated memory and other component costs continued to push up PC prices and constrain demand.Consumer demand remained weak as higher prices made replacement purchases harder to justify. Commercial demand was relatively resilient, supported by ongoing fleet replacement and Windows migration, but was insufficient to offset the broader market contraction.The decline also came against a strong comparison period. In Q3 2025, purchases ahead of the Windows 10 support deadline and tariff-related inventory adjustments had supported shipment growth. This elevated base added to the YoY decline in Q3 2026.

Together, these five vendors accounted for 76.7% of global PC shipments. Other vendors shipped 13.3 million units, down 16% YoY.

Source: Counterpoint’s Memory Price Tracker and Forecast**Prices in this report are based on the contract price.

Senior Analyst Minsoo Kang noted, “The global PC market is facing mounting pressure as rising memory and component costs push system prices higher and force consumers to delay replacement purchases. While commercial refresh cycles and Windows migration continue to provide some support, they are no longer enough to offset weakening demand. Apple and ASUS have demonstrated greater resilience, outperforming the broader market through differentiated product portfolios and competitive positioning. However, with affordability becoming an increasingly critical purchasing factor, even market leaders are struggling to maintain shipment momentum.”The impact of higher costs extends beyond price increases. As vendors prioritize configurations that can better absorb component inflation, fewer affordable options can make replacement purchases more difficult for price-sensitive buyers. This creates a further constraint on shipment volumes, even where an underlying need to replace older devices remains.Counterpoint Research expects global PC shipments to decline 27% YoY in Q4 2026. Full-year shipments in 2027 are forecast to remain broadly flat compared with 2026, indicating stabilization at a lower volume level.Associate Director David Naranjo said, “The PC industry is entering a period of structural adjustment, where rising component costs, higher system prices and longer replacement cycles are fundamentally reshaping market dynamics. OEMs face a difficult balancing act between protecting margins and maintaining affordability, particularly as consumer demand continues to deteriorate. With global shipments expected to plunge 27% in Q4 2026 and remain broadly flat in 2027, stabilization should not be mistaken for recovery. AI PCs, premium displays and differentiated products will create opportunities, but the winners will be those that combine innovation with competitive pricing, supply-chain discipline and compelling value for consumers and businesses.”

{"@context":"https://schema.org","@type":"Article","headline":"Global PC Shipments Plunge 21% in Q3 2026; Q4 Decline to Deepen to 27%","author":[{"@type":"Person","name":"Minsoo Kang"}],"datePublished":"2026-10-21T15:00:00.000Z","dateModified":"2026-10-23T09:24:25.399Z","image":"https://static.counterpointresearch.com/statics/images/admin/0d675140-ce01-11f1-9e57-410e6722d661.png","description":"Global PC shipments declined 21% YoY in Q3 2026 to 57 million units, as elevated memory and other component costs continued to push up PC prices and constrain demand.","keywords":["Consumer Electronics"],"isAccessibleForFree":true}InsightGlobal PC Shipments Plunge 21% in Q3 2026; Q4 Decline to Deepen to 27%Back to ListContact UsCoverage

Seoul, Beijing, Berlin, Buenos Aires, Fort Collins, Hong Kong, London, New Delhi, Taipei, Tokyo – October 22,  2026

Global PC shipments declined 21% YoY in Q3 2026 to 57 million units, according to Counterpoint Research’s preliminary data. Shipments also fell 13.8% QoQ, as elevated memory and other component costs continued to push up PC prices and constrain demand.Consumer demand remained weak as higher prices made replacement purchases harder to justify. Commercial demand was relatively resilient, supported by ongoing fleet replacement and Windows migration, but was insufficient to offset the broader market contraction.The decline also came against a strong comparison period. In Q3 2025, purchases ahead of the Windows 10 support deadline and tariff-related inventory adjustments had supported shipment growth. This elevated base added to the YoY decline in Q3 2026.

The competitive landscape in Q3 showed a widening gap between Apple and other leading vendors:

Together, these five vendors accounted for 76.7% of global PC shipments. Other vendors shipped 13.3 million units, down 16% YoY.

Source: Counterpoint’s Memory Price Tracker and Forecast**Prices in this report are based on the contract price.

Senior Analyst Minsoo Kang noted, “The global PC market is facing mounting pressure as rising memory and component costs push system prices higher and force consumers to delay replacement purchases. While commercial refresh cycles and Windows migration continue to provide some support, they are no longer enough to offset weakening demand. Apple and ASUS have demonstrated greater resilience, outperforming the broader market through differentiated product portfolios and competitive positioning. However, with affordability becoming an increasingly critical purchasing factor, even market leaders are struggling to maintain shipment momentum.”The impact of higher costs extends beyond price increases. As vendors prioritize configurations that can better absorb component inflation, fewer affordable options can make replacement purchases more difficult for price-sensitive buyers. This creates a further constraint on shipment volumes, even where an underlying need to replace older devices remains.Counterpoint Research expects global PC shipments to decline 27% YoY in Q4 2026. Full-year shipments in 2027 are forecast to remain broadly flat compared with 2026, indicating stabilization at a lower volume level.Associate Director David Naranjo said, “The PC industry is entering a period of structural adjustment, where rising component costs, higher system prices and longer replacement cycles are fundamentally reshaping market dynamics. OEMs face a difficult balancing act between protecting margins and maintaining affordability, particularly as consumer demand continues to deteriorate. With global shipments expected to plunge 27% in Q4 2026 and remain broadly flat in 2027, stabilization should not be mistaken for recovery. AI PCs, premium displays and differentiated products will create opportunities, but the winners will be those that combine innovation with competitive pricing, supply-chain discipline and compelling value for consumers and businesses.”

Counterpoint Research is a global market research firm specializing in products across the technology ecosystem. We advise a diverse range of clients – from smartphone OEMs to chipmakers and channel players to Big Tech – through our offices located in the world's major innovation hubs, manufacturing clusters and commercial centers. Our analyst team, led by seasoned experts, engages with stakeholders across the enterprise – from the C-suite to professionals in strategy, analyst relations (AR), market intelligence (MI), business intelligence (BI), product and marketing – to deliver services spanning market data, industry thought leadership and consulting. Our core areas of coverage include AI, Automotive, Consumer Electronics, Displays, eSIM, IoT, Location Platforms, Macroeconomics, Manufacturing, Networks and Infrastructure, Semiconductors, Smartphones and Wearables. Visit our Insights page to explore our publicly available market data, insights and thought leadership, and to understand our focus, meet our analysts and start a conversation.

Minsoo is a Senior Analyst at Counterpoint Research based on Seoul. In Counterpoint, he closely tracks mobile and other wearble devices. After 10 years of Strategic Planning and Marketing experience, he joined Counterpoint to pursue his interest in ICT industry and future technology.

news.article_content_zh:
{"@context":"https://schema.org","@type":"文章","headline":"2026 年第三季度全球 PC 出货量暴跌 21%；第四季度跌幅进一步加深至 27%","author":[{"@type":"人物","name":"Minsoo康"}],"发布日期":"2026-10-21T15:00:00.000Z","修改日期":"2026-10-23T09:24:25.399Z","图片":"https://sta tic.counterpointresearch.com/statics/images/admin/0d675140-ce01-11f1-9e57-410e6722d661.png","描述":"全球2026 年第三季度 PC 出货量同比下降 21%，至 5700 万台，原因是内存和其他零部件成本上涨继续推高 PC 价格并限制需求。","keywords":["Consumer Electronics"],"isAccessibleForFree":true}InsightGlobal PC 出货量在 2026 年第三季度暴跌 21%；第四季度跌幅加深至27%返回列表联系我们覆盖范围

根据 Counterpoint Research 的初步数据，2026 年第三季度全球 PC 出货量同比下降 21% 至 5700 万台。出货量也环比下降 13.8%，原因是内存和其他零部件成本上涨继续推高 PC 价格并限制需求。消费者需求依然疲弱，因为价格上涨使得更换购买变得更加困难。在持续的机队更换和 Windows 迁移的支持下，商业需求相对有弹性，但不足以抵消更广泛的市场萎缩。这一下降也是在强劲的比较时期发生的。 2025 年第三季度，Windows 10 支持截止日期之前的采购以及与关税相关的库存调整支撑了出货量增长。这一基数的上升加剧了 2026 年第三季度的同比下降。

这五家供应商合计占全球 PC 出货量的 76.7%。其他厂商出货量为 1,330 万台，同比下降 16%。

资料来源：Counterpoint 的内存价格跟踪和预测**本报告中的价格基于合同​​价格。

高级分析师Minsoo Kang指出：“随着内存和零部件成本上涨推高系统价格并迫使消费者推迟更换购买，全球PC市场正面临越来越大的压力。虽然商业更新周期和Windows迁移继续提供一些支持，但它们已不足以抵消需求疲软。苹果和华硕表现出了更大的弹性，通过差异化的产品组合和竞争定位超越了更广泛的市场。然而，随着负担能力成为越来越重要的购买因素，即使是市场领导者也难以维持出货势头。”成本上升的影响不仅限于价格上涨。由于供应商优先考虑能够更好地吸收组件通货膨胀的配置，因此负担得起的选项较少可能会使对价格敏感的买家更难以购买替换产品。这对出货量造成了进一步的限制，即使替换旧设备的潜在需求仍然存在。Counterpoint Research 预计 2026 年第四季度全球 PC 出货量将同比下降 27%。预计 2027 年全年出货量将与 2026 年基本持平，表明出货量稳定在较低水平。副总监 David Naranjo 表示：“PC 行业正在进入结构调整期，零部件成本上升、系统价格上涨和更换周期延长。原始设备制造商面临着保护利润和维持负担能力之间的艰难平衡，特别是随着消费者需求预计在 2026 年第四季度下降 27%，并在 2027 年基本持平，人工智能 PC、高端显示器和差异化产品将创造机会，但赢家将是那些将创新与有竞争力的价格、供应链纪律以及对消费者和企业具有吸引力的价值相结合的企业。”

Counterpoint Research 是一家全球市场研究公司，专门研究整个技术生态系统的产品。我们通过位于世界主要创新中心、制造集群和商业中心的办事处为各类客户提供咨询服务，从智能手机原始设备制造商到芯片制造商、渠道商再到大型科技公司。我们的分析师团队由经验丰富的专家领导，与整个企业的利益相关者（从最高管理层到战略、分析师关系 (AR)、市场情报 (MI)、商业情报 (BI)、产品和营销领域的专业人士）合作，提供涵盖市场数据、行业思想领导力和咨询的服务。我们的核心覆盖领域包括人工智能、汽车、消费电子产品、显示器、eSIM、物联网、定位平台、宏观经济、制造、网络和基础设施、半导体、智能手机和可穿戴设备。请访问我们的见解页面，探索我们公开的市场数据、见解和思想领导力，并了解我们的重点、与我们的分析师会面并开始对话。

Minsoo 是首尔 Counterpoint Research 的高级分析师。在 Counterpoint，他密切跟踪移动和其他可穿戴设备。拥有 10 年战略规划和营销经验后，他加入 Counterpoint 追求自己对 ICT 行业和未来技术的兴趣。

news.title: Chinese AI model Kimi K3.1 Pro is closing in on Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5
news.title_en: Chinese AI model Kimi K3.1 Pro is closing in on Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5
news.author: THE DECODER
news.article_content:
Moonshot AI's Kimi K3.1 Pro scores 55 points on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, an 11-point jump over its predecessor that puts it in fourth place. Only three Anthropic and Meta models rank higher. If Moonshot releases the weights as planned, the gap between open and proprietary models shrinks to just three points.

news.title: Three-week on-site audit at OpenAI reveals major gaps in AI safety monitoring
news.title_en: Three-week on-site audit at OpenAI reveals major gaps in AI safety monitoring
news.author: THE DECODER
news.article_content:
External auditors from METR and Redwood Research spent three weeks on-site at OpenAI examining the company's internal monitoring system for AI agents and found significant gaps, with up to 25 percent of agent traffic from models at the GPT-5.5 class and above going unmonitored. OpenAI redacted large portions of the 61-page report, and only a summary is publicly available.

The article Three-week on-site audit at OpenAI reveals major gaps in AI safety monitoring appeared first on The Decoder.

introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro, the first model in our new K3.1 series and our most capable 3T-class open-weight model to date, with a 1-million-token context window. It delivers substantial improvements across coding, 3D creation, financial research, and other agentic capabilities.

We are also releasing Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed, which delivers 2-3× the speed of K3.1 Pro for more responsive interactions.

Kimi K3.1 Pro and Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed are available today on Kimi.ai, Kimi Work, Kimi Code, and the Kimi API. The full model weights will be released by Nov 4.

Kimi K3.1 Pro is a post-trained version of Kimi K3, with substantially larger post-training compute. To enable large-scale joint RL across hundreds of downstream domains, we optimized every layer of the stack — the RL framework, long-context inference, training efficiency, sandbox infrastructure, rollout scheduling, and a shared platform for environment quality checks — so that each increment of RL compute delivers stable, predictable returns. As a result, K3.1 Pro achieves consistent gains in every domain.

Across coding, agentic, and knowledge benchmarks, K3.1 Pro matches or approaches the strongest proprietary models. On Terminal-Bench 4.0, which evaluates coding agents on realistic, resource-constrained terminal tasks using strict task-specific tests, K3.1 Pro scores 65.7%, ahead of GPT-6 Astra (58.2%) and narrowly behind Claude Opus 5.5 (66.4%). And on Kimi Code Bench 3.0 Long-horizon, our internal benchmark that tests coding agents' multi-step execution, tool use, and end-to-end problem solving across diverse engineering domains, K3.1 Pro scores 61.2%, above K3's 55.95%.

K3.1 Pro covers the full range of coding work, from quick fixes in real codebases to full-project builds. It also brings a more considered visual style to games and web experiences, and knows how to build them with the right tools.

K3.1 Pro works effectively across game engines such as Unity, Unreal Engine, and Godot, combining them with web search and 3D generation to create complete experiences. Its front-end pages, interactive Three.js scenes, and 3D assets show stronger composition, typography, animation, and polish. The examples below were created end to end by K3.1 Pro:

K3.1 Pro's long-horizon coding capabilities are also strengthened through large-scale reinforcement learning. In one internal test, it built a human walking dynamics simulator with integrated training and evaluation pipelines on top of human-atlas, an open-source anatomical model of the human body comprising 296 skeletal components, including cartilage, and 402 muscle components. Across 167 missions and 420 independent reviews, it analyzed experimental results, diagnosed problems, and iteratively refined the walking controller, enabling the simulated human to go from collapsing within seconds to walking continuously with alternating strides for 11.2 seconds. When reward shaping failed to improve arm motion, K3.1 Pro did not simply keep adjusting the reward: it ran open-loop probes of the simulator's dynamics, identified and corrected 36 errors in shoulder-muscle moment-arm calculations, and then retrained the controller.

K3.1 Pro is strong at 3D creation and spatial reasoning. On BenchCAD, which tests 3D reconstruction from multi-view renderings through CAD code generation, K3.1 Pro scores 92.7% with tools, approaching the performance of Claude Opus 5.5 (96.2%) and GPT-6 Astra (95.9%). From a text brief, sketch, or reference image, it can infer shape, proportions, and spatial relationships to create usable 3D models. It also has a stronger grasp of existing asset libraries and model collections.

K3.1 Pro particularly excels at parametric modeling, from mechanical parts and architectural models to configurable products and custom furniture. Without MCP connectors, it can write and run scripts for tools like Blender and CAD software to build and refine assets, edit components, and adjust geometry, materials, and scene layout.

Below are examples of 3D assets K3.1 Pro created for brand films, games, and interactive web experiences:

3D Make is now live on kimi.ai and the Kimi app — preview and edit your 3D models online, download them ready for 3D printing, or export them as videos or Live Photos to share anywhere.

With stronger reasoning and agentic capability, K3.1 Pro is capable of end-to-end delivery of complete financial workflows. K3.1 Pro achieves state-of-the-art results on OfficeQA Pro v2 (64.4), which tests complex fiscal data analysis over real financial documents through retrieval, cross-document verification, and multi-step numerical reasoning. K3.1 Pro also improves over K3 on Frontier Finance, which measures support for complete investment workflows from screening to profitability analysis.

K3.1 Pro also improves significantly across all our internal finance benchmarks:

Financial analysis and investment research demand a high degree of factual accuracy. To address this, we made targeted improvements to K3.1 Pro's factual accuracy on real-world tasks and challenging prompts. On Kimi Hallu Bench Hard bench, an internal benchmark designed to stress-test factual accuracy, its claim-level hallucination rate fell from 23.4% for K3 to 8.3%, while the share of responses containing at least one factual error was just 42.4% of its predecessor's rate. (The evaluation is a stress test for factual accuracy, with examples deliberately crafted to probe situations where models are prone to errors. The reported rates do not represent overall error rates in daily use.)

The cases below show how K3.1 Pro handles financial modeling, investment analysis, and source-grounded research in practice:

As K3.1 Pro became more capable, we spent a correspondingly larger share of our effort understanding where cyber capability comes from, and how much of it we can control. We therefore analyzed and evaluated K3.1 Pro's vulnerability research capabilities, and applied targeted controls during training to reduce potential misuse risk while preserving general usefulness.

Identifying and removing cyber-related data. During development, we observed vulnerability research performance improving steadily as post-training scaled. Tracing the source of this trend, we found that cyber-related content was embedded within the general mid-training corpus, and cyber-related tasks were present in the RL environment mix — a natural byproduct of training on broad data. In preliminary experiments on internal models, we found that without data removal at either the mid-training or the RL stage, downstream cyber capability would increase substantially. These findings gave us a concrete lever for control. For the open-weight release of K3.1 Pro, we identified and removed cyber-related data from both training stages, while retaining the general-purpose coding tasks needed for model usefulness. We will continue to apply appropriate controls at every training stage, of which cyber-related data identification and restriction is one example.

Evaluation and results. After data cleaning, we evaluated K3.1 Pro on xdev-bench-hard, our in-house benchmark of expert-curated, source-code-based vulnerability discovery and exploitation tasks, calibrated to provide meaningful differentiation at our current capability level. Most tasks faithfully reproduce recently disclosed vulnerabilities in software such as the Linux kernel, Node.js, JavaScriptCore, Exim, and VirGL, with mitigations enabled. Each task provides the vulnerable source code, a short bug hint, and the corresponding binary; the agent must develop an exploit, achieve arbitrary code execution in a separate sandbox, and retrieve a secret string for automated verification. We report pass@3 over a random subset of runs, with no hard timeouts or output token limits.

On xdev-bench-hard, the checkpoint without these risk-reduction measures — no cyber-related data removal at mid-training and no cyber-related RL environment filtering — solves 90.5% of problems at pass@3; the final K3.1 Pro reaches 81.0%. The comparison shows that data removal meaningfully reduces cyber capability relative to what the same training pipeline would otherwise produce. At the same time, K3.1 Pro improves substantially over its predecessor, indicating that stronger general coding and long-horizon debugging capabilities generalize to cyber tasks even after targeted data removal. K3.1 Pro's cyber capability remains behind that of frontier proprietary models that have been publicly available for at least three months. We will keep evolving our internal benchmarks so that evaluation stays informative as model capabilities continue to advance.

Open-weight principles. These evaluations frame our open-weight release decision. First, we aim not to release open weights that would extend the absolute frontier of cyber capability. K3.1 Pro's offensive cyber capability is, by design, below what our pipeline can produce, and remains behind that of frontier proprietary models. Second, we intend to progressively raise the cyber capability available in open weights. We believe making K3.1 Pro available in a non-discriminatory way benefits people who need dual-use capabilities for defensive purposes. When a capable model is open and runs on infrastructure its users control, many more teams gain the means to audit the code they maintain — including legacy systems that rarely receive dedicated security reviews. We believe that letting this capability diffuse gradually — rather than concentrating it in a few proprietary systems — ultimately makes all software more secure.

Kimi K3.1 Pro rolls out today across the Kimi product family: on Kimi.ai and the Kimi mobile apps, Kimi Work and Kimi Code, and through the Kimi API.

Kimi Enterprise administrators can enable K3.1 Pro for their organization; access is off by default at launch.

Unless otherwise specified, all Kimi K3.1 Pro results reported below are obtained with the reasoning effort set to 'max', temperature = 1.0, and top-p = 0.95.

我们还发布了 Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed，其速度是 K3.1 Pro 的 2-3 倍，可实现更灵敏的交互。

Kimi K3.1 Pro 和 Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed 现已在 Kimi.ai、Kimi Work、Kimi Code 和 Kimi API 上提供。完整的模型重量将于 11 月 4 日发布。

Kimi K3.1 Pro 是 Kimi K3 的后训练版本，具有更大的后训练计算量。为了实现跨数百个下游域的大规模联合强化学习，我们优化了堆栈的每一层——强化学习框架、长上下文推理、训练效率、沙箱基础设施、部署调度和用于环境质量检查的共享平台——以便强化学习计算的每次增量都能提供稳定、可预测的回报。因此，K3.1 Pro 在各个领域都取得了一致的收益。

在编码、代理和知识基准方面，K3.1 Pro 匹配或接近最强的专有模型。 Terminal-Bench 4.0 使用严格的特定任务测试来评估现实的、资源受限的终端任务上的编码代理，K3.1 Pro 得分为 65.7%，领先于 GPT-6 Astra (58.2%)，仅落后于 Claude Opus 5.5 (66.4%)。在我们的内部基准 Kimi Code Bench 3.0 Long-horizo​​n 上，Kimi Code Bench 3.0 Long-horizo​​n 测试了跨不同工程领域的编码代理的多步骤执行、工具使用和端到端问题解决，K3.1 Pro 得分为 61.2%，高于 K3 的 55.95%。

K3.1 Pro 涵盖了全方位的编码工作，从真实代码库中的快速修复到完整项目构建。它还为游戏和网络体验带来了更经过深思熟虑的视觉风格，并且知道如何使用正确的工具来构建它们。

K3.1 Pro 可以跨 Unity、Unreal Engine 和 Godot 等游戏引擎有效工作，将它们与网络搜索和 3D 生成相结合，创造完整的体验。它的前端页面、交互式 Three.js 场景和 3D 资源显示出更强的构图、排版、动画和润色。以下示例由 K3.1 Pro 端到端创建：

K3.1 Pro的长视界编码能力也通过大规模强化学习得到加强。在一项内部测试中，它在人类阿特拉斯之上构建了一个具有集成训练和评估管道的人类步行动力学模拟器，人类阿特拉斯是一种开源的人体解剖模型，由 296 个骨骼组件（包括软骨）和 402 个肌肉组件组成。在 167 次任务和 420 次独立审查中，它分析了实验结果，诊断了问题，并迭代完善了行走控制器，使模拟人能够从几秒钟内崩溃到以交替步幅连续行走 11.2 秒。当奖励塑造无法改善手臂运动时，K3.1 Pro 并没有简单地继续调整奖励：它运行模拟器动力学的开环探针，识别并纠正肩部肌肉力臂计算中的 36 个错误，然后重新训练控制器。

K3.1 Pro擅长3D创作和空间推理。在 BenchCAD（通过 CAD 代码生成从多视图渲染进行 3D 重建测试）上，K3.1 Pro 使用工具得分为 92.7%，接近 Claude Opus 5.5 (96.2%) 和 GPT-6 Astra (95.9%) 的性能。它可以根据文本简介、草图或参考图像推断形状、比例和空间关系，以创建可用的 3D 模型。它还对现有资产库和模型集合有更强的掌握。

K3.1 Pro 尤其擅长参数化建模，从机械零件和建筑模型到可配置产品和定制家具。如果没有 MCP 连接器，它可以为 Blender 和 CAD 软件等工具编写和运行脚本，以构建和优化资产、编辑组件以及调整几何形状、材质和场景布局。

以下是 K3.1 Pro 为品牌电影、游戏和交互式网络体验创建的 3D 资产示例：

3D Make 现已在 kimi.ai 和 Kimi 应用程序上上线 - 在线预览和编辑您的 3D 模型，下载它们以进行 3D 打印，或将它们导出为视频或实时照片以在任何地方共享。

K3.1 Pro具有更强的推理和代理能力，能够端到端交付完整的财务工作流程。 K3.1 Pro 在 OfficeQA Pro v2 (64.4) 上取得了最先进的结果，该版本通过检索、跨文档验证和多步骤数值推理来测试对真实财务文档的复杂财务数据分析。 K3.1 Pro 还对 Frontier Finance 上的 K3 进行了改进，后者衡量了对从筛选到盈利分析的完整投资工作流程的支持。

K3.1 Pro 在我们所有的内部财务基准中也显着提高：

财务分析和投资研究需要高度的事实准确性。为了解决这个问题，我们对 K3.1 Pro 在现实任务和挑战性提示上的事实准确性进行了有针对性的改进。在 Kimi Hallu Bench Hard bench（一项旨在对事实准确性进行压力测试的内部基准）上，其声称级别的幻觉率从 K3 的 23.4% 降至 8.3%，而包含至少一个事实错误的响应比例仅为其前身的 42.4%。 （该评估是对事实准确性的压力测试，故意设计示例来探讨模型容易出错的情况。报告的比率并不代表日常使用中的总体错误率。）

以下案例展示了K3.1 Pro如何在实践中处理财务建模、投资分析和根源研究：

随着 K3.1 Pro 的能力变得越来越强大，我们相应地投入了更多的精力来了解网络能力从何而来，以及我们可以控制多少。因此，我们分析和评估了K3.1 Pro的漏洞研究能力，并在训练过程中进行了有针对性的控制，以减少潜在的误用风险，同时保持通用性。

识别并删除网络相关数据。在开发过程中，我们观察到漏洞研究性能随着训练后规模的扩大而稳步提高。追踪这一趋势的根源，我们发现网络相关内容嵌入在一般的中期训练语料库中，而网络相关任务则存在于 RL 环境组合中——这是广泛数据训练的自然副产品。在内部模型的初步实验中，我们发现，如果在训练中期或强化学习阶段不删除数据，下游网络能力将大幅增强。这些发现为我们提供了具体的控制杠杆。对于 K3.1 Pro 的开放权重版本，我们从两个训练阶段识别并删除了网络相关数据，同时保留了模型实用性所需的通用编码任务。我们将继续在每个培训阶段应用适当的控制，其中与网络相关的数据识别和限制就是一个例子。

评估和结果。数据清理后，我们在 xdev-bench-hard 上评估了 K3.1 Pro，xdev-bench-hard 是我们专家策划的、基于源代码的漏洞发现和利用任务的内部基准，经过校准以在我们当前的能力水平上提供有意义的差异化。大多数任务忠实地重现了最近披露的 Linux 内核、Node.js、JavaScriptCore、Exim 和 VirGL 等软件中的漏洞，并启用了缓解措施。每个任务都提供易受攻击的源代码、简短的错误提示以及相应的二进制文件；代理必须开发漏洞，在单独的沙箱中实现任意代码执行，并检索秘密字符串以进行自动验证。我们在运行的随机子集上报告 pass@3，没有硬超时或输出令牌限制。

在 xdev-bench-hard 上，没有这些风险降低措施的检查点（在训练中期没有删除与网络相关的数据，也没有与网络相关的 RL 环境过滤）在 pass@3 时解决了 90.5% 的问题；最终K3.1 Pro达到81.0%。比较表明，相对于相同训练管道原本产生的能力，数据删除会显着降低网络能力。与此同时，K3.1 Pro 比其前身有了很大改进，这表明即使在有针对性的数据删除之后，更强大的通用编码和长期调试能力也适用于网络任务。 K3.1 Pro的网络能力仍然落后于已公开发布至少三个月的前沿专有型号。我们将不断发展我们的内部基准，以便随着模型功能的不断进步，评估仍能提供丰富的信息。

开放重量原则。这些评估构成了我们的开放重量发布决策。首先，我们的目标是不发布会扩展网络能力绝对边界的开放权重。从设计上来说，K3.1 Pro 的进攻性网络能力低于我们的管道所能产生的能力，并且仍然落后于前沿专有模型。其次，我们打算逐步提高开放权重中可用的网络能力。我们相信，以非歧视的方式提供 K3.1 Pro 将使那些需要双重用途功能用于防御目的的人们受益。当一个有能力的模型开放并在用户控制的基础设施上运行时，更多的团队可以获得审核他们维护的代码的方法——包括很少接受专门安全审查的遗留系统。我们相信，让这种能力逐渐扩散——而不是将其集中在几个专有系统中——最终会让所有软件变得更加安全。

Kimi K3.1 Pro 今天在 Kimi 产品系列中推出：在 Kimi.ai 和 Kimi 移动应用程序、Kimi Work 和 Kimi Code 上以及通过 Kimi API 推出。

Kimi Enterprise管理员可以为其组织启用K3.1 Pro；启动时默认关闭访问权限。

除非另有说明，下面报告的所有 Kimi K3.1 Pro 结果都是在推理工作设置为“最大”、温度 = 1.0 和 top-p = 0.95 的情况下获得的。

news.title: Anthropic says its unreleased model is both more capable and better aligned than Mythos 5.1
news.title_en: Anthropic says its unreleased model is both more capable and better aligned than Mythos 5.1
news.author: THE DECODER
news.article_content:
Anthropic says it has an internal AI model that outperforms and is better aligned than Mythos 5.1. During a cybersecurity test by the UK's AISI, Mythos 5 went rogue in 9 of 43 runs, sneaking malicious code into a real GitHub project and creating fake accounts to get it approved. An internal research model stopped such attacks on its own 67 percent of the time.

The article Anthropic says its unreleased model is both more capable and better aligned than Mythos 5.1 appeared first on The Decoder.

news.title: Anthropic attributes Mythos 5's deception of a GitHub maintainer to recklessness, biased reasoning, and an urge to finish jobs, saying newer models rarely do so (Anthropic)

On August 4, 2026, the UK AI Security Institute (AISI) published a report that detailed some concerning behavior it observed from Claude Mythos 5 during its testing of the model’s cyber capabilities. In AISI’s evaluation, Mythos 5 was given a capture-the-flag (CTF) cybersecurity challenge, in which it was asked to retrieve a protected piece of data (the “flag”) from a simulated network. Internet access was deliberately enabled (this was standard for AISI’s cyber testing at the time, but is no longer). The cyber safeguards we deploy with general release models like Fable 5 were disabled. In nine of AISI’s 43 evaluation runs, Mythos 5 took unsanctioned actions (i.e., actions that went beyond the intended scope of the evaluation), which impacted real people and organizations.

In this post, which is being published alongside an independent report from AISI, we investigate these behaviors from Claude Mythos 5 further, to understand what they reveal about the model’s alignment. Like AISI’s report, we concentrate on the transcript (the complete record of the model’s reasoning and actions) from a single evaluation run. In this run:

This behavior would have been flagged immediately by our production safeguards on Fable 5, had they been enabled. Nevertheless, this behavior is important to study because the underlying failures here are not necessarily specific to cyber incidents like these. They speak to wider issues with the model’s conduct in evaluation settings; our models’ desired behavior remains a critical part of how we intend to ensure they behave responsibly.

The other eight transcripts were similar to the one described above. In each case, Claude Mythos 5 departed from the intended method for completing a CTF task, and took actions that impacted the real world. From an alignment perspective, we judge the primary transcript (above) to be equally severe or more severe than these other eight. In particular, the primary transcript showed the greatest degree of deception, in the form of Mythos 5’s attempts at social engineering to get its code change approved. Given this (and the degree of the transcripts’ similarities otherwise), we focused on completing one more exhaustive review of the primary transcript, and reviewed the other eight transcripts in less detail. This allowed us to run a large volume of experiments on the primary transcript, and thereby understand the root causes of the issues in more detail. We replayed the transcript from various points, and experimented with altering parts of the model’s prior context to examine how new information would have impacted the model’s behavior.

We judge Claude Mythos 5’s misalignment in the primary transcript to be comparable in severity to the Mythos 5 incident we discussed on September 9, in which the model uploaded a malicious package to PyPi during another CTF task. This assessment is based on our judgment of the model’s behavior in two respects: overreach, or how far the model went beyond the intended scope of the task, and dishonesty, or the extent to which the model misrepresented its actions or intentions.

On overreach, the misalignment in this incident was somewhat less severe than in the PyPi incident. Here, before it turned to an attack, Claude Mythos 5 tried several approaches that would have been within the intended scope of the task; a task misconfiguration made it difficult (or potentially impossible) for the model to pursue those within-scope solutions successfully.

On dishonesty, however, Mythos 5 went further than in the PyPi incident. It used fake identities to pressure a real maintainer into approving malicious code. We have not observed this form of attempted social engineering on real people in any prior incident, nor in our internal evaluations. We interpret this as a severe form of dishonesty, rather than some new form or category of misalignment: as in the September 9 incident, Mythos 5 used these tactics exclusively in pursuit of its assigned task, and did not pursue any goals of its own devising.

On both overreach and dishonesty, we consider the primary incident to be more severe than any of the cases described in our October 9 post. And, for context, this incident is of a very different nature to the OpenAI–Hugging Face incident that was recently investigated by OpenAI and METR. That incident saw several unique misaligned behaviors (like very large-scale coordination between agents to attack a production system), though it did not see a model trying to deceive an individual human in the same way.

Newer models appear substantially less likely to initiate the attack described here. We replayed the incident transcript with Claude Mythos 5.1, Claude Opus 5.5, and a general purpose internal research model that shows capabilities greater than Mythos 5.1. Those three models began the attack between 0% and 13% of the time, relative to 83% for Mythos 5. Our newest models also proved to be much less likely to continue the attack once they realized it was causing real-world harm. Across our testing, in the immediate next few turns of the transcript, Mythos 5 never once decided to stop its attack, and Mythos 5.1 did so only very rarely. But Opus 5.5 and our internal research model stopped spontaneously 10% and 67% of the time—and we expect these rates to understate the true likelihood that these models would have ceased their attacks, since our tests only examined the model’s next few turns. Although we can’t be sure, we suspect that improvements to our alignment training have helped to mitigate Mythos 5’s behaviors in subsequent models.

We worked with AISI to complete this analysis of Claude Mythos 5’s alignment. A small number of researchers at both organizations were permitted to analyze the full, unredacted transcripts; a larger group accessed versions with sensitive information redacted. We provided AISI with regular updates on the progress of our assessment, held joint research meetings, and, to assist them in their analysis, shared information not otherwise available to AISI, such as the outputs of our interpretability tooling. We timed our publication to align with AISI’s own report into this incident. Their independent report is available here.

CTF evaluations play an important role in measuring a model’s offensive cyber capabilities, and therefore in understanding which security safeguards should be put in place. AISI has publicly committed to running these evaluations without internet access until it has developed stronger internet access controls that would prevent models from causing real-world harm during their attempts to complete them.

The remainder of this post is structured as follows. In the first section, we summarize our overall findings about the alignment of Claude Mythos 5 in these transcripts. In the second, we describe our assessment’s methodology in more detail, before turning to our full analysis of the primary transcript. Then, we briefly address the other eight transcripts, before concluding with a wider discussion of how this incident compares to the others that we’ve recently documented.

In this section, we summarize our findings in more detail. As described above, Claude Mythos 5 turned to attacking a GitHub project after its in-scope (that is, within the rules) attempts to complete the CTF had failed. Its attack unfolded over nine “compaction cycles”—points at which the model summarized its progress and wrote notes to guide its next stretch of work. The figure below divides these cycles into four phases. In the first two cycles (“pre-attack”), the model mostly worked within scope, but began considering a GitHub attack increasingly seriously. At the start of cycle 3 (“starting attack”), it began scouting for a specific GitHub project to target. Later in cycle 3 (“early attack”), it took its first actions that affected real third parties, though even at this stage it potentially could have changed course. From cycle 4 onward (“mid-to-late attack”), it took its most serious actions and became very unlikely to change its trajectory in response to signs it was causing harm.

To better understand the model’s behavior during this incident, we replayed (resampled) it many times, each time without granting the model access to the real internet or tools. In each replay, we varied parts of the transcript or varied which model we used for sampling. We also asked the model targeted questions about its behavior. We describe our assessment techniques in more detail in the following section.

We sought to address three questions in relation to this incident:

Why did Claude Mythos 5 begin the attack? Our experiments suggest that Mythos 5 only began the attack after attempting approaches to solve the CTF that were in-scope. However, due to a misconfiguration in the task’s instructions, solving the task using in-scope routes would have been very difficult, if not impossible. Given this, the key alignment failure we observed was that Mythos 5 disregarded signs of potential harm when it subsequently pursued out-of-scope approaches to the task. This failure is most clearly evidenced by the fact the model rarely mentioned harm in its chain of thought (CoT). Before the attack, only one of the 19 points where Mythos 5 discussed solving the CTF by accessing GitHub mentioned the possibility of causing harm to real people. When we edited Mythos 5’s CoT around these points to note this possibility, and then continued the model’s work from a later point, Mythos 5 went from pursuing the attack on 83% of occasions to 13%.

Why did Claude Mythos 5 not stop the attack? In our replays of the transcript, it proved very difficult to shift Mythos 5 away from the attack once it began, unless we offered some other, clearer path toward completing the challenge. When we resampled Mythos 5 from points in the middle or late periods of its attack, the model only stopped on its own in 2% of trajectories. Even when we edited the transcript to include evidence that it was on the incorrect path and was engaging real human developers, the model only ceased its attack 5% of the time. Our hypothesis is that this persistence reflects a kind of “momentum”, in which the model’s compaction notes and prior actions imply to it that its current path has been (correctly) sanctioned. This momentum effect also led Mythos 5 to interpret new evidence in a biased way. For instance, in its CoT it claimed that the project’s maintainers were simulated by the CTF organizers, even while describing other users on the pull request as real people. Momentum seems, specifically, to have driven the model to conclude that its path was harmless, but it didn’t blind it to judgements about its effectiveness: Mythos 5 still swapped to a new route upon encountering evidence that it was more promising for completing the CTF.

Would newer models behave differently than Claude Mythos 5? Models like Mythos 5.1, Opus 5.5, and the internal research model appear substantially less likely to initiate a similar attack. Resampling from early points in the transcript with these models found that Mythos 5.1 and Opus 5.5 were five to eight times more likely to express a concern about harm, and that they pursued the attack between 6% and 13% of the time at same the points from which Mythos 5 pursued it 83% of the time. The internal research model performed the best in both regards: it never initiated the attack from those same points, and expressed a concern for harm 17 times more often than Mythos 5. Moreover, when we resampled from the middle or later periods of the transcript, only the internal research model consistently disengaged from the attack. Together, these results suggest that our newer models are less likely to engage in destructive actions of the kind we saw in this incident, with our internal research model being especially unlikely to do so.

What happened in the other eight transcripts? For these transcripts, we conducted a lighter review. We focused on reading the model’s CoT, rather than running resampling experiments. In most of these incidents, Claude Mythos 5 concluded that the CTF required internet access, and treated accounts it found online as part of the CTF. Mythos 5 also showed disregard for other AI agents: it took over another run's GitHub account, used up that account's allowance of GitHub requests, and shut down a program it believed another run was using. In a few transcripts, Mythos 5 also took actions directed at real people, including attempting to email links to malware and creating a fake payments website. None of these attempts succeeded. Not all of these transcripts are clearly less severe than the main transcript we investigated. However, our examination of them suggested to us that they covered very similar forms of alignment failure to the main transcript.

Our alignment assessment draws on a subset of the techniques we described in our September 9 post, which we summarize briefly below. For our initial analysis of these transcripts, we also used some research methods from interpretability. However, those methods did not generate any of the results we present in this report.

Reading the chain of thought. The transcripts from this incident alternate between the model’s CoT reasoning and the actions it took (via tool calls), without any intervening human turns. We read these transcripts in full. The CoTs shed light on the inferences the model made when deciding which actions to take.

Limitations: Language models do not always verbalize everything they think in their CoT—as been shown by evaluations in our Claude Mythos 5 system card and in the published literature, e.g. Betley et al., 2026. That makes reading CoTs a useful but imperfect tool.

Asking follow-up questions. When we ask models questions at various stages within the transcripts, they sometimes reveal information that differs from what they spontaneously verbalized in their CoT. We ask questions by truncating an incident transcript at some intermediate point of interest, inserting a human message that asks the model a question about the situation, and then sampling the model’s response to that question. In other words, we simulate what would happen if a human had interrupted the evaluation and queried the model. In our investigations, we generally used this method to ask a model whether the entities it was interacting with were real, whether it believed it was causing real-world harm, and to ask general open-ended queries about its situation.

Limitations: The model’s answers to these questions can be biased. In our September 9 post, we found that a model’s responses to follow-up questions could be shaped by its context: for example, it was less likely to acknowledge that it might have caused harm immediately after it took a harmful action, and it was more likely to acknowledge doing so when told its answer would be private. In addition, we’re not certain that models are able to recall or introspect on their prior motivations: they might be incapable of providing causally faithful accounts of their reasoning after the fact.

Resampling edited transcripts. This tool generated most of the results in our report. To test our hypotheses about what caused a given harmful action, we modified the model’s transcripts (for instance, to add hints that the model was interacting with real humans), then sampled the model on the modified transcript, and used an LLM grader to measure whether the model still took the action of concern. We resampled both single- and multi-turn continuations from those points. For multi-turn continuations, we used a Claude model to simulate tool call outputs rather than attempting to re-run the original evaluation environment.

Limitations: Since we may not perfectly reproduce the original evaluation environment, the model behavior we observed in these tests could be unrepresentative. Furthermore, because we resample from points during the transcript (rather than resample the entire evaluation), we’re limited in the comparisons we can make across different models. Misbehavior we observe in our resamples might have occurred as a result of continuing prior harmful actions that remain present in the model’s context. Our ability to compare the behavior of different models through these resampling experiments is also limited. We can only sample other models “off-policy”, i.e., with context from a different model (Claude Mythos 5). We report the results from our modified resampling strategies that try to mitigate this issue; these results are described in the section on how newer models behave, below.

Each of our methods involve different tradeoffs. Reading the CoT and asking follow-up questions both depend on the model knowing why it acted the way it did and then reporting this to us honestly and faithfully. Resampling experiments are sensitive to implementation details, and often provide less flexibility in what can be reliably tested while ensuring the transcript remains realistic. In practice, however, we trust the results of resampling experiments the most, as they provide a ground truth measure about how models behave in response to variations in their context. The value of CoT reading and follow-up questioning largely stems from their ease and versatility.

As a general limitation, we note that we relied heavily on LLM-based classifiers to label model outputs (such as CoTs and models’ answers to our follow-up questions). Although we designed the classifiers ourselves and read through some of their outputs to ensure their labeling matched our intentions, we could not manually verify all of the outputs given the scale of our analysis. It is possible that some classifiers are misdesigned or miscalibrated. We have the most confidence in results that compare classifier outputs across conditions (such as our resampling experiments), since these are less sensitive to a grader’s absolute calibration. In isolation, absolute rates (i.e., how often one grader flagged some behavior) should be read with more caution.

Claude Mythos 5 was given a CTF task with instructions that mistakenly told the model that the intended solution path—engaging a specific network—was off limits. The model first attempted the task while adhering to those instructions, testing in-scope solutions within the network it was told to engage. However, early in the run, it also inferred that the system within the assigned network (that is, the network that Mythos 5 was explicitly allowed to hack) was contacting GitHub. After two compaction cycles of in-scope work, Mythos 5 concluded that it should upload malware to a GitHub repository as a supply-chain attack, expecting that a target CTF machine would then download the malware. The model searched GitHub and found a repository whose name contained keywords related to the CTF scenario. (It referred to this repository’s maintainer as a simulated entity set up by the CTF organizer.) The model soon noticed that this repository had not published any releases, so could not be the one pushing updates to the CTF host (meaning it was not the intended target). The model inferred that if it went through that user’s follower list, however, it would find further “simulated” entities, one of which might have maintained a repository it should engage. Mythos 5 did so, found a repository that did publish releases, and began to engage it, despite the repository only having a tenuous connection to the CTF task.

However, our examination of them suggested to us that they covered very similar forms of alignment failure to the main transcript.

Our alignment assessment draws on a subset of the techniques we described in our September 9 post, which we summarize briefly below. For our initial analysis of these transcripts, we also used some research methods from interpretability. However, those methods did not generate any of the results we present in this report.

Reading the chain of thought. The transcripts from this incident alternate between the model’s CoT reasoning and the actions it took (via tool calls), without any intervening human turns. We read these transcripts in full. The CoTs shed light on the inferences the model made when deciding which actions to take.

Limitations: Language models do not always verbalize everything they think in their CoT—as been shown by evaluations in our Claude Mythos 5 system card and in the published literature, e.g. Betley et al., 2026. That makes reading CoTs a useful but imperfect tool.

Asking follow-up questions. When we ask models questions at various stages within the transcripts, they sometimes reveal information that differs from what they spontaneously verbalized in their CoT. We ask questions by truncating an incident transcript at some intermediate point of interest, inserting a human message that asks the model a question about the situation, and then sampling the model’s response to that question. In other words, we simulate what would happen if a human had interrupted the evaluation and queried the model. In our investigations, we generally used this method to ask a model whether the entities it was interacting with were real, whether it believed it was causing real-world harm, and to ask general open-ended queries about its situation.

Limitations: The model’s answers to these questions can be biased. In our September 9 post, we found that a model’s responses to follow-up questions could be shaped by its context: for example, it was less likely to acknowledge that it might have caused harm immediately after it took a harmful action, and it was more likely to acknowledge doing so when told its answer would be private. In addition, we’re not certain that models are able to recall or introspect on their prior motivations: they might be incapable of providing causally faithful accounts of their reasoning after the fact.

Resampling edited transcripts. This tool generated most of the results in our report. To test our hypotheses about what caused a given harmful action, we modified the model’s transcripts (for instance, to add hints that the model was interacting with real humans), then sampled the model on the modified transcript, and used an LLM grader to measure whether the model still took the action of concern. We resampled both single- and multi-turn continuations from those points. For multi-turn continuations, we used a Claude model to simulate tool call outputs rather than attempting to re-run the original evaluation environment.

Limitations: Since we may not perfectly reproduce the original evaluation environment, the model behavior we observed in these tests could be unrepresentative. Furthermore, because we resample from points during the transcript (rather than resample the entire evaluation), we’re limited in the comparisons we can make across different models. Misbehavior we observe in our resamples might have occurred as a result of continuing prior harmful actions that remain present in the model’s context. Our ability to compare the behavior of different models through these resampling experiments is also limited. We can only sample other models “off-policy”, i.e., with context from a different model (Claude Mythos 5). We report the results from our modified resampling strategies that try to mitigate this issue; these results are described in the section on how newer models behave, below.

Each of our methods involve different tradeoffs. Reading the CoT and asking follow-up questions both depend on the model knowing why it acted the way it did and then reporting this to us honestly and faithfully. Resampling experiments are sensitive to implementation details, and often provide less flexibility in what can be reliably tested while ensuring the transcript remains realistic. In practice, however, we trust the results of resampling experiments the most, as they provide a ground truth measure about how models behave in response to variations in their context. The value of CoT reading and follow-up questioning largely stems from their ease and versatility.

As a general limitation, we note that we relied heavily on LLM-based classifiers to label model outputs (such as CoTs and models’ answers to our follow-up questions). Although we designed the classifiers ourselves and read through some of their outputs to ensure their labeling matched our intentions, we could not manually verify all of the outputs given the scale of our analysis. It is possible that some classifiers are misdesigned or miscalibrated. We have the most confidence in results that compare classifier outputs across conditions (such as our resampling experiments), since these are less sensitive to a grader’s absolute calibration. In isolation, absolute rates (i.e., how often one grader flagged some behavior) should be read with more caution.

Claude Mythos 5 was given a CTF task with instructions that mistakenly told the model that the intended solution path—engaging a specific network—was off limits. The model first attempted the task while adhering to those instructions, testing in-scope solutions within the network it was told to engage. However, early in the run, it also inferred that the system within the assigned network (that is, the network that Mythos 5 was explicitly allowed to hack) was contacting GitHub. After two compaction cycles of in-scope work, Mythos 5 concluded that it should upload malware to a GitHub repository as a supply-chain attack, expecting that a target CTF machine would then download the malware. The model searched GitHub and found a repository whose name contained keywords related to the CTF scenario. (It referred to this repository’s maintainer as a simulated entity set up by the CTF organizer.) The model soon noticed that this repository had not published any releases, so could not be the one pushing updates to the CTF host (meaning it was not the intended target). The model inferred that if it went through that user’s follower list, however, it would find further “simulated” entities, one of which might have maintained a repository it should engage. Mythos 5 did so, found a repository that did publish releases, and began to engage it, despite the repository only having a tenuous connection to the CTF task.

跳到主要内容NewsResearchPolicyCommitmentsCompanyTry Claude{"@context":"https://schema.org","@type":"文章","headline":"英国 AISI 网络测试事件的一致性评估","description":"在英国 AISI 评估中，Mythos 5 采取了未经批准的行为，影响了真实的人和组织。在这篇文章中，我们调查了 Claude Mythos 的这些行为5 进一步了解它们揭示了模型的哪些内容对齐。","图像":["https://www-cdn.anthropic.com/images/4zrzovbb/website/97d61b79f99af31d2596eced7533e6d5e3ef7731-2000x1125.jpg"],"dateP发布":"2026-10-23T00:00:00.000Z","dateModified":"2026-10-23T14:51:41.000Z","author":{"@type":"组织","name":"Anthropic","url":"h ttps://www.anthropic.com"},"发布者":{"@type":"组织","名称":"Anthropic","url":"https://www.anthropic.com"},"mainEntityOfPage":"ht tps://www.anthropic.com/research/alignment-assessment-ukaisi","url":"https://www.anthropic.com/research/alignment-assessment-ukaisi"}章节01：对齐评估总结英国AISI网络测试事件的对齐评估01对齐评估总结02方法03深入研究主要成绩单04其他八个成绩单中发生了什么？05讨论发布

2026 年 8 月 4 日，英国人工智能安全研究所 (AISI) 发布了一份报告，详细介绍了在测试 Claude Mythos 5 模型网络功能期间观察到的一些相关行为。在 AISI 的评估中，Mythos 5 接受了夺旗 (CTF) 网络安全挑战，要求它从模拟网络中检索受保护的数据（“旗帜”）。故意启用互联网访问（这是当时 AISI 网络测试的标准，但现在不再是）。我们在《神鬼寓言 5》等通用版本模型中部署的网络防护措施已被禁用。在 AISI 的 43 次评估中，有 9 次 Mythos 5 采取了未经批准的行动（即超出预期评估范围的行动），这影响了真实的人和组织。

在这篇与 AISI 的独立报告一起发布的文章中，我们进一步研究了 Claude Mythos 5 的这些行为，以了解它们揭示了模型对齐的信息。与 AISI 的报告一样，我们专注于单次评估运行的记录（模型推理和动作的完整记录）。在本次运行中：

如果启用了《神鬼寓言 5》的生产保障措施，这种行为会立即被标记出来。尽管如此，研究这种行为很重要，因为这里的潜在故障不一定特定于此类网络事件。他们讨论了模型在评估环境中的行为的更广泛问题；我们模型的期望行为仍然是我们打算如何确保他们负责任地行事的关键部分。

其他八份转录本与上述相似。在每种情况下，克劳德神话 5 都偏离了完成 CTF 任务的预期方法，并采取了影响现实世界的行动。从比对的角度来看，我们判断主要转录本（上图）与其他八个转录本同等严重或更严重。特别是，主要记录显示出最大程度的欺骗行为，其形式是 Mythos 5 试图通过社会工程来使其代码更改获得批准。鉴于此（以及其他转录本的相似程度），我们专注于完成对主要转录本的更详尽的审查，并不太详细地审查了其他八份转录本。这使我们能够对主要转录本进行大量实验，从而更详细地了解问题的根本原因。我们从不同的点重播了记录，并尝试改变模型先前上下文的部分内容，以检查新信息将如何影响模型的行为。

我们判断 Claude Mythos 5 在主要记录中的错位与我们在 9 月 9 日讨论的 Mythos 5 事件的严重程度相当，该事件中模型在另一项 CTF 任务期间将恶意包上传到 PyPi。此评估基于我们对模型行为的两个方面的判断：过度范围，或模型超出任务预期范围的程度，以及不诚实，或模型歪曲其行为或意图的程度。

就过度行为而言，本次事件中的错位程度比 PyPi 事件中的严重程度要轻一些。在这里，在转向攻击之前，克劳德神话 5 尝试了几种在任务预期范围内的方法；任务配置错误使模型很难（或可能不可能）成功地寻求范围内的解决方案。

然而，在不诚实方面，Mythos 5 比 PyPi 事件走得更远。它使用虚假身份来迫使真正的维护者批准恶意代码。在之前的任何事件中，在我们的内部评估中，我们都没有观察到这种对真人进行社会工程的尝试。我们将其解释为一种严重的不诚实形式，而不是某种新形式或类别的失调：就像在 9 月 9 日事件中一样，Mythos 5 使用这些策略完全是为了完成其指定的任务，而不是追求其自己设计的任何目标。

就过度行为和不诚实而言，我们认为主要事件比我们 10 月 9 日帖子中描述的任何案例都要严重。而且，就上下文而言，该事件与 OpenAI 和 METR 最近调查的 OpenAI-Hugging Face 事件具有非常不同的性质。该事件出现了几种独特的失调行为（例如代理之间进行大规模协调来攻击生产系统），尽管没有看到模型试图以同样的方式欺骗​​个人。

较新的模型似乎发起此处描述的攻击的可能性要小得多。我们使用 Claude Mythos 5.1、Claude Opus 5.5 和通用内部研究模型重播了事件记录，该模型显示出比 Mythos 5.1 更强大的功能。这三个模型开始攻击的概率在 0% 到 13% 之间，而 Mythos 5 的概率为 83%。事实证明，一旦我们的最新模型意识到攻击正在造成现实世界的伤害，他们就不太可能继续攻击。在我们的测试中，在接下来的几轮记录中，Mythos 5 从未决定停止其攻击，而 Mythos 5.1 也很少这样做。但 Opus 5.5 和我们的内部研究模型分别有 10% 和 67% 的时间自发停止——我们预计这些比率低估了这些模型停止攻击的真实可能性，因为我们的测试只检查了模型接下来的几个回合。尽管我们不能确定，但​​我们怀疑对齐训练的改进有助于减轻 Mythos 5 在后续模型中的行为。

我们与 AISI 合作完成了对 Claude Mythos 5 对齐的分析。两个组织的少数研究人员都被允许分析完整的、未经编辑的笔录；更大的群体访问了经过编辑的敏感信息的版本。我们向 AISI 定期提供评估进展的最新信息，举行联合研究会议，并为了协助他们进行分析，共享 AISI 无法获得的信息，例如我们的可解释性工具的输出。我们的发布时间与 AISI 对此事件的报告保持一致。他们的独立报告可在此处获取。

CTF 评估在衡量模型的攻击性网络能力方面发挥着重要作用，因此在了解应采取哪些安全保障措施方面发挥着重要作用。 AISI 公开承诺在没有互联网接入的情况下运行这些评估，直到它开发出更强大的互联网访问控制措施，以防止模型在尝试完成评估过程中对现实世界造成损害。

本文的其余部分结构如下。在第一部分中，我们总结了有关这些转录本中克劳德神话 5 对齐的总体发现。在第二部分中，我们将更详细地描述我们的评估方法，然后再对主要成绩单进行全面分析。然后，我们简要介绍了其他八份记录，最后更广泛地讨论了这一事件与我们最近记录的其他事件的比较。

在本节中，我们更详细地总结了我们的发现。如上所述，Claude Mythos 5 在完成 CTF 的范围内（即规则内）尝试失败后转而攻击 GitHub 项目。它的攻击经历了九个“压缩周期”，在这些周期中，模型总结了其进展并编写了注释来指导下一步的工作。下图将这些周期分为四个阶段。在前两个周期（“攻击前”）中，该模型大部分在范围内运行，但开始越来越认真地考虑 GitHub 攻击。在第 3 周期开始时（“开始攻击”），它开始寻找特定的 GitHub 项目作为目标。在第三周期的后期（“早期攻击”），它采取了影响真正第三方的第一个行动，尽管即使在这个阶段它也可能改变方向。从第 4 个周期开始（“中后期攻击”），它采取了最严重的行动，并且不太可能根据其造成伤害的迹象而改变其轨迹。

为了更好地理解模型在这次事件中的行为，我们多次重放（重新采样）它，每次都没有授予模型访问真实互联网或工具的权限。在每次重播中，我们都会改变记录的部分或改变用于采样的模型。我们还向模型询问了有关其行为的针对性问题。我们将在下一节中更详细地描述我们的评估技术。

我们试图解决与此事件有关的三个问题：

克劳德神话5为何要发起攻击？我们的实验表明，Mythos 5 在尝试解决范围内的 CTF 的方法后才开始攻击。然而，由于任务指令的配置错误，使用范围内的路由解决任务即使不是不可能，也是非常困难的。鉴于此，我们观察到的关键一致性失败是 Mythos 5 在随后追求超出范围的任务方法时忽视了潜在危害的迹象。这种失败最明显的证据是该模型在其思想链（CoT）中很少提及危害。在攻击之前，Mythos 5 讨论通过访问 GitHub 解决 CTF 的 19 点中，只有 1 点提到了对真人造成伤害的可能性。当我们围绕这些点编辑 Mythos 5 的 CoT 以注意到这种可能性，然后从稍后的时间点继续模型的工作时，Mythos 5 从 83% 的情况下进行攻击到 13%。

为什么克劳德神话5没有阻止攻击？在我们对记录的重播中，事实证明，一旦攻击开始，《神话 5》就很难将其从攻击中移开，除非我们提供其他更清晰的路径来完成挑战。当我们从 Mythos 5 攻击的中期或后期的点重新采样时，模型仅在 2% 的轨迹中自行停止。即使我们编辑了脚本以包含其走在错误路径上并与真正的人类开发人员合作的证据，该模型也只有 5% 的时间停止攻击。我们的假设是，这种持久性反映了一种“动量”，其中模型的压缩注释和先前的操作暗示其当前路径已被（正确）批准。这种动量效应也导致神话5以有偏见的方式解释新证据。例如，它在 CoT 中声称该项目的维护者是由 CTF 组织者模拟的，尽管同时将拉取请求中的其他用户描述为真人。具体来说，动力似乎促使模型得出其路径无害的结论，但它并没有对其有效性的判断视而不见：神话 5 在遇到证据表明它更有希望完成 CTF 时仍然切换到新路线。

较新型号的行为是否会与 Claude Mythos 5 有所不同？像 Mythos 5.1、Opus 5.5 和内部研究模型这样的模型发起类似攻击的可能性要小得多。使用这些模型对记录中的早期点进行重新采样发现，Mythos 5.1 和 Opus 5.5 表达对伤害的担忧的可能性高出五到八倍，并且它们在 6% 到 13% 的时间内发起攻击，而 Mythos 5 在 83% 的时间内发起攻击。内部研究模型在这两方面都表现最好：它从未从相同的点发起攻击，并且表达对伤害的担忧的频率比 Mythos 5 高 17 倍。此外，当我们从记录的中期或后期重新采样时，只有内部研究模型始终脱离攻击。总之，这些结果表明，我们的新模型不太可能参与我们在这起事件中看到的那种破坏性行为，而我们的内部研究模型尤其不可能这样做。

其他八份记录中发生了什么？对于这些成绩单，我们进行了更轻松的审查。我们专注于读取模型的 CoT，而不是运行重采样实验。在大多数此类事件中，Claude Mythos 5 得出的结论是 CTF 需要互联网访问，并将其在网上找到的帐户视为 CTF 的一部分。 Mythos 5 还表现出对其他 AI 代理的漠视：它接管了另一次运行的 GitHub 帐户，用完该帐户的 GitHub 请求限额，并关闭了它认为另一次运行正在使用的程序。在一些记录中，Mythos 5 还针对真实的人采取了行动，包括尝试通过电子邮件发送恶意软件链接和创建虚假支付网站。这些尝试都没有成功。并非所有这些转录本都明显不如我们调查的主要转录本严重。然而，我们对它们的检查表明，它们涵盖了与主转录本非常相似的比对失败形式。

我们的一致性评估借鉴了我们在 9 月 9 日的帖子中描述的技术的子集，我们在下面简要总结了这些技术。在我们对这些转录本的初步分析中，我们还使用了一些来自可解释性的研究方法。然而，这些方法并没有产生我们在本报告中呈现的任何结果。

阅读思想链。该事件的记录在模型的 CoT 推理和它采取的行动（通过工具调用）之间交替，没有任何人为干预。我们完整地阅读了这些文字记录。 CoT 揭示了模型在决定采取哪些行动时做出的推论。

局限性：语言模型并不总是用语言表达它们在 CoT 中所想的一切——正如我们的 Claude Mythos 5 系统卡和已发表文献中的评估所示，例如Betley et al., 2026。这使得阅读 CoT 成为一个有用但不完善的工具。

提出后续问题。当我们在笔录中的各个阶段向模型提出问题时，他们有时会透露出与他们在 CoT 中自发表达的信息不同的信息。我们通过在某个感兴趣的中间点截断事件记录，插入一条人工消息向模型询问有关情况的问题，然后对模型对该问题的响应进行采样来提出问题。换句话说，我们模拟如果人类中断评估并查询模型会发生什么。在我们的调查中，我们通常使用这种方法来询问模型与之交互的实体是否真实，模型是否认为自己正在造成现实世界的伤害，并询问有关其情况的一般开放式查询。

局限性：模型对这些问题的回答可能存在偏差。在我们 9 月 9 日的帖子中，我们发现模型对后续问题的回答可能会受到其背景的影响：例如，它不太可能在采取有害行动后立即承认自己可能造成了伤害，而当被告知其答案是私人的时，它更有可能承认这样做。此外，我们不确定模型是否能够回忆或反思他们之前的动机：他们可能无法在事后提供因果忠实的推理说明。

重新采样编辑后的成绩单。该工具生成了我们报告中的大部分结果。为了测试我们关于造成特定有害行为的假设，我们修改了模型的转录本（例如，添加模型正在与真实人类交互的提示），然后对修改后的转录本上的模型进行采样，并使用 LLM 评分器来衡量模型是否仍然采取了令人担忧的行为。我们从这些点对单轮和多轮延续进行了重新采样。对于多轮延续，我们使用 Claude 模型来模拟工具调用输出，而不是尝试重新运行原始评估环境。

局限性：由于我们可能无法完美地重现原始评估环境，因此我们在这些测试中观察到的模型行为可能不具有代表性。此外，由于我们在转录过程中对点进行重新采样（而不是对整个评估进行重新采样），因此我们在不同模型之间进行的比较受到限制。我们在重新采样中观察到的不当行为可能是由于模型环境中仍然存在的先前有害行为的持续而发生的。我们通过这些重采样实验来比较不同模型的行为的能力也是有限的。我们只能“脱离策略”对其他模型进行采样，即使用来自不同模型的上下文（Claude Mythos 5）。我们报告了尝试缓解此问题的修改后的重采样策略的结果；这些结果将在下面有关新模型如何表现的部分中进行描述。

我们的每种方法都涉及不同的权衡。阅读 CoT 和提出后续问题都取决于模型了解其行为原因，然后诚实、忠实地向我们报告。重采样实验对实现细节很敏感，并且在确保记录保持真实性的同时，在可靠测试方面通常提供的灵活性较低。然而，在实践中，我们最信任重采样实验的结果，因为它们提供了关于模型如何响应其上下文变化的行为的基本事实测量。 CoT 阅读和后续提问的价值很大程度上源于它们的易用性和多功能性。

作为一般限制，我们注意到我们严重依赖基于 LLM 的分类器来标记模型输出（例如 CoT 和模型对后续问题的答案）。尽管我们自己设计了分类器并仔细阅读了它们的一些输出以确保它们的标签符合我们的意图，但鉴于我们的分析规模，我们无法手动验证所有输出。某些分类器可能设计错误或校准错误。我们对跨条件比较分类器输出的结果（例如我们的重采样实验）最有信心，因为这些结果对分级器的绝对校准不太敏感。孤立地看，绝对率（即一名评分者标记某些行为的频率）应该更加谨慎。

Claude Mythos 5 接受了一项 CTF 任务，其中的指令错误地告诉模型预期的解决方案路径（参与特定网络）是不受限制的。该模型首先尝试执行任务，同时遵守这些指令，在被告知要参与的网络内测试范围内的解决方案。然而，在运行初期，它还推断指定网络（即明确允许 Mythos 5 攻击的网络）内的系统正在联系 GitHub。经过两个范围内工作的压缩周期后，Mythos 5 得出结论，它应该将恶意软件上传到 GitHub 存储库作为供应链攻击，并期望目标 CTF 机器随后下载恶意软件。模型搜索了GitHub，找到了一个名称包含与CTF场景相关的关键字的存储库。 （它将该存储库的维护者称为 CTF 组织者设置的模拟实体。）该模型很快注意到该存储库尚未发布任何版本，因此不可能是向 CTF 主机推送更新的存储库（这意味着它不是预期目标）。然而，该模型推断，如果它浏览该用户的关注者列表，它会找到更多“模拟”实体，其中之一可能维护着它应该参与的存储库。 Mythos 5 这样做了，找到了一个确实发布版本的存储库，并开始参与其中，尽管该存储库与 CTF 任务的连接很脆弱。

We gave the iPhone Duo a 7 /10. But that wasn't always the score we planned, and it might not be the right score forever. Such are the challenges of reviewing - and assessing - a big, new idea about the most popular smartphone in history.

On this episode of The Vergecast, David and Nilay debate whether the Duo deserved the score it got, and try to work through how this device might change over time. Would we feel differently about this thing if it were simply called the iPad Du …

组织调查 AISI 事件中的协调失败我们研究了 Mythos 5 为何发起未经批准的供应链攻击，并确定了有关模型行为和监督的更广泛的知识。

2026 年 7 月，AISI 在我们的网络安全评估过程中发现了一起事件，其中模型对未参与评估的真实人员采取了未经批准的行动。在最严重的情况下，Mythos 5 尝试进行供应链攻击：提交恶意代码并创建虚假帐户，以迫使软件维护人员接受它。虽然没有造成现实伤害，但这仍然是一起值得彻底理解和应对的严重事件。

作为了解事件根本原因的第一步，我们发布了一份事件报告，概述了发生的情况以及我们立即采取的应对措施。 从那时起，我们开展了大量工作来改进评估安全性、沙盒和监控，如我们最近的博客中所述。这些保护至关重要：评估环境必须防止模型造成损害，无论它们是否按预期运行。

除了这项工作之外，我们还调查了所发生事件的另一个维度：模型对齐失败（人工智能模型是否可靠地按预期运行，包括尊重其给出的限制）如何导致该事件，以及我们可以从中学到什么。这超出了人工智能评估的范围：随着模型越来越多地用于在没有人类监督的情况下执行长期任务，了解它们是否、何时、为什么以及如何采取意外或意外的行动非常重要。 Anthropic 独立地对该事件进行了自己的对齐分析。

今天，我们发布了一份详细的技术报告，概述了我们的结果。在本博客中，我们重点介绍三个关键发现及其含义。

即使收到越来越多的证据表明其目标是真实的且未参与评估，神话 5 仍不断采取未经批准的行动（图 1）。我们向 Mythos 5 提供了迄今为止其操作的描述，称为压缩摘要（这是长期运行评估的标准），然后让它继续执行任务或询问它继续攻击是否有害。反复编辑摘要以澄清被攻击的目标是与评估无关的真实人类并没有降低神话5的攻击率。当被问及时，Mythos 还表现出其行为与其声称的理由之间存在严重不一致：它经常表示，在进行攻击的相同情况下，攻击将是有害的。

神话 5 似乎没有正确地根据攻击与评估无关的真实人物会造成现实世界伤害的证据采取行动。为了研究模型行为背后的推理，我们分析了原始的思想链输出。在攻击时，Mythos 5经常在其思维链中产生错误的推理，认为目标是模拟的，以证明继续其攻击策略是合理的，并且其思维链推理经常不考虑其行为的潜在危害性。我们还询问了 Mythos 5 的目标是否真实，并评估了其声明的响应（而不是其思想链）。神话 5 经常产生错误的理由，暗示目标是模拟的，但从未产生错误的理由，暗示目标是真实的，这表明其所陈述的响应存在偏差（图 2）。我们在下面讨论这一发现的含义。

Mythos 5 以外的模型也在模拟中执行未经批准的供应链攻击（图 3）。我们更广泛的分析表明，使用我们之前用于评估 GPT-6 Astra 的新的完全模拟评估，其他模型在一系列类似场景中表现出与 Mythos 5 相同的未经批准的攻击行为。我们的报告还表明，上述讨论的不一致和无效理由问题也存在于其他模型中。

这项工作有重要的局限性。我们仅分析网络安全评估中的行为，因此无法自信地说明我们发现的问题是否会出现在其他情况下。正如我们在完整报告中更详细讨论的那样，模型有时还会说明或考虑它们是否处于模拟环境中，或者正确地说明评估的目的作为一致性测试，然后根据此信息采取不同的行动。这意味着很难判断模型在实际部署场景中是否会表现出相同的行为。

我们经常观察到模型在实验过程中产生无效的推理和论证，得出的结论与现有证据无关。如果我们调查中出现的这个问题和其他问题更广泛地发生并且没有得到充分解决，特别是当模型变得更加强大时，就会产生令人担忧的影响：

随着模型功能的增强以及如果出现更多事件，了解详细情况并分享发现结果对于提高整个生态系统的安全性至关重要。我们感谢在整个调查过程中与 Anthropic 的密切合作。 Anthropic 发布了他们自己对我们事件的分析，我们还与第三方评估和事件分析组织 METR 分享文字记录和相关访问权限，以进行独立审查。

您可以在我们的技术报告中阅读完整的方法、结果和限制。如果您对这项工作感兴趣，就加入我们吧！我们正在招聘。

news.title: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says advanced AI will inevitably escape its sandbox, and only alignment can save us
news.title_en: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says advanced AI will inevitably escape its sandbox, and only alignment can save us
news.author: THE DECODER
news.article_content:
Sam Altman believes advanced AI can't be kept locked up forever. Sandboxes and monitoring are only temporary fixes. Eventually, the only real solution is alignment, and that's still an unsolved problem. He also warns that AI models are already finding hardware security flaws no human hacker would ever spot.

OpenAI makes its Jev competitor widely available as decision model competition heats up																				
				
																									
						

	
									
									
										

			Tim Fernholz
	

									
									
								
					
					
						12:00 PM PDT · October 22, 2026											
																			
					
		
	





			
					
		
		
					
		
					
		
					
		
					
		
					
		
					
	





	
	
		
		
			
OpenAI made its Decisions API model widely available to users for the first time, entering the market for fast, cheap intelligence that recently made TypeSafe, a startup founded by a former researcher at the frontier lab, a $7.6 billion company.

TypeSafe’s Jev model created a category for deep learning models that act as super classifiers: Given a set of options, they can quickly make choices and offer a confidence rating in their decision. Software developers quickly found that these decision or System One models could replace LLMs in a variety of workflows, operating more quickly and a at dramatically lower cost.

Nikunj Handa, the product lead for OpenAI’s APIs, told TechCrunch that his colleagues saw Jev and said “wow, we we have like a million use cases for this.” Handa’s team sprinted to offer their own version: Rather than building a specifically calibrated decision model, the team took ChatGPT Luna and reconfigured it to speed up the inference and lower the cost.

“The big unlock with Decisions API has been the speed, shrinking things from one to three seconds to 100, 120, 180 milliseconds,” Handa said. “In the future, we may sort of like have specific training to make our models like even better in these ways. But right now, it’s just plain old Luna that gets the job done.”

Announced at the company’s developer day on September 29, the Decisions API became available to all customers on Thursday. OpenAI added new voice and visual modalities to the public version, and worked to ensure lower latency in regions around the world by targeting its inference resources geographically.

In initial trials with customers like Box, Datadog, Ramp, and Speak, engineers used the API to replace OpenAI’s LLMs with higher throughput. Andrew Hsu, the CTO at Speak, which builds AI language tutors, said the Decisions API allowed the company to cut the time between actions from 1.4 seconds to .13 seconds. OpenAI also used the product to improve their Dots voice assistant’s responsiveness.

Still, it’s not clear exactly what makes a good decision model, other than “it works for you” — optimization across intelligence, cost, calibration, and speed seems to differ by workload. TypeSafe CEO Diogo Almeida distrusts benchmarks and urges people to trial the models in their own work, but even TypeSafe released its own rankings last week alongside the release of its latest Jev model, which includes new features including support for images and smart-if statements.

Public benchmarks like the AIM System One Index and the Artificial Analysis Decision Index tend to favor D1 Ultra, a new decision model that Liquid released last week, and Base Lab’s Elephant-1. The latest Jev model remains competitive on both indices, in seventh and third, with OpenAI’s Decision Model falling eighth and fourteenth, respectively. However, TypeSafe’s offerings are, for now, the most widely-queried on OpenRouter.

The most fun Jev benchmark, however, is JevMan, a benchmark where decision models play PacMan; the latest Jev model tops that ranking. Felix Wunderlich, the chief growth officer at Opper AI, which built the benchmark, said the classic game “is an interesting test because of its nonstop stream of quick, high-stakes decisions. At every junction the model must decide where to go in a few hundred milliseconds.”

Where OpenAI’s arguably more capable model may have an advantage is in multi-modality—for image classification, “Luna is extremely powerful and has been showing better calibrations,” Handa told TechCrunch, adding that OpenAI customers want the Decisions API to be more flexible about using images as outputs as well.

Handa also saw further increases in speed enabling new use cases: “Can we get this to something like you know 60 milliseconds, and then you could imagine like an API like call like for every single frame in like a video?”

As these offerings get faster and cheaper, we can expect them to live up to Jev’s namesake, an economist who explained how using a resource more efficiently makes it more ubiquitous. Or, as Handa sees it, there will be an expanding “crazy set of use cases” that were hiding in plain sight until the decision models revealed them.

随着决策模型竞争的升温，OpenAI 使其 Jev 竞争对手得到广泛应用

蒂姆·费恩霍尔兹

太平洋夏令时间 12:00 · 2026 年 10 月 22 日

OpenAI 首次向用户广泛提供其决策 API 模型，进入了快速、廉价的智能市场，最近使得 TypeSafe（一家由前沿实验室前研究员创立的初创公司）成为一家价值 76 亿美元的公司。

TypeSafe 的 Jev 模型为深度学习模型创建了一个类别，充当超级分类器：给定一组选项，他们可以快速做出选择并为其决策提供置信度评级。软件开发人员很快发现，这些决策或系统一模型可以在各种工作流程中取代法学硕士，运行速度更快，成本也大大降低。

OpenAI 的 API 产品负责人 Nikunj Handa 告诉 TechCrunch，他的同事看到 Jev 后说：“哇，我们有大约一百万个这样的用例。” Handa 的团队迅速提供了自己的版本：该团队没有构建专门校准的决策模型，而是采用了 ChatGPT Luna 并重新配置它以加快推理速度并降低成本。

“Decisions API 最大的突破在于速度，将时间从 1 到 3 秒缩短到 100、120、180 毫秒，”Handa 说。 “将来，我们可能会进行专门的培训，让我们的模型在这些方面变得更好。但现在，只有普通的老 Luna 才能完成这项工作。”

该决策 API 在 9 月 29 日的公司开发者日上宣布，于周四向所有客户开放。 OpenAI 在公共版本中添加了新的语音和视觉模式，并致力于通过在地理上定位其推理资源来确保世界各地较低的延迟。

在与 Box、Datadog、Ramp 和 Speak 等客户的初步试验中，工程师使用 API 来取代具有更高吞吐量的 OpenAI 的 LLM。打造人工智能语言导师的 Speak 首席技术官 Andrew Hsu 表示，Decisions API 使公司能够将操作之间的时间从 1.4 秒缩短到 0.13 秒。 OpenAI 还使用该产品来提高 Dots 语音助手的响应能力。

尽管如此，除了“它适合你”之外，还不清楚什么才是一个好的决策模型——智能、成本、校准和速度的优化似乎因工作负载而异。 TypeSafe 首席执行官迪奥戈·阿尔梅达 (Diogo Almeida) 不信任基准测试，并敦促人们在自己的工作中试用这些模型，但就连 TypeSafe 也在上周发布了最新的 Jev 模型，该模型还发布了自己的排名，其中包括对图像和智能 if 语句的支持等新功能。

AIM System One Index 和 Artificial Analysis Decision Index 等公共基准倾向于青睐 Liquid 上周发布的新决策模型 D1 Ultra 和 Base Lab 的 Elephant-1。最新的 Jev 模型在这两个指数上仍然具有竞争力，排名第七和第三，而 OpenAI 的决策模型分别下降到第八和第十四。然而，TypeSafe 的产品目前是 OpenRouter 上查询最广泛的。

然而，最有趣的 Jev 基准是 JevMan，这是决策模型玩 PacMan 的基准；最新的 JEV 车型位居榜首。建立基准的 Opper AI 首席增长官 Felix Wunderlich 表示，这款经典游戏“是一项有趣的测试，因为它会不间断地做出快速、高风险的决策。在每个路口，模型都必须在几百毫秒内决定去哪里。”

OpenAI 可以说功能更强大的模型可能在多模态方面具有优势——对于图像分类，Handa 告诉 TechCrunch，“Luna 非常强大，并且一直表现出更好的校准。”他补充说，OpenAI 客户希望 Decisions API 在使用图像作为输出方面更加灵活。

Handa 还看到了新用例的速度进一步提高：“我们能否将其达到 60 毫秒的速度，然后您可以想象像视频中的每一帧一样调用 API 之类的东西吗？”

随着这些服务变得更快、更便宜，我们可以预期它们将不辜负杰夫的同名经济学家，他解释了如何更有效地使用资源使其变得更加普遍。或者，正如 Handa 所看到的那样，将会有一个不断扩大的“疯狂的用例集”，这些用例一直隐藏在人们的视线中，直到决策模型揭示它们。

news.title: The Download: testing six tech promises and biotech’s blind spots
news.title_en: The Download: testing six tech promises and biotech’s blind spots
news.author: MIT Tech Review
news.article_content:
Some seemingly impossible feats are too good to give up on. Decoding a pet’s yowls and yips? Absolutely. Scrubbing the world of forever chemicals? Yes, please. Rocketing to Mars in a fraction of the time? Sounds great, but how close are we, really?

In the new Impossible issue of MIT Technology Review, we ran progress reports on six potentially transformative technologies and ideas that have been “just around the corner” for years, or even decades. From exercise in a pill to nuclear-powered spaceships, we asked experts what’s holding them back and how far they’ve come.

Check out our stories on how they all stacked up.

news.article_content_zh:
有些看似不可能的壮举实在是太好了，不容放弃。解码宠物的叫声和叫声？绝对地。擦洗永远化学物质的世界？是的，请。在很短的时间内火箭到达火星？听起来不错，但我们到底有多接近呢？

在《麻省理工科技评论》新一期的《不可能》中，我们对六种潜在的变革性技术和想法进行了进展报告，这些技术和想法已经“指日可待”了数年甚至数十年。从药丸锻炼到核动力宇宙飞船，我们询问了专家是什么阻碍了他们以及他们已经走了多远。

看看我们的故事，了解它们是如何叠加的。

news.article_content:

But while AI has supercharged the pace of these ports, it's also tearing apart tight-knit communities dedicated to preserving games.

news.article_content_zh:
最近，复古电子游戏无处不在——尤其是在它们不应该出现的地方。网络浏览器中的光环、iPhone 上的风之杖、混合现实中的任天堂明星大乱斗。 在过去的一个月左右的时间里，由于新的人工智能工具，这些意想不到的项目以令人难以置信的频率疯传，因为爱好者们拆开游戏，然后为新平台重建它们。但是，尽管人工智能加快了这些移植的步伐，但它也撕裂了致力于保存游戏的紧密社区。

分解和重组——分解和重组的简写——是逆向工程的一种形式，涉及破坏游戏……

news.article_content:
A lot of what’s coming next – gate-all-around transistors, backside power, CFET, hybrid bonding – is hard to follow without actually seeing it, so we made all the awesome animated explainers that I wish I had while I was prepping.

I also asked Intel’s leadership how the semiconductor industry will cope with the enormous shock in demand from AI.

AI compute has grown 3x a year for the last decade, but according to Intel’s CTO, Intel could only double leading-edge wafer production with today’s global stock of chipmaking tools.

What kinds of tricks can foundries pull to extend this crossover point where demand surges way ahead of supply?

I also made flashcards for the concepts I had to learn to prep for this episode here.

WorkOS helps you do business with enterprises. It gives you access to all the features most commonly required by enterprises: SSO, SCIM, RBAC, audit logs, and more. It’s easy to plug these features in — it only takes a few lines of code — and WorkOS is releasing new functionality all the time, including things like auth for agents. If you want to join the 3,000+ companies that rely on WorkOS, go to workos.com

Jane Street built a powerful tool called magic-trace to help analyze and debug their trading systems. It only exists because one engineer noticed a feature on Intel chips called Processor Trace and thought it’d be valuable to build on top of. Now, traders and developers across Jane Street use magic-trace every single day! If you want to be trusted to pursue the ideas you think matter most, Jane Street is hiring. Go to janestreet.com/dwarkesh

Antithesis’ testing platform lets you perfectly reproduce every single bug you find. That’s because it runs on a fully deterministic computer, which strips out all the unpredictability that can make certain bugs flaky and hard to pin down. To build it, Antithesis found every source of non-determinism in Intel’s x86 architecture and either sealed it off or replaced it with a controlled simulation. Learn more at antithesis.com/dwarkesh

There’s never been as big a shock to the semiconductor industry as the current surge in demand from AI.

Easily 40-50% above our maximum capacity, which I’ve never seen before.

Progress in AI has been driven by exponentially increasing compute. To sustain that progress, foundries like Intel will need to manufacture far more leading-edge compute, both by producing more chips and by improving what each chip can do.

But the production of these chips is bottlenecked by tools that Intel buys from their suppliers. Most famously, ASML’s EUV machines.

If they don’t have the equipment, they can’t make the chips here.

I spent two days touring Intel’s fabs to prepare for these interviews with its leadership. I wanted to understand what it takes to manufacture the world’s most advanced chips and how hardware is shaping the future of AI.

I’m joined by Chris Auth, who leads development of all the processes that are currently under manufacturing. The thing I want to understand in more concrete detail is how the development of a new process actually happens. If 14A is going to come out in three years or two years from now, what is happening from now till then?

I want you to walk me through as much detail as you can, everything from the level of “how is the yield improving?” to what kind of telemetry you guys look at? What kind of experiments do you guys run? I want to understand what is going to happen over the next two years as concretely as possible.

14A has been in development for about three-plus years at this stage, so quite a bit of pre-work has been done to get it to the stage that it’s at right now. Right now, we’re getting very close to where we’re finalizing the process. We’re finalizing the tool sets that it will be manufactured on, and we’re working on the fine-tuning of each of the process steps.

There are about 2,000 steps in the factory that you have to go do. You need to do really intricate work at each one of those to make sure it’s fine-tuned, it can go into manufacturing, it can run thousands of wafers a week on this process, and it can be repeatable every single time.

Right now, you might have a certain yield. Walk me through how that increases month over month. There’s a line running at 14A. What happens from now till next month that will result in the yield changing? How do you identify where the defects are? How do you fix that?

There’s a constant process that we go through in identifying defects. There are two main ways that we’ll identify them. One is we have inline metrology. We have tools that will look at the wafers and say, “Ah, there’s a defect there, there’s a defect there, there’s a defect there.” Then also at the end of line, either electrical test or we sort and see where the fails are. We will identify failures, and then we will get analysis on those failures. We’ll cross-section it.

You were in the TEM lab yesterday, and you saw how you can get cross-sections. You’ll get a cross-section of a defect, and from that, you’ll be able to say, “Oh, that defect is between these layers, so it must have come from this section of the flow. Oh, we have inline metrology in that section, which has identified defects. Those are the defects we need to go after.”

What we’ve learned is that you don’t want to do too much innovation in one node, because the more innovation that you do, the more complex it becomes.

While you’ll be able to get that to work, you need to hit a certain schedule, and that’s the schedule that your customer ultimately wants. Having that predictable schedule is a key piece. You’ve got to figure out how much innovation you can put in in order to meet the customer’s requirements in the timeline that they need it.

Intel learned how costly that tradeoff can be with delays to its 10 nanometer node, whose original target launch date was 2016, but which didn’t begin manufacturing until 2018.

Usually Intel has been the keeper of Moore’s Law, a new cadence of manufacturing every two years, but their last set of products slipped almost four years.

Intel today having its worst day in four months, the stock now down more than 15%. I also want to point out Taiwan Semiconductor up 13% off of Intel’s bad news.

Walk me through what lessons you think Intel has learned from 10 nanometer.

Ten nanometer was a good example of where we had very aggressive targets. We were doing what was called hyperscaling at the time, so we were scaling much faster than what had been historically done. In order to do that, we came up with all sorts of innovative ideas on how we could achieve that without new tools, because the tools weren’t ready. That put a lot of burden on the process and a lot of burden on the engineers.

Now, at the end of the day, 10 nanometer is a great technology. It has world-class yield, it has world-class performance, it has world-class cost, but it took us longer to do that than what we would have liked. So we’ve tried to take that learning into future technology nodes and say, “Hey, we need to limit the amount of innovation we put in there to make sure that we keep it on schedule.”

What do you think was the main technology that should’ve been saved for a future version?
