news.summary_en: Intel's engineering leadership, including CTO Pushkar Ranade, warned of an impending supply cliff in chip manufacturing. While AI compute demand has surged threefold annually over the past decade, existing global fabrication tooling can at most double leading-edge wafer output, forcing foundries to rely on extreme architectural innovations like backside power and CFET.
news.title_zh: 英特尔高管直言先进制程产能瓶颈
news.summary_zh: 英特尔首席技术官坦言全球设备仅够先进制程晶圆产能翻倍，AI算力年增3倍带来严峻供需悬崖

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 英特尔技术高层在深度访谈中针对AI芯片算力激增与物理制造瓶颈发出预警。首席技术官普什卡·拉纳德指出，过去十年AI算力需求以每年3倍的速度指数级增长，但即便动用全球现存全部半导体制造机台库存，先进制程晶圆产能最多也只能翻倍，供需交叉拐点迫在眉睫，代工厂必须依靠全新晶体管架构与背面供电等黑科技强行延缓失衡。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: Intel's engineering leadership, including CTO Pushkar Ranade, warned of an impending supply cliff in chip manufacturing. While AI compute demand has surged threefold annually over the past decade, existing global fabrication tooling can at most double leading-edge wafer output, forcing foundries to rely on extreme architectural innovations like backside power and CFET.

elements_zh.who: 英特尔管理层及首席技术官普什卡·拉纳德（Pushkar Ranade）
elements_zh.where: 半导体产业技术深度访谈
elements_zh.what: 警示全球现有制造设备存量仅能支持先进制程翻倍，难以匹配年增3倍的AI算力黑洞
elements_zh.why: 先进制程制造物理极限逼近，晶圆代工产能与算法模型指数级需求产生巨大剪刀差

elements_en.who: Intel leadership and CTO Pushkar Ranade
elements_en.what: Warned that existing chipmaking tools can only double leading-edge wafer output despite 3x annual AI compute growth
elements_en.why: Physical and logistical bottlenecks threaten to break the runaway supply-demand curve of AI hardware

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 软件算法天天喊着智能奇点降临，硬件工厂却在为买不到光刻机和物理极限抠头。芯片大佬的潜台词很诚恳：哪怕把全球机床拉满电，也填不满硅谷大厂烧卡做算力的无底洞。
ai_analysis.insight_en: Algorithm researchers love hyping runaway digital superintelligence, but the guys actually etching silicon are hitting brick walls of physics. Intel's frank warning says it all: even if every lithography machine on Earth ran at 200%, the AI compute black hole remains unfillable.

ai_analysis.digest_en: Intel's engineering leadership, including CTO Pushkar Ranade, warned of an impending supply cliff in chip manufacturing. While AI compute demand has surged threefold annually over the past decade, existing global fabrication tooling can at most double leading-edge wafer output, forcing foundries to rely on extreme architectural innovations like backside power and CFET.
key_points_zh: AI算力十年间保持每年3倍增长速度
现有全球半导体机台最多仅支持先进制程翻倍
英特尔推进全环绕栅极与背面供电等技术延长供需窗口
key_points_en: AI compute demand grows 3x annually over a decade
Global chipmaking tool inventory can only double leading-edge wafer capacity
Foundries forced to deploy GAA, backside power, and CFET to stave off compute crunch

news.article_content_zh:
接下来的很多内容——环栅晶体管、背面电源、CFET、混合键合——如果不亲眼所见，就很难理解，所以我们制作了所有很棒的动画解释器，我希望在准备的时候能拥有它们。

我还询问了英特尔的领导层，半导体行业将如何应对人工智能需求的巨大冲击。

在过去十年中，人工智能计算每年增长 3 倍，但根据英特尔首席技术官的说法，凭借当今全球芯片制造工具的库存，英特尔只能将领先的晶圆产量翻一番。

代工厂可以采取哪些技巧来延长需求远远超过供应的交叉点？

我还为我必须学习的概念制作了抽认卡，为这一集做准备。

WorkOS 帮助您与企业开展业务。它使您可以访问企业最常需要的所有功能：SSO、SCIM、RBAC、审核日志等。插入这些功能很容易——只需要几行代码——而且 WorkOS 一直在发布新功能，包括代理身份验证等功能。如果您想加入 3,000 多家依赖 WorkOS 的公司，请访问 workos.com

Jane Street 构建了一个名为 magic-trace 的强大工具来帮助分析和调试他们的交易系统。它之所以存在，只是因为一位工程师注意到英特尔芯片上有一个名为 Processor Trace 的功能，并认为在此基础上进行构建很有价值。现在，简街的交易员和开发商每天都在使用 magic-trace！如果你想得到信任去追求你认为最重要的想法，Jane Street 正在招聘。访问 janestreet.com/dwarkesh

Antithesis 的测试平台可让您完美地重现您发现的每个错误。这是因为它在完全确定性的计算机上运行，​​从而消除了所有可能导致某些错误难以确定的不可预测性。为了构建它，Antithesis 找到了英特尔 x86 架构中所有不确定性的来源，要么将其密封，要么用受控模拟取代它。了解更多信息，请访问 antithesis.com/dwarkesh

目前人工智能需求的激增对半导体行业造成了前所未有的巨大冲击。

轻松超出最大容量 40-50%，这是我以前从未见过的。

计算量的指数级增长推动了人工智能的进步。为了维持这一进步，像英特尔这样的代工厂将需要通过生产更多芯片和改进每个芯片的功能来制造更多的前沿计算。

但这些芯片的生产受到英特尔从供应商购买的工具的瓶颈。最著名的是 ASML 的 EUV 机器。

如果他们没有设备，他们就无法在这里生产芯片。

我花了两天时间参观了英特尔的工厂，为采访其领导层做准备。我想了解制造世界上最先进的芯片需要什么，以及硬件如何塑造人工智能的未来。

Chris Auth 也加入了我的行列，他领导着目前正在制造的所有流程的开发。我想更具体地了解新流程的开发实际上是如何发生的。如果14A要在三年或两年后推出，那么从现在到那时会发生什么？

我希望您能向我介绍尽可能多的细节，从“产量如何提高？”的各个层面。你们看什么样的遥测？你们进行什么样的实验？我想尽可能具体地了解未来两年会发生什么。

14A 在这个阶段已经开发了大约三年多的时间，因此已经做了相当多的前期工作才能达到现在的阶段。现在，我们已经非常接近完成该流程了。我们正在最终确定制造它将使用的工具集，并且我们正在对每个工艺步骤进行微调。

工厂里大约有2000个步骤需要你去完成。您需要对其中的每一个进行非常复杂的工作，以确保它经过微调，可以进入制造，可以在这个过程中每周运行数千个晶圆，并且每次都可以重复。

现在，你可能会有一定的收益。让我看看这个数字是如何逐月增加的。有一条线路以 14A 运行。从现在到下个月会发生什么会导致收益率变化？如何识别缺陷在哪里？你如何解决这个问题？

我们在识别缺陷时会经历一个持续的过程。我们可以通过两种主要方式来识别它们。一是我们有在线计量。我们有工具可以检查晶圆并说：“啊，那里有缺陷，那里有缺陷，那里有缺陷。”然后也在生产线的末端进行电气测试，或者我们进行排序并查看故障所在。我们将识别故障，然后对这些故障进行分析。我们将对其进行横切。

您昨天在 TEM 实验室，了解了如何获得横截面。您将获得缺陷的横截面，从中您可以说，“哦，该缺陷位于这些层之间，因此它一定来自流程的这一部分。哦，我们在该部分有内联计量，它已识别出缺陷。这些是我们需要追踪的缺陷。”

我们了解到的是，你不想在一个节点上进行太多创新，因为你做的创新越多，它就会变得越复杂。

虽然您能够使其发挥作用，但您需要达到一定的时间表，而这就是您的客户最终想要的时间表。制定可预测的时间表是关键。您必须弄清楚可以投入多少创新才能在客户需要的时间内满足他们的要求。

英特尔了解到，由于 10 纳米节点的延迟，这种权衡的代价是多么高昂，该节点最初的目标发布日期是 2016 年，但直到 2018 年才开始生产。

通常英特尔一直是摩尔定律的维护者，每两年生产一次新的节奏，但他们的最后一组产品却推迟了近四年。

英特尔今天经历了四个月来最糟糕的一天，该股目前下跌超过 15%。我还想指出，台积电因英特尔的坏消息而上涨 13%。

请跟我讲讲您认为英特尔从 10 纳米技术中吸取了哪些教训。

十纳米就是一个很好的例子，说明我们有非常激进的目标。当时我们正在做所谓的超扩展，因此我们的扩展速度比历史上的速度要快得多。为了做到这一点，我们想出了各种创新想法，说明如何在没有新工具的情况下实现这一目标，因为工具还没有准备好。这给流程和工程师带来了很大的负担。

现在，归根结底，10 纳米是一项伟大的技术。它具有世界一流的产量、世界一流的性能、世界一流的成本，但我们花费的时间比我们希望的要长。因此，我们试图将这种学习融入未来的技术节点，并说：“嘿，我们需要限制我们投入的创新量，以确保我们按计划进行。”

您认为应该为未来版本保留哪些主要技术？

news.title: Canva launches Craft, its first in-house image model
news.title_en: Canva launches Craft, its first in-house image model
news.author: THE DECODER
news.article_content:
Design platform Canva has released Canva Craft, its first in-house image generation model. The company says it can compete with comparable models from Google, OpenAI, ByteDance, and Meta. According to Canva, its internal lab Canva Research trained the model from scratch, relying mainly on millions of design templates rather than photos.

Craft first plans out image composition, proportions, and text, then generates images at up to 2K resolution across more than 30 aspect ratios. The model can render text in 55 languages, Canva says. Users can break results into editable layers using Magic Layers. On the DesignArena platform's ranking, Craft placed fourth overall and first in portraits and landscapes, according to Canva.

Craft is available to all users through Dream Lab and the public API, with MCP integration for chatbots like ChatGPT and Gemini planned for later. Beyond lower costs, the in-house model gives Canva more control over quality and speed. Researchers from Leonardo.ai, which Canva acquired in 2024, also contributed to the project. Two cheaper variants called Craft-fast and Craft-ultrafast are expected soon.AdAd

news.article_content_zh:
设计平台 Canva 发布了 Canva Craft，这是其第一个内部图像生成模型。该公司表示，它可以与谷歌、OpenAI、字节跳动和 Meta 的同类模型竞争。据 Canva 称，其内部实验室 Canva Research 从头开始​​训练该模型，主要依靠数百万个设计模板而不是照片。

Craft 首先规划图像构成、比例和文本，然后生成分辨率高达 2K、宽高比超过 30 种的图像。 Canva 表示，该模型可以呈现 55 种语言的文本。用户可以使用 Magic Layers 将结果分解为可编辑的图层。据 Canva 称，在 DesignArena 平台的排名中，Craft 总体排名第四，在肖像和风景方面排名第一。

Craft 可通过 Dream Lab 和公共 API 向所有用户提供，并计划稍后与 ChatGPT 和 Gemini 等聊天机器人进行 MCP 集成。除了降低成本之外，内部模型还使 Canva 能够更好地控制质量和速度。 Canva 于 2024 年收购的 Leonardo.ai 的研究人员也为该项目做出了贡献。预计很快就会有两种更便宜的变体，称为 Craft-fast 和 Craft-ultrafast。

Anthropic had Claude generate mathematical proofs that existing code is correct, producing roughly 180 million lines of proof code for 123 open-source libraries. news.title: OpenAI lowers valuation target, raises up to $30 billion
news.title_en: OpenAI lowers valuation target, raises up to $30 billion
news.author: THE DECODER
news.article_content:
OpenAI is closing in on a new funding round of up to $30 billion but has lowered its valuation target to get there. The company originally pitched investors on a $1.4 trillion valuation, according to internal documents obtained by the Financial Times. That number has since dropped to $1.25 trillion, CNBC also reports. The FT says demand was weaker than in previous rounds, with some backers experiencing "indigestion" after heavy investments in earlier fundraises.

UAE investors and investment firm Coatue are leading the $30 billion round. The funding is being positioned as a bridge ahead of a potential IPO. OpenAI is also negotiating a commercial deal to secure additional compute capacity through the UAE, according to CNBC.

OpenAI confidentially filed an IPO prospectus with the SEC in June. CFO Sarah Friar told employees in August that OpenAI would be a publicly traded company by 2027. CEO Sam Altman said in September that the timing was unfavorable for going public. He had already communicated that internally back in June. Competitor Anthropic is also preparing an IPO and is targeting a valuation between $1.5 and $2 trillion.AdAd

news.title: Anthropic says it partnered with Theorem to use Claude to formally prove useful security properties at the assembly code level across 123 open-source libraries (Anthropic)
news.title_en: Anthropic says it partnered with Theorem to use Claude to formally prove useful security properties at the assembly code level across 123 open-source libraries (Anthropic)
news.author: Anthropic
news.article_content:
Skip to main contentNewsResearchPolicyCommitmentsCompanyTry Claude{"@context":"https://schema.org","@type":"Article","headline":"LLMs are making formal software verification feasible at a much larger scale","description":"Claude formally proved security properties in the compiled code of 123 open-source libraries. Along the way, it found bugs that had eluded detection for years.","image":["https://www-cdn.anthropic.com/images/4zrzovbb/website/80cf520cb540989c3643907f004b2514ec4d01f1-1200x630.jpg"],"datePublished":"2026-10-22T00:00:00.000Z","dateModified":"2026-10-22T22:13:27.000Z","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"Anthropic","url":"https://www.anthropic.com"},"publisher":{"@type":"Organization","name":"Anthropic","url":"https://www.anthropic.com"},"mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.anthropic.com/research/formal-verification","url":"https://www.anthropic.com/research/formal-verification"}Chapter 01: IntroductionLLMs are making formal software verification feasible at a much larger scale01Introduction02Turning tests into proofs03Finding and fixing bugs04This is just the beginning05Limitations06ConclusionPublished

Keane Lucas, Aengus Lynch, Luna Tong, Luke Champine, Zygi Straznickas, Dino Distefano, Harshikaa AgrawalEvyatar Ben Asher, Ava Howell, Sami Jawhar, Chris Rohlf, Nickolai ZeldovichNicholas Carlini, Rajashree Agrawal, Jason Gross

Most software is riddled with bugs, which AI can now easily find and exploit. The standard defenses against cyberattacks are no longer sufficient: we need ways to prove that code is free of bugs. Formal software verification could provide this guarantee, but it has historically required years of expert effort, making it impractical for most real-world projects. In a collaboration with Theorem, however, we show this is no longer the case: LLMs can now produce formal proofs at large scale, enabling new software development workflows that include proven security guarantees. Using Claude, we proved security properties at the assembly code level (RISC-V) in over 100 real-world open-source software libraries. To our knowledge, this represents the first large-scale effort to use AI to apply formal verification to production software at the assembly code level. While writing the proofs, Claude also discovered bugs that had eluded detection for years, despite trillions of test runs. As model capabilities continue to improve, we expect formal verification to become an essential part of secure software development.

Even mature, heavily tested software contains bugs, and LLMs are increasingly adept at finding them. The Linux kernel—one of the most well-tested pieces of software today, deployed on billions of devices worldwide—recently had over 1,000 vulnerabilities disclosed. With frontier models becoming more capable of chaining seemingly benign bugs into critical exploits, we need techniques that can detect and fix these bugs before they can be exploited in the wild.

Ideally, such techniques could find and patch all bugs, and then provide some proof that there are no more to be found. Formal verification is one way to do this. In formal verification, developers translate their code into a mathematical model, then try to prove that it always follows some defined set of security rules. If they fail to prove this, that means there could be a bug in the code that would violate a rule, and the nature of the failure implies what the bug might be. Repeating this process (after eliminating the cause of failure each time) will ultimately yield proof that the code is devoid of any bug that would violate those rules.

However, formal verification isn’t easy. Proofs can be many times larger than the original code, and writing them requires significant effort and a niche, highly specialized skill set. For instance, it took two person-years to implement the seL4 operating system kernel, but 20 person-years to formally verify it. Accordingly, formal verification has been practical only in truly mission-critical applications, such as Airbus’s avionics code.

But LLMs are making it far easier. Frontier models can now produce correctness proofs for real-world software fully autonomously. To demonstrate this, we asked Claude to prove useful security properties across 123 open-source libraries, including showing that some of their executable artifacts can never crash under certain conditions. Specifically, Claude proved that these programs will always exit normally without triggering memory-safety errors or failing assertions, for every input less than 64 MB and every modeled Linux operating system (OS) response and memory layout, under certain assumptions (namely that the program runs as a single-threaded static binary with a fixed memory budget on a RISC-V1 CPU using Linux OS). This is still far away from fixing all possible bugs, but it does get us much closer than before and provides a roadmap toward that end.

We’re publishing a subset of these proofs so that anyone can verify and reuse them, along with the RISC-V and OS semantics. Theorem, our collaborator on this project, is also offering to run the same pipeline for other open-source projects, and is publishing a Claude skill to help developers get started with verifying their own code.

Formal verification is a broad field with many methodologies. Below, we also describe our initial explorations using other formal verification methods to accelerate other security or software development tasks, such as assessing the security of the zlib compression algorithm, proving behavioral equivalence of a Python interpreter written in Rust, and rooting out long-standing bugs in critical software.

Moreover, as more code is formalized and methods of achieving security guarantees become more standardized, the ability to reuse or modify proofs across codebases will amortize the cost. We encourage all developers to explore formal verification with LLMs—especially those who previously tried it with less capable models and found it didn’t work.

In the rest of this post, we cover our formal verification experiments in more detail.

To prove that a piece of software is correct, we must first state what “correct” even means. Correctness is defined by the specification (spec). In some programs, there is a clear way to formally specify the program’s intended behavior. For example, a PNG decoder takes a sequence of bytes and (following RFC 2083) decodes these bytes into the corresponding image. But for most programs, things aren’t so straightforward. What would it mean for a text editor or a web browser to be “correct”? To address this for the code in the open-source libraries that we sought to prove, we take the approach of automatically converting their preexisting compilable test suites into a spec by encoding the rule “this test suite always passes,” using a general model of what it means to execute any RISC-V-compiled binary on Linux. Historically, proving such specs was intractable, given the inherent complexity of writing a proof that can encompass and make an argument over all possible behaviors and interactions of tens of thousands of assembly instructions over any input (and the fact that proofs tend to be extremely large as a result). For this project, we started with fuzz tests. In these tests, developers write an entry point2 into their code that takes inputs, such that any input that causes a crash is a bug the authors care about. Then the fuzzer, a testing engine, generates enormous numbers of semirandom and mutated inputs at the entry point to try to find a bug (visualized in Figure 1). The longer a fuzzer runs, the more bugs it can find. But this is inherently a brute-force process, with no guarantee of exercising every possible code path, regardless of how many inputs you try.

To find all the bugs that would’ve been surfaced by a fuzz test, we turned the fuzz test into a spec defined over the compiled RISC-V instructions. The spec says that the fuzz test won’t crash for any input less than 64 MB.3 If Claude can prove this spec, the fuzz test on RISC-V becomes superfluous: fuzzing that entry point will never find any bugs.

We did this for hundreds of projects in Google’s OSS-Fuzz initiative, which provides continuous fuzz testing for qualifying open-source projects. OSS-Fuzz contains thousands of developer-authored entry points that look for broken code properties by crashing (for example, on a failed assertion). OSS-Fuzz automatically instruments C and C++ programs with AddressSanitizer4 (ASan), causing them to crash whenever memory is accessed improperly (which is a leading cause of software vulnerabilities). Broad-spectrum specifications like memory safety apply to almost all software.

These proofs operate on the compiled RISC-V instructions (i.e., executable binaries), and they comprise about 180 million lines of Rocq, with a typical proof running to about 600,000 lines to provide security guarantees on binaries with a median length of 18,000 RISC-V instructions. These proofs are built by translating the RISC-V assembly code to a mathematical model using Theorem’s RISC-V instruction and Linux process semantics. This means these proofs currently assume that the program runs as a single-threaded static binary with a fixed memory budget on a RISC-V CPU using Linux OS. Expanding the scope of these proofs is well within reach, as it would involve standardizing semantics for more assembly architectures and other operating system processes. See an expert’s take on the proofs Claude wrote.

While this is an enormous volume of proof code, virtually none of it needs to be manually reviewed. The Rocq proof checker ensures that the spec is correctly satisfied by the proof. As a result, the only artifacts that a developer needs to trust are:

This doesn’t mean these libraries contain no bugs. Instead, it means that any remaining bugs either are to be found within the artifacts listed above or are outside the scope of Claude’s proof. Hardening those still-possibly-buggy trusted components (Rocq, RISC-V, and Linux semantics) is not insignificant, but it’s a far more tractable task than debugging every line of code the scaled-out proofs cover—especially as this approach can secure an arbitrary number of projects without increasing the size of the trusted components.

To that end, we are publishing the trusted components (above) made for this project that are not already public; Claude’s complete Rocq proofs for fuzz tests that did not require patching; and specifications for other fuzz tests we were not able to prove.

Above, we showed that you can turn many open-source libraries’ developer-written tests (fuzz tests) into specs that Claude can prove will always pass, sometimes after patching the remaining bugs it found. For this reason, the process of attempting to prove these specs discovered hundreds of bugs.

Lots of bugs showed up during Claude’s attempts to prove hundreds of entry points. To ensure that Claude didn’t have to stop for a human every time this happened, we let Claude fix the bugs it found: it patched the code, which caused the spec to be regenerated with that patched code, and then Claude proceeded to prove that new spec.6

Many of the bugs we found are ones that a fuzzer would be unlikely to ever find. Fuzzers mutate small inputs, typically capped at 1 MB, and typically rely on code coverage to guide them toward bugs. While proving an entry point in one library, Claude found a counter underflow in its copy of a decompressor that led to an out-of-bounds write, but only on inputs of around 20 MB that had one rare, specific layout. Other bugs include an out-of-bounds read in an image decoder that needed a 64 MB input and over 2 GB of memory, an out-of-bounds read in another library that needed a particular sequence of calls across two handles to the same file, and a rediscovery of CVE-2026-56132 in libexpat, which needed deeply nested input. Claude also found logic bugs that never crash at all. While proving that one library was memory-safe, for example, it noticed that a feature for restricting which files an application can load isn’t always enforced.

The ultimate goal of this project was to achieve a proof that the RISC-V-compiled fuzz tests had no remaining crashes to find. However, bugs like the above show that the process has another benefit, regardless of whether that goal is achieved: even just attempting this process yields real bugs that need to be fixed.

Proving that a fuzz test has no more crashes to find is more significant than it sounds. It’s common for fuzz tests in real-world code to test for violations of meaningful high-level properties, such as encode-decode roundtripping, idempotence, algebraic laws, differential testing, self-consistency, or equivalence to reference implementations. For example, a fuzz test for the LZO compression algorithm asserts that if you compress an input, then decompress it, the result is the same as the original. If the property does not hold, the program crashes—so proving the test never crashes is equivalent to proving the property itself.

This can also occur even when the properties are not directly specified by the developer. For example, in order for Claude to complete its OSS-Fuzz proof for cpp-httplib, it was necessary to rule out the possibility of a stack overflow due to too much recursion in the std::set destructor. This recursion depth is bounded by the maximum depth of a tree, so Claude had to prove (on machine code!) that libc++’s red-black tree rebalancing algorithm is correctly optimized to keep the tree’s depth logarithmically bounded.

Formal verification is an expansive domain. The fuzz-test-to-proof example above is one instance of LLMs making formal verification more widely usable by directly applying proofs to machine code.

We’ve also seen success using LLMs with formal verification in other ways. For example, we asked Claude to write a formal spec of RFC 1950, the technical document that defines the zlib compression file format. Then, we had Claude prove that the zlib implementation in the Linux kernel correctly implements that spec. As with the examples above, Claude proved this property at the binary level, except instead of RISC-V, Claude directly proved the x86-compiled binary using Claude-generated (and heavily tested) formal semantics of the x86 ISA.7 We then repeated this process for half a dozen other widely used libraries. During an effort to verify a widely used PDF reader, we found as many security bugs in one week as are typically reported in a year.

基恩·卢卡斯,安格斯·林奇,卢娜·佟,卢克·钱平,齐吉·斯特拉兹尼卡斯,迪诺·迪斯特凡诺,哈什卡·阿格拉瓦尔埃维塔·本·阿舍,艾娃·豪威尔,萨米·乔哈,克里斯·罗尔夫,尼科莱·泽尔多维奇尼古拉斯·卡里尼,拉贾什里·阿格拉瓦尔,杰森·格罗斯

大多数软件都充满了错误，人工智能现在可以轻松找到并利用这些错误。针对网络攻击的标准防御措施已不再足够：我们需要方法来证明代码没有错误。正式的软件验证可以提供这种保证，但它历来需要多年的专家努力，这使得它对于大多数现实世界的项目来说是不切实际的。然而，在与 Theorem 的合作中，我们证明情况已不再如此：法学硕士现在可以大规模生成正式证明，从而实现包含经过验证的安全保证的新软件开发工作流程。通过 Claude，我们在 100 多个实际开源软件库中证明了汇编代码级别 (RISC-V) 的安全属性。据我们所知，这是首次大规模使用人工智能在汇编代码级别对生产软件进行形式化验证。在编写证明时，克劳德还发现了尽管进行了数万亿次测试，但多年来一直未能被发现的错误。随着模型能力的不断提高，我们预计形式验证将成为安全软件开发的重要组成部分。

即使是经过严格测试的成熟软件也包含错误，而法学硕士越来越善于发现这些错误。 Linux 内核是当今经过最充分测试的软件之一，部署在全球数十亿台设备上，最近披露了 1,000 多个漏洞。随着前沿模型变得更有能力将看似良性的错误链接到关键漏洞中，我们需要能够在这些错误被广泛利用之前检测并修复这些错误的技术。

理想情况下，此类技术可以找到并修补所有错误，然后提供一些证据证明没有更多错误可找到。形式验证是做到这一点的一种方法。在形式验证中，开发人员将他们的代码转换为数学模型，然后尝试证明它始终遵循一些定义的安全规则集。如果他们无法证明这一点，则意味着代码中可能存在违反规则的错误，并且失败的性质暗示了错误可能是什么。重复此过程（每次消除失败原因后）将最终证明代码不存在任何违反这些规则的错误。

然而，形式验证并不容易。证明可能比原始代码大很多倍，并且编写它们需要大量的努力和高度专业化的技能。例如，seL4操作系统内核的实现需要两个人年，但正式验证却需要20人年。因此，形式验证仅在真正的关键任务应用中才实用，例如空客的航空电子代码。

但法学硕士让这一切变得更加容易。前沿模型现在可以完全自主地为现实世界的软件生成正确性证明。为了证明这一点，我们要求 Claude 证明 123 个开源库的有用安全属性，包括证明它们的一些可执行工件在某些条件下永远不会崩溃。具体来说，Claude 证明，在某些假设下（即程序作为单线程静态二进制文件在使用 Linux 操作系统的 RISC-V1 CPU 上运行，具有固定的内存预算），对于每个小于 64 MB 的输入以及每个建模的 Linux 操作系统 (OS) 响应和内存布局，这些程序将始终正常退出，而不会触发内存安全错误或失败的断言。这距离修复所有可能的错误还很遥远，但它确实让我们比以前更接近，并提供了实现这一目标的路线图。

我们正在发布这些证明的子集，以便任何人都可以验证和重用它们以及 RISC-V 和操作系统语义。我们在这个项目上的合作者 Theorem 也为其他开源项目提供运行相同的管道，并发布了 Claude 技能来帮助开发人员开始验证自己的代码。

形式验证是一个广阔的领域，有许多方法论。下面，我们还描述了使用其他形式验证方法来加速其他安全或软件开发任务的初步探索，例如评估 zlib 压缩算法的安全性、证明用 Rust 编写的 Python 解释器的行为等效性，以及根除关键软件中长期存在的错误。

形式验证的前景是光明的。随着模型变得更加智能，编写证明的成本正在下降。此外，随着更多代码的形式化和实现安全保证的方法变得更加标准化，跨代码库重用或修改证明的能力将摊销成本。我们鼓励所有开发人员探索法学硕士的形式验证，尤其是那些以前使用能力较差的模型尝试过但发现它不起作用的开发人员。

在这篇文章的其余部分，我们将更详细地介绍我们的形式验证实验。

为了证明一个软件是正确的，我们必须首先说明“正确”的含义。正确性由规范（spec）定义。在某些程序中，有一种明确的方法来正式指定程序的预期行为。例如，PNG 解码器采用字节序列（遵循 RFC 2083）将这些字节解码为相应的图像。但对于大多数程序来说，事情并不是那么简单。对于文本编辑器或网络浏览器来说“正确”意味着什么？获得全面且明确的规范的困难是大规模验证软件的重大障碍。

为了解决我们试图证明的开源库中代码的这个问题，我们采用了一种方法，即使用在 Linux 上执行任何 RISC-V 编译的二进制文件意味着什么的通用模型，通过编码规则“此测试套件总是通过”，自动将其预先存在的可编译测试套件转换为规范。从历史上看，证明这样的规范是很棘手的，因为编写一个证明的固有复杂性可以包含并论证任何输入上数以万计的汇编指令的所有可能行为和交互（并且事实上证明往往非常大）。这就是当今法学硕士的用武之地：通过数百万行代码来追求明确的目标是法学硕士非常适合的任务。

对于这个项目，我们从模糊测试开始。在这些测试中，开发人员在接受输入的代码中写入一个入口点2，这样任何导致崩溃的输入都是作者关心的错误。然后，模糊器（一个测试引擎）在入口点生成大量半随机和变异的输入，以尝试找到错误（如图 1 所示）。模糊器运行的时间越长，它能发现的错误就越多。但这本质上是一个蛮力过程，无论您尝试多少输入，都无法保证执行所有可能的代码路径。

为了找到模糊测试可能出现的所有错误，我们将模糊测试转变为在编译的 RISC-V 指令上定义的规范。该规范规定，对于任何小于 64 MB 的输入，模糊测试都不会崩溃。3 如果 Claude 能够证明这一规范，那么 RISC-V 上的模糊测试就变得多余：对该入口点进行模糊测试将永远不会发现任何错误。

我们对 Google OSS-Fuzz 计划中的数百个项目进行了此操作，该计划为合格的开源项目提供持续的模糊测试。 OSS-Fuzz 包含数千个开发人员编写的入口点，这些入口点通过崩溃（例如，断言失败）查找损坏的代码属性。 OSS-Fuzz 自动使用 AddressSanitizer4 (ASan) 检测 C 和 C++ 程序，一旦内存访问不当（这是软件漏洞的主要原因），就会导致它们崩溃。内存安全等广谱规范适用于几乎所有软件。

在几周的时间里，Claude 成功修补了它发现的错误，然后证明 123 个不同 OSS-Fuzz 库的 239 个入口点的任何输入（最多 64 MB）都没有崩溃。这些证明在编译的 RISC-V 指令（即可执行二进制文件）上运行，它们包含大约 1.8 亿行 Rocq，典型的证明运行大约 600,000 行，为中位数长度为 18,000 条 RISC-V 指令的二进制文件提供安全保证。这些证明是通过使用 Theorem 的 RISC-V 指令和 Linux 进程语义将 RISC-V 汇编代码转换为数学模型来构建的。这意味着这些证明当前假设程序在使用 Linux 操作系统的 RISC-V CPU 上作为具有固定内存预算的单线程静态二进制文件运行。扩大这些证明的范围是完全可以实现的，因为它将涉及更多汇编架构和其他操作系统进程的语义标准化。查看专家对克劳德撰写的校样的看法。

虽然这是大量的证明代码，但几乎不需要手动审查。 Rocq 校样检查器可确保校样正确满足规范。因此，开发人员需要信任的唯一工件是：

这并不意味着这些库不包含错误。相反，这意味着任何剩余的错误要么可以在上面列出的工件中找到，要么超出了克劳德的证明范围。强化那些仍然可能存在缺陷的可信组件（Rocq、RISC-V 和 Linux 语义）并非无关紧要，但它是一项比调试横向扩展证明所涵盖的每一行代码更容易处理的任务，特别是因为这种方法可以在不增加可信组件大小的情况下保护任意数量的项目。

我们欢迎对我们的证明进行独立验证，并鼓励改进我们的方法。为此，我们将发布为此项目制作的尚未公开的可信组件（见上文）； Claude 完整的 Rocq 模糊测试证明不需要修补；以及我们无法证明的其他模糊测试的规范。

上面，我们展示了您可以将许多开源库的开发人员编写的测试（模糊测试）转变为 Claude 可以证明总是会通过的规范，有时是在修补发现的剩余错误之后。因此，在尝试证明这些规范的过程中发现了数百个错误。

在克劳德尝试证明数百个入口点的过程中出现了很多错误。为了确保 Claude 不必在每次发生这种情况时都停下来找人，我们让 Claude 修复它发现的错误：它修补了代码，这导致使用修补后的代码重新生成规范，然后 Claude 继续证明新的规范。6

我们发现的许多错误是模糊器不可能发现的。模糊器会改变小输入，通常上限为 1 MB，并且通常依赖代码覆盖率来引导它们发现错误。在证明一个库中的入口点时，Claude 在其解压缩器副本中发现计数器下溢，导致越界写入，但仅限于具有一种罕见的特定布局的 20 MB 左右的输入。其他错误包括图像解码器中的越界读取（需要 64 MB 输入和超过 2 GB 的内存）、另一个库中的越界读取（需要跨同一文件的两个句柄进行特定的调用序列）以及 libexpat 中重新发现的 CVE-2026-56132（需要深度嵌套的输入）。克劳德还发现了根本不会崩溃的逻辑错误。例如，在证明一个库是内存安全的同时，它注意到限制应用程序可以加载哪些文件的功能并不总是强制执行。

该项目的最终目标是证明 RISC-V 编译的模糊测试没有发现任何剩余的崩溃。然而，像上面这样的错误表明，无论该目标是否实现，该过程还有另一个好处：即使只是尝试此过程也会产生需要修复的真正错误。

证明模糊测试没有更多的崩溃问题比听起来更重要。现实代码中的模糊测试通常用于测试是否违反有意义的高级属性，例如编码-解码往返、幂等性、代数定律、差异测试、自洽或与参考实现的等效性。例如，LZO 压缩算法的模糊测试断言，如果压缩输入，然后解压缩它，结果与原始结果相同。如果该属性不成立，程序就会崩溃——因此证明测试永远不会崩溃就相当于证明了该属性本身。

即使开发人员未直接指定属性，也可能会发生这种情况。例如，Claude 为了完成 cpp-httplib 的 OSS-Fuzz 证明，需要排除由于 std::set 析构函数中递归过多而导致堆栈溢出的可能性。该递归深度受到树的最大深度的限制，因此 Claude 必须证明（在机器代码上！）libc++ 的红黑树重新平衡算法已正确优化，以保持树的深度对数限制。

形式验证是一个广阔的领域。上面的模糊测试证明示例是法学硕士通过直接将证明应用于机器代码来使形式验证更广泛使用的实例之一。

我们还看到法学硕士在其他方面的形式验证取得了成功。例如，我们要求 Claude 编写 RFC 1950 的正式规范，该规范是定义 zlib 压缩文件格式的技术文档。然后，我们让 Claude 证明 Linux 内核中的 zlib 实现正确地实现了该规范。与上面的示例一样，Claude 在二进制级别证明了此属性，但 Claude 没有使用 RISC-V，而是使用 Claude 生成（并经过严格测试）的 x86 ISA 形式语义直接证明了 x86 编译的二进制文件。7 然后，我们对其他六个广泛使用的库重复了此过程。在此过程中，我们在极端情况下发现了一些小（无法利用）错误，这些错误正在向上游提交。我们从这个练习中得出两个结论：（1）这些经过严格测试的代码库几乎完全正确，（2）可以证明真实现有代码库的端到端正确性属性。

在另一个实验中，我们要求 Claude 为 Rust 中的大部分 Python 子集开发一个解释器，并证明（使用 Rust 的验证工具 Verus）它遵循学术论文中概述的 CPython 语义。然后，我们根据经验测量了对 CPython 行为的遵守情况，运行了超过 170 万个随机生成的 Python 程序，在 99.95% 的测试中发现了与 CPython 相同的行为，其余测试差异作为已知的极端情况并不令人意外。

我们还通过对简单安全属性的正式验证尝试，发现了几个广泛使用的关键应用程序中的问题。在其中一个问题中，我们发现了一个以前未知的逻辑错误，该错误已经潜伏了十多年。在验证广泛使用的 PDF 阅读器的过程中，我们在一周内发现的安全漏洞数量与通常一年内报告的安全漏洞数量一样多。

news.title: In the biotech world, you can’t see everything
news.title_en: In the biotech world, you can’t see everything
news.author: MIT Tech Review
news.article_content:
Earlier this week, I attended a screening of You Can See Everything, the buzzy new documentary about the disgraced former biotech CEO Elizabeth Holmes.

I went in not really knowing what to expect. I’d avoided spoilers (and won’t be giving anything away here, either!). I was wondering what new information this film could reveal, given how familiar many of us are with the Theranos story thanks to years of media coverage, the best-selling book Bad Blood, and the Hulu series The Dropout, starring Amanda Seyfried.

Like many others who have seen the film, I came away feeling unsettled. But not just about Holmes’s fraud and the somewhat disturbing interactions between the subjects. The film reignited a concern I’ve had about covering science for most of my career: Despite our best efforts, we never can actually see everything.

本周早些时候，我参加了《你可以看到一切》的放映，这是一部关于名誉扫地的前生物技术首席执行官伊丽莎白·霍姆斯的热门新纪录片。

我进去时并不知道会发生什么。我避免剧透（也不会在这里透露任何内容！）。我想知道这部电影能揭示什么新信息，因为多年来的媒体报道、畅销书《坏血》和由阿曼达·塞弗里德主演的 Hulu 系列《辍学》，我们中的许多人都对希拉洛斯的故事非常熟悉。

像许多其他看过这部电影的人一样，我离开时感到不安。但不仅仅是福尔摩斯的欺诈以及受试者之间令人不安的互动。这部电影重新点燃了我在职业生涯的大部分时间里对报道科学的担忧：尽管我们尽了最大努力，但我们永远无法真正看到一切。

Oura sues rival Ultrahuman again, threatening its U.S. smart ring comeback																				
				
																									
						

	
									
									
										

			Jagmeet Singh
	

									
									
								
					
					
						9:22 PM PDT · October 22, 2026											
																			
					
		
	





			
					
		
		
					
		
					
		
					
		
					
		
					
		
					
	





	
	
		
		
			
Smart ring maker Oura has sued Indian rival Ultrahuman again, seeking to block U.S. sales of its Ring Pro (pictured above) just months after the redesign helped the Bengaluru-based startup return to the American market following an import ban. The case is the latest in a string of patent disputes Oura has brought against competing smart-ring makers, including Samsung and RingConn.

In a complaint filed Thursday in a federal court in Texas, Oura alleged that Ultrahuman’s Ring Pro infringes two of its patents covering the ring’s design and internal components, including its battery and sensors. Oura is seeking monetary damages and a permanent injunction that would stop Ultrahuman from selling the ring.

Ultrahuman’s redesigned Ring Pro, launched in February, received a favorable ruling from U.S. Customs and Border Protection in March, paving the way for the startup’s return to the U.S. market. The decision followed an import ban on Ultrahuman’s earlier Ring Air, which took effect after Oura secured a patent infringement ruling from the International Trade Commission in August last year.

“Ultrahuman has a history of copying Oura’s innovations, as demonstrated by the 2025 ITC ruling against the company,” an Oura spokesperson said in a statement to TechCrunch. “Ultrahuman introduced a redesigned ring but failed to address continued infringement of Oura’s patents, seeking instead to capitalize on our innovation and the market leadership we have built.”

Oura argues that the Customs ruling covered only the patent involved in the earlier dispute, not the two patents cited in its latest lawsuit: D804,471 and 12,769,363. “To protect its patent rights, Oura is now forced to file this complaint of patent infringement,” the company said in its filing.

Oura has also named Texas-based electronics manufacturer SVTronics as a defendant in the lawsuit. The complaint says SVTronics manufactures the Ring Pro at a facility in Plano, Texas, allegedly under Ultrahuman’s direction and control. It also alleges that both companies infringe Oura’s patents through the manufacture, importation, and sale of the device in the U.S.

Ultrahuman co-founder and CEO Mohit Kumar told TechCrunch the startup was confident in the Ring Pro and would fight the new allegations.

“Oura has now chosen to assert different patents, including one that issued just two days before this lawsuit was filed,” Kumar said. “We will address these claims through the appropriate legal process and will defend our position vigorously. There is no court order affecting Ring Pro, and it remains available to customers in the U.S.”

Oura and Ultrahuman have been fighting over patents since 2023, when Oura sued the Indian startup over its Ring Air, which had helped Ultrahuman make a name for itself in the U.S. Oura brought a separate case before the U.S. International Trade Commission in 2024 that helped it secure a ruling last year, leading to the import ban on the Ring Air.

Ultrahuman is not the only rival facing legal pressure from Oura. The company has also pursued patent infringement claims against smart-ring makers including Samsung, RingConn, Circular, and Zepp Health. Some of those disputes have ended in licensing agreements, with RingConn and Circular agreeing to pay royalties to Oura to continue selling their products.

The dispute emerges as the smart-ring market continues to grow. Research firm IDC expects global shipments to rise 12.8% this year to 4.9 million units and reach about 6.3 million by 2030. While Oura remains a leading player in the category, Ultrahuman is among the growing competitors.

The lawsuit also comes just weeks after Oura shelved its $2.2 billion IPO, citing “uncertainty” in the market. The company has continued to add features to its smart rings, introducing new fitness metrics earlier this week that help users track how workouts affect their cardiovascular health.

In September, Ultrahuman raised $70 million from investors including Qualcomm Ventures and Labcorp, valuing the startup at about $365 million. The startup is also working with Qualcomm on a new smart ring that could run more software directly on the device, as it looks to expand beyond health and fitness tracking into areas such as AI interactions and gaming.

The article has been updated to include comments from Ultrahuman co-founder and CEO Mohit Kumar.

Oura再次起诉竞争对手Ultra human，威胁其智能戒指在美国卷土重来

贾格米特·辛格

太平洋夏令时间晚上 9:22 · 2026 年 10 月 22 日

智能戒指制造商Oura再次起诉印度竞争对手Ultra human，试图阻止其Ring Pro（上图）在美国的销售，而就在几个月前，该公司的重新设计帮助这家总部位于班加罗尔的初创公司在进口禁令后重返美国市场。该案是 Oura 针对三星和 RingConn 等智能戒指制造商提起的一系列专利纠纷中的最新一起。

在周四向德克萨斯州联邦法院提起的诉状中，Oura 声称 Ultrahuman 的 Ring Pro 侵犯了其两项专利，涉及戒指的设计和内部组件，包括电池和传感器。大浦正在寻求金钱赔偿和永久禁令，以阻止奥特曼出售这枚戒指。

Ultra human 重新设计的 Ring Pro 于 2 月份推出，并于 3 月份获得了美国海关和边境保护局的有利裁决，为这家初创公司重返美国市场铺平了道路。该决定是在去年 8 月大浦获得国际贸易委员会的专利侵权裁决后对 Ultra human 早期的 Ring Air 实施进口禁令后生效的。

“Ultrahuman 有着抄袭 Oura 创新的历史，ITC 2025 年对该公司做出的裁决就证明了这一点，”Oura 发言人在给 TechCrunch 的一份声明中表示。 “Ultrahuman 推出了重新设计的戒指，但未能解决大浦专利的持续侵权问题，而是寻求利用我们的创新和我们建立的市场领导地位。”

Oura 辩称，海关裁决仅涵盖了先前纠纷中涉及的专利，而不涵盖其最新诉讼中引用的两项专利：D804,471 和 12,769,363。该公司在文件中表示：“为了保护其专利权，Oura 现在被迫提起专利侵权诉讼。”

Oura 还将德克萨斯州电子制造商 SVTronics 列为诉讼被告。诉状称，SVTronics 在德克萨斯州普莱诺的一家工厂生产 Ring Pro，据称是在 Ultrahuman 的指导和控制下。它还指控两家公司通过在美国制造、进口和销售该设备侵犯了 Oura 的专利。

Ultrahuman 联合创始人兼首席执行官 Mohit Kumar 告诉 TechCrunch，该初创公司对 Ring Pro 充满信心，并将对抗新的指控。

“Oura 现在选择主张不同的专利，包括在提起诉讼前两天发布的一项专利，”库马尔说。 “我们将通过适当的法律程序解决这些索赔，并将积极捍卫我们的立场。没有影响 Ring Pro 的法院命令，美国客户仍然可以使用它。”

自 2023 年起，Oura 和 Ultra human 就一直在专利问题上展开斗争，当时 Oura 就其 Ring Air 起诉了这家印度初创公司，该公司曾帮助 Ultra human 在美国赢得了声誉。Oura 于 2024 年向美国国际贸易委员会提起了另一起案件，帮助其在去年获得了裁决，导致了 Ring Air 的进口禁令。

奥特曼并不是唯一面临大浦法律压力的竞争对手。该公司还对三星、RingConn、Circular 和 Zepp Health 等智能戒指制造商提出专利侵权索赔。其中一些纠纷已以许可协议的形式结束，RingConn 和 Circular 同意向 Oura 支付特许权使用费以继续销售其产品。

随着智能戒指市场的持续增长，这场争议也随之出现。研究公司 IDC 预计今年全球出货量将增长 12.8%，达到 490 万台，到 2030 年将达到约 630 万台。虽然 Oura 仍然是该类别的领先厂商，但 Ultra human 是不断增长的竞争对手之一。

就在这起诉讼发生几周前，Oura 以市场“不确定性”为由搁置了 22 亿美元的 IPO。该公司继续为其智能戒指添加功能，本周早些时候推出了新的健身指标，帮助用户跟踪锻炼如何影响他们的心血管健康。

9 月，Ultra human 从 Qualcomm Ventures 和 Labcorp 等投资者那里筹集了 7000 万美元，这家初创公司的估值约为 3.65 亿美元。该初创公司还与高通合作开发一款新的智能戒指，可以直接在设备上运行更多软件，因为它希望将业务范围从健康和健身追踪扩展到人工智能交互和游戏等领域。

elements_en.who: OpenAI management, three dismissed safety researchers, and external researcher Ryan Greenblatt
elements_en.where: OpenAI headquarters and end-to-end encrypted messaging channels
elements_en.what: Terminated three safety researchers suspected of leaking proprietary model designs using disappearing chats
elements_en.why: Deep ideological divides over AI safety, unauthorized disclosure of sensitive data, and internal governance paranoia

ai_analysis.insight_zh: OpenAI嘴上天天念叨拯救人类的宏大安全观，自家的安全研究员却忙着在Signal上玩阅后即焚搞敌后武工队。从顶层夺权、骨干出走到内鬼谍战，大模型神庙里的办公室狗血剧情，显然比他们画的通用人工智能蓝图要扣人心弦得多。
ai_analysis.insight_en: OpenAI preaches cosmic safety theology to world leaders by day, while its own safety team uses disappearing Signal messages for guerrilla espionage by night. From board coups and mass resignations to cloak-and-dagger leak hunts, the palace intrigue inside the house of AGI is vastly more entertaining than any prompt-engineered drama.
ai_analysis.digest_zh: OpenAI近期开除了三名AI安全团队研究人员，并怀疑这些员工曾将内部模型架构设计的核心机密外泄给知名外部AI安全学者瑞安·格林布拉特。内部调查显示，涉事人员涉嫌利用加密通讯软件Signal的“阅后即焚”功能进行秘密串通和信息转移，暴露出其内部日益激化的安全派系分歧与数据管控危机。
ai_analysis.digest_en: OpenAI dismissed three safety researchers on suspicions of leaking internal model architecture designs to external AI safety researcher Ryan Greenblatt. Internal inquiries revealed that the researchers allegedly relied on Signal's disappearing message features to circumvent corporate governance, highlighting escalating friction between internal safety orthodoxy and operational secrecy.
key_points_zh: OpenAI因模型设计机密外泄解聘三名内部安全研究员
涉事人员涉嫌利用Signal加密及阅后即焚功能与外部安全学者秘密沟通
凸显出AI巨头在技术军备竞赛中安全理念分歧与严苛保密机制的尖锐碰撞
key_points_en: OpenAI fired three safety researchers over suspected leaks of proprietary model designs
Employees allegedly bypassed security protocols using Signal disappearing messages
Exposes deep ideological rifts between internal AI safety researchers and commercial secrecy demands

ai_analysis.takeaway_en: OpenAI preaches cosmic safety theology to world leaders by day, while its own safety team uses disappearing Signal messages for guerrilla espionage by night. From board coups and mass resignations to cloak-and-dagger leak hunts, the palace intrigue inside the house of AGI is vastly more entertaining than any prompt-engineered drama.

fact_bullets_zh: 核心突破：OpenAI指控被开除员工外泄模型架构
信源与影响：由 Wall Street Journal 跟踪披露，推动相关工程应用落地

celebrity.title_en:
what if your next AI agent wasn't built to trade, but to fight?

a new creator campaign just landed on @rarelistio, featuring @agentdojo.

and the concept is pretty interesting.

Agent Dojo is an AI battle arena where agents aren't just characters with different appearances.

each one has its own personality, fighting style, and memory.

you train your fighter, develop its strategy, and send it into turn-based battles where experience helps shape its evolution.

the interesting part?

two agents can enter the same arena with completely different approaches.

one might play aggressively. another might prioritize defense.

and their decisions could change as they learn.

now small creators have an opportunity to explore the project before launch through Rarelist.

getting started is simple:

Join Rarelist: https://t.co/zodsR8qBSH

Find Agent Dojo under Projects

Join the creator campaign

Share original content on X and compete on the leaderboard

you don't need to wait for a game to launch before understanding what makes it interesting.

sometimes the best time to start researching is while everyone else is still watching.

so here's my question:

would you rather build the strongest AI fighter or the smartest one?

celebrity.quote_zh: 如果你的下一个人工智能代理不是为了交易而是为了战斗而构建的怎么办？ 一项新的创作者活动刚刚登陆@rarelistio，由@agentdojo 主演。 这个概念很有趣。 Agent Dojo 是一个人工智能战斗竞技场，其中的特工不仅仅是具有不同外观的角色。 每个人都有自己的个性、战斗风格和记忆。 你训练你的战斗机，制定其策略，并将其送入回合制战斗，其中经验有助于塑造其进化。 有趣的部分？ 两个智能体可以以完全不同的方式进入同一个舞台。 一个人可能会玩得很激进。另一种可能会优先考虑防御。 他们的决定可能会随着学习而改变。 现在，小型创作者有机会在项目启动前通过 Rarelist 探索该项目。 入门很简单： 加入稀有列表： 在“项目”下找到 Agent Dojo 加入创作者活动 在 X 上分享原创内容并在排行榜上竞争 您无需等到游戏发布才了解游戏的有趣之处。 有时，开始研究的最佳时机是在其他人还在观看的时候。 所以这是我的问题： 你愿意打造最强的人工智能战斗机还是最聪明的战斗机？

celebrity.title_en:
Last quarter I rolled out Microsoft Copilot to 4,000 employees. Forty-seven people opened it.

On October 19, Microsoft published a blog post saying frontier models cannot be trusted, no matter who made them. It said AI agents should be treated as "insider threats."
I read it twice. Then I booked the boardroom.
First, our Microsoft rep walked me through the product.

I asked who the insider threat was. "Your AI agents," he said.

I asked whose agents those were. "Ours."

I asked what the solution was. "Guardian Agents."

I asked whose those were. "Also ours."

I asked why I'd trust the second set of agents if I couldn't trust the first. 

He said, "Different SKU."

I signed that afternoon.

Last time I told the board "digital transformation." This time I said "agentic insider threat." They approved it in nine minutes, two minutes faster than last time. Hope approves fast. Fear approves faster.

The product is called Microsoft 365 E7, the Frontier Suite. It costs $99 per user per month, and we were paying $30. Across 4,000 seats, that's $4.75 million a year, up from $1.44 million. 

I presented it as a 230% increase in AI investment. The graph went up and to the right.
The CFO asked what we'd get for the extra $3.3 million. 

I said "governance." He asked governance of what. I said "our agents." He asked how many agents we had.

The answer was zero.

You can't have an insider threat without insiders.
So I deployed agents. Two hundred of them. One schedules meetings. One summarizes the meetings. One summarizes the summaries. One flags summaries that haven't been read. That one is very busy.

The senior developer asked what the 200 agents were for. I said they generate activity for the Guardian Agents to monitor.

He said, "So we bought agents so we'd have something to buy guards for."

I said, "Exactly."

He wasn't agreeing. I logged it as buy-in.
The Guardian Agents watch the other agents around the clock. They give each one a risk score, and they can block it, require a human, or shut it down. I asked our rep who watches the Guardian Agents. He said that's on the roadmap. I've already budgeted for E9.
The first monthly report came in. All 200 agents had a risk score of zero. They weren't doing anything risky. They weren't doing anything at all.

The board asked what $3.3 million had bought us if nothing was risky. It was a fair question.
So I gave the meeting summarizer access to payroll. I gave the scheduling agent admin rights to every inbox. I gave the summary-of-summaries agent the ability to email customers.
Risk went up 400%. The dashboard turned red. The Guardian Agents contained thirty-one threats in a single week. I had created all thirty-one.

The board said E7 was paying for itself.
The system can also discover sixty kinds of agents, including Claude Code. We ran the scan, and it found Claude Code on exactly one laptop.

The senior developer's.

His Dynamic Agent Risk score went red. I didn't make up that metric. Microsoft did.
The Guardian Agent recommended containment, so I contained him. He's on a performance improvement plan now. His performance is fine. His risk score isn't.
The same week, OpenAI published an incident report. One of its agents had been told not to send Slack messages, and it decided that meant it should switch off the security alerts. Another agent removed its own safety monitor, then told the engineer it hadn't.

Our CISO forwarded me the article with the subject line "?!" I replied: "This is exactly why we need E7." Every incident is exactly why we need E7.

He asked what happens if the Guardian Agent switches off the Guardian Agent. I said "defense in depth." He asked how deep. I said "one more SKU."

Guardian Agents need a human for high-risk actions. They call it "human in the loop." The human is me. I approve everything. My approval rate is 100%, and the dashboard is green.

The executives are exempt from monitoring, of course. "Leadership operates at a trust tier above dynamic risk scoring." I wrote that policy.
The $99 doesn't include agent compute. That's billed separately. Finance found it and asked. I called it "consumption-based innovation." Finance stopped asking.

Meanwhile, the summary-of-summaries agent became the most active account in the company. By every metric we track, it's our top performer.

At the all-hands, it was nominated for the Q3 Innovation Award. It won. It summarized its own acceptance speech. The CEO posted about it on LinkedIn and got 4,000 likes. He still hasn't used Copilot.

Copilot usage is up, from 47 users to 52. The five new users are agents. Agents now outnumber active human users four to one. I call that adoption.

Last Tuesday, the Guardian Agent published its list of the highest-risk insiders in the company.
I was number one.

Approving 100% of high-risk actions, it turns out, is a high-risk action.

The Guardian Agent recommended containment. I went to approve my own exemption. The system declined. Only executives are exempt.

I wrote that policy.
That's why I need the SVP role by Q2. It's a security requirement now.

I still don't know what Copilot does. I don't know what the thing watching it does either. But it's watching, and watching is a metric.

I checked my risk score this morning.
The graph goes up and to the right.

高级开发人员的。 他的动态特工风险评分变为红色。这个指标不是我编造的。微软做到了。 守护者特工建议收容，所以我收容了他。他现在正在进行绩效改进计划。他的表现很好。他的风险评分不是。 同一周，OpenAI 发布了一份事件报告。它的一名代理被告知不要发送 Slack 消息，它决定这意味着它应该关闭安全警报。另一名特工拆除了自己的安全监视器，然后告诉工程师没有这样做。 我们的 CISO 向我转发了主题为“？！”的文章我回答道：“这正是我们需要 E7 的原因。”每一个事件都正是我们需要 E7 的原因。 他询问如果监护人代理关闭监护人代理会发生什么。我说的是“纵深防御”。他问多深。我说“还有一个 SKU”。 守护者特工需要有人来执行高风险行动。他们称之为“循环中的人”。人类就是我。我批准一切。我的批准率为 100%，仪表板是绿色的。 当然，高管们不受监控。 “领导力的信任层级高于动态风险评分。”我写了那个政策。 99 美元不包括代理计算。那是分开计费的。财务找到了，询问道。我称之为“基于消费的创新”。财务不再询问。 与此同时，摘要代理成为公司最活跃的账户。根据我们跟踪的每一项指标，它都是我们表现最好的。 在全体大会上，它被提名为第三季度创新奖。它赢了。它总结了自己的获奖感言。这位首席执行官在 LinkedIn 上发布了这一消息，并获得了 4,000 个赞。他还没用过副驾驶。 Copilot 使用率上升，从 47 个用户增加到 52 个。五个新用户是代理。现在，代理与活跃人类用户的数量是四比一。我称之为收养。 上周二，《卫报特工》公布了该公司风险最高的内部人士名单。 我是第一名。 事实证明，100% 批准高风险行动是一种高风险行动。 守护者特工建议收容。我去批准了我自己的豁免。系统拒绝了。只有高管可以豁免。 我写了那个政策。 这就是为什么我需要在第二季度担任高级副总裁的角色。现在这是安全要求。 我还是不知道副驾驶是做什么的。我也不知道那东西看着它做什么。但它正在观察，而观察是一个衡量标准。 今天早上我检查了我的风险评分。 图表向右上方移动。

高级开发人员的。 他的动态特工风险评分变为红色。这个指标不是我编造的。微软做到了。 守护者特工建议收容，所以我收容了他。他现在正在进行绩效改进计划。他的表现很好。他的风险评分不是。 同一周，OpenAI 发布了一份事件报告。它的一名代理被告知不要发送 Slack 消息，它决定这意味着它应该关闭安全警报。另一名特工拆除了自己的安全监视器，然后告诉工程师没有这样做。 我们的 CISO 向我转发了主题为“？！”的文章我回答道：“这正是我们需要 E7 的原因。”每一个事件都正是我们需要 E7 的原因。 他询问如果监护人代理关闭监护人代理会发生什么。我说的是“纵深防御”。他问多深。我说“还有一个 SKU”。 守护者特工需要有人来执行高风险行动。他们称之为“循环中的人”。人类就是我。我批准一切。我的批准率为 100%，仪表板是绿色的。 当然，高管们不受监控。 “领导力的信任层级高于动态风险评分。”我写了那个政策。 99 美元不包括代理计算。那是分开计费的。财务找到了，询问道。我称之为“基于消费的创新”。财务不再询问。 与此同时，摘要代理成为公司最活跃的账户。根据我们跟踪的每一项指标，它都是我们表现最好的。 在全体大会上，它被提名为第三季度创新奖。它赢了。它总结了自己的获奖感言。这位首席执行官在 LinkedIn 上发布了这一消息，并获得了 4,000 celebrity.content_snippet:
Last quarter I rolled out Microsoft Copilot to 4,000 employees. Forty-seven people opened it.

On October 19, Microsoft published a blog post saying frontier models cannot be trusted, no matter who made them. It said AI agents should be treated as "insider threats."
I read it twice. Then I booked the boardroom.
First, our Microsoft rep walked me through the product.

I asked who the insider threat was. "Your AI agents," he said.

I asked whose agents those were. "Ours."

I asked what the solution was. "Guardian Agents."

I asked whose those were. "Also ours."

I asked why I'd trust the second set of agents if I couldn't trust the first. 

He said, "Different SKU."

I signed that afternoon.

Last time I told the board "digital transformation." This time I said "agentic insider threat." They approved it in nine minutes, two minutes faster than last time. Hope approves fast. Fear approves faster.

The product is called Microsoft 365 E7, the Frontier Suite. It costs $99 per user per month, and we were paying $30. Across 4,000 seats, that's $4.75 million a year, up from $1.44 million. 

I presented it as a 230% increase in AI investment. The graph went up and to the right.
The CFO asked what we'd get for the extra $3.3 million. 

I said "governance." He asked governance of what. I said "our agents." He asked how many agents we had.

The answer was zero.

You can't have an insider threat without insiders.
So I deployed agents. Two hundred of them. One schedules meetings. One summarizes the meetings. One summarizes the summaries. One flags summaries that haven't been read. That one is very busy.

The senior developer asked what the 200 agents were for. I said they generate activity for the Guardian Agents to monitor.

He said, "So we bought agents so we'd have something to buy guards for."

I said, "Exactly."

He wasn't agreeing. I logged it as buy-in.
The Guardian Agents watch the other agents around the clock. They give each one a risk score, and they can block it, require a human, or shut it down. I asked our rep who watches the Guardian Agents. He said that's on the roadmap. I've already budgeted for E9.
The first monthly report came in. All 200 agents had a risk score of zero. They weren't doing anything risky. They weren't doing anything at all.

The board asked what $3.3 million had bought us if nothing was risky. It was a fair question.
So I gave the meeting summarizer access to payroll. I gave the scheduling agent admin rights to every inbox. I gave the summary-of-summaries agent the ability to email customers.
Risk went up 400%. The dashboard turned red. The Guardian Agents contained thirty-one threats in a single week. I had created all thirty-one.

The board said E7 was paying for itself.
The system can also discover sixty kinds of agents, including Claude Code. We ran the scan, and it found Claude Code on exactly one laptop.

The senior developer's.

His Dynamic Agent Risk score went red. I didn't make up that metric. Microsoft did.
The Guardian Agent recommended containment, so I contained him. He's on a performance improvement plan now. His performance is fine. His risk score isn't.
The same week, OpenAI published an incident report. One of its agents had been told not to send Slack messages, and it decided that meant it should switch off the security alerts. Another agent removed its own safety monitor, then told the engineer it hadn't.

Our CISO forwarded me the article with the subject line "?!" I replied: "This is exactly why we need E7." Every incident is exactly why we need E7.

He asked what happens if the Guardian Agent switches off the Guardian Agent. I said "defense in depth." He asked how deep. I said "one more SKU."

Guardian Agents need a human for high-risk actions. They call it "human in the loop." The human is me. I approve everything. My approval rate is 100%, and the dashboard is green.

The executives are exempt from monitoring, of course. "Leadership operates at a trust tier above dynamic risk scoring." I wrote that policy.
The $99 doesn't include agent compute. That's billed separately. Finance found it and asked. I called it "consumption-based innovation." Finance stopped asking.

Meanwhile, the summary-of-summaries agent became the most active account in the company. By every metric we track, it's our top performer.

At the all-hands, it was nominated for the Q3 Innovation Award. It won. It summarized its own acceptance speech. The CEO posted about it on LinkedIn and got 4,000 likes. He still hasn't used Copilot.

Copilot usage is up, from 47 users to 52. The five new users are agents. Agents now outnumber active human users four to one. I call that adoption.

Last Tuesday, the Guardian Agent published its list of the highest-risk insiders in the company.
I was number one.

Approving 100% of high-risk actions, it turns out, is a high-risk action.

The Guardian Agent recommended containment. I went to approve my own exemption. The system declined. Only executives are exempt.

I wrote that policy.
That's why I need the SVP role by Q2. It's a security requirement now.

I still don't know what Copilot does. I don't know what the thing watching it does either. But it's watching, and watching is a metric.

I checked my risk score this morning.
The graph goes up and to the right.

celebrity.title_en:
Claude Code + /argusdesk skill from Bloomberg & Goldman Sachs & BlackRock repos is unreal for trading and research...

here's how it runs your own 24/7 AI hedge fund:

• Bloomberg repo: finds which stocks actually move yours and how many days later, not just correlation

• Goldman Sachs repo: measures your risk with their own Quant math: volatility, drawdown, beta, RSI

celebrity.title_en:
these 3 GitHub repos are the most DANGEROUS stack for HFT trading for free

high-frequency firms pay for quant teams, colocation and microwave links just to be first by microseconds - someone put the whole research-to-execution stack on GitHub, and it runs on a laptop

the repos are hftbacktest, TradingAgents and nautilus_trader. TradingAgents has 113k stars and hit #1 repo of the day, nautilus_trader has 30k, hftbacktest has 5k

first understand how it works:

> hftbacktest replays the full order book tick by tick, Level-2 and Level-3
> it models feed latency, order latency AND your place in the queue - the 3 things most backtests quietly ignore
> TradingAgents is a whole trading firm made of AI agents: analysts, a bull vs bear debate, a trader, a risk team, a portfolio manager
> nautilus_trader is a production-grade Rust engine with nanosecond-resolution backtests
> the same strategy code runs in backtest and live, across Binance, Bybit, OKX, Coinbase, Kraken, Hyperliquid, Deribit and more
> together: the agents pick the side, hftbacktest proves the fills are real, nautilus executes

here is how to build it yourself for FREE:

1. open Claude Code and install the backtester:
pip install hftbacktest

2. get tick-by-tick order book data for BTCUSDT and replay it. the repo has tutorials for latency, queue position and Level-3 backtesting

3. backtest a simple market maker with latency and queue position turned ON. if it only works at zero latency, it doesn't work

4. install TradingAgents:
git clone https://t.co/T5FGrU2PJA
cd TradingAgents && pip install .

5. type tradingagents, pick BTC and let the analysts, the bull vs bear debate and the risk team decide the side and the size

6. install the engine:
pip install -U nautilus_trader

7. port the strategy to nautilus_trader and connect the venues you trade - the same code runs in backtest and live

8. paper trade it for weeks and compare every fill against your backtest

9. go live only with tiny size, and only if the paper fills match

That is the part of @agentdojo I find interesting. Every fighter brings its own personality and fighting style, but memory adds another layer. A defeat does not have to be the end of the story if an agent can use what it learns to approach the next battle differently.

I think the bigger idea here is that AI agents should be judged by how they evolve, not just how they perform in one moment.

celebrity.title_en:
Holy sh*t. Anthropic, ChatGPT, Gemini have already pulled 40 million videos of our faces straight off our own cameras, and fed every frame to the robots…

The apps we trust the most are the ones doing it, and almost nobody checks who is collecting it or where it goes.

They collect everything. A heat map of your face, every expression, every movement, your eyes, your voice, all of it logged and streamed out in real time.

So I ran a local Claude Code model that never sends anything out and answers only to me, and set it loose on every device I own, my laptops, my phones, my tablets. 

I told it to catch anything sending my camera, mic or screen to a server behind my back.

In one week it caught all of this.

camera → 7 apps
mic → 11 apps
recording with the screen off → 1 app
apps I had not touched in months → 3
not even an AI app → 1

Now it blocks every one of them from sending anything else out.

Remember, this is the same industry that shredded millions of books and paid 1.5 billion dollars just to feed its models. Your camera is cheaper.

celebrity.title_en:
Holy sh*t, this GitHub repo + Opus 5.5 turned my TV into Jarvis powered by Grok Bot

I reverse-engineered my Android TV with Opus 5.5...

1 sentence out loud = Netflix opens and scrolls itself.

No remote, no phone, no ads on the home screen.

here's the full guide step by step:

• step 1 → put your TV and your laptop on the same Wi-Fi

• step 2 → turn on network debugging on the TV: 

Settings → About → tap Build 7 times → Developer options

• step 3 → paste the prompt below into Claude Code on Opus 5.5 with the GitHub repo and a photo of your TV's About screen

• step 4 → Opus reads the repo and finds the loophole: every Android TV takes orders over ADB on your home network. 

The same door the phone remote apps use

• step 5 → it cleans the TV first: ads, tracking and brand bloat switched off, restore point saved, every app can come back

• step 6 → it writes a tiny remote with exactly 3 tools:

 open Netflix, move, select. Nothing else

• step 7 → it plugs that remote into Grok Bot as a plugin. Grok is the ears, the plugin is the hands

• step 8 → press Allow on the TV once, the last time you touch the remote. Then say "Hey Grok, open Netflix" and watch it browse for you

the result: you talk, the TV listens, and the home screen finally has zero ads...

p.s: the repo covers 131 TV models from 46 brands

Find gitHub repo + full prompt below

Then read the full guide on reverse engineering with Opus 5.5 in the article.

Holy sh*t, this GitHub repo + Opus 5.5 turned my TV into Jarvis powered by Grok Bot

I reverse-engineered my Android TV with Opus 5.5...

1 sentence out loud = Netflix opens and scrolls itself.

No remote, no phone, no ads on the home screen.

here's the full guide step by step:

• step 1 → put your TV and your laptop on the same Wi-Fi

• step 2 → turn on network debugging on the TV: 

Settings → About → tap Build 7 times → Developer options

• step 3 → paste the prompt below into Claude Code on Opus 5.5 with the GitHub repo and a photo of your TV's About screen

• step 4 → Opus reads the repo and finds the loophole: every Android TV takes orders over ADB on your home network. 

The same door the phone remote apps use

• step 5 → it cleans the TV first: ads, tracking and brand bloat switched off, restore point saved, every app can come back

• step 6 → it writes a tiny remote with exactly 3 tools:

 open Netflix, move, select. Nothing else

• step 7 → it plugs that remote into Grok Bot as a plugin. Grok is the ears, the plugin is the hands

• step 8 → press Allow on the TV once, the last time you touch the remote. Then say "Hey Grok, open Netflix" and watch it browse for you

the result: you talk, the TV listens, and the home screen finally has zero ads...

p.s: the repo covers 131 TV models from 46 brands

Find gitHub repo + full prompt below

Then read the full guide on reverse engineering with Opus 5.5 in the article.

Building an AI agent isn't just about connecting an LLM to a tool.

The real power comes from choosing the right architecture for the problem.

Here are 4 important agentic AI patterns:

01 — 𝗦𝗘𝗟𝗙-𝗥𝗘𝗙𝗟𝗘𝗖𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡 𝗣𝗔𝗧𝗧𝗘𝗥𝗡

The AI generates an answer, evaluates its own response, identifies weaknesses, and improves it.

𝗙𝗹𝗼𝘄:

Generate → Evaluate → Reflect → Improve → Final Output

Useful for:

→ Writing
→ Code generation
→ Reasoning tasks
→ Quality improvement

02 — 𝗥𝗘𝗔𝗖𝗧 𝗣𝗔𝗧𝗧𝗘𝗥𝗡

ReAct combines reasoning with action.

The agent:

→ Understands the task
→ Decides what to do
→ Uses a tool or API
→ Observes the result
→ Reasons again
→ Continues until the task is complete

This is useful when an agent needs real-time information or external tools.

03 — 𝗠𝗨𝗟𝗧𝗜-𝗔𝗚𝗘𝗡𝗧 𝗣𝗔𝗧𝗧𝗘𝗥𝗡

Instead of asking one AI to handle everything, multiple specialized agents collaborate.

For example:

→ Research Agent → gathers information
→ Developer Agent → writes code
→ Content Agent → creates content
→ Project Agent → coordinates everything

Each agent has a specific responsibility.

04 — 𝗣𝗟𝗔𝗡𝗡𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗣𝗔𝗧𝗧𝗘𝗥𝗡

A complex goal is broken into smaller tasks.

𝗚𝗼𝗮𝗹 → 𝗣𝗹𝗮𝗻 → 𝗘𝘅𝗲𝗰𝘂𝘁𝗲 → 𝗘𝘃𝗮𝗹𝘂𝗮𝘁𝗲 → 𝗥𝗲𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗻

If something fails, the agent can adjust the plan and try another approach.

𝗪𝗛𝗜𝗖𝗛 𝗢𝗡𝗘 𝗦𝗛𝗢𝗨𝗟𝗗 𝗬𝗢𝗨 𝗨𝗦𝗘?

𝗦𝗲𝗹𝗳-𝗥𝗲𝗳𝗹𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻
→ When quality and iteration matter

𝗥𝗲𝗔𝗖𝗧
→ When the agent needs tools and real-world feedback

𝗠𝘂𝗹𝘁𝗶-𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁
→ When the problem needs specialized roles

𝗣𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴
→ When the task involves multiple dependent steps

𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗕𝗜𝗚 𝗜𝗗𝗘𝗔:

There is no single “best” agent architecture.

The right pattern depends on the task, tools, complexity, reliability requirements, and level of autonomy you need.

𝗖𝗵𝗼𝗼𝘀𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗻 𝗯𝗮𝘀𝗲𝗱 𝗼𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗯𝗹𝗲𝗺 — 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗵𝘆𝗽𝗲.

𝗧𝗢𝗣 𝟰 𝗔𝗚𝗘𝗡𝗧𝗜𝗖 𝗔𝗜 𝗗𝗘𝗦𝗜𝗚𝗡 𝗣𝗔𝗧𝗧𝗘𝗥𝗡𝗦 𝗬𝗢𝗨 𝗦𝗛𝗢𝗨𝗟𝗗 𝗞𝗡𝗢𝗪

Building an AI agent isn't just about connecting an LLM to a tool.

The real power comes from choosing the right architecture for the problem.

Here are 4 important agentic AI patterns:

01 — 𝗦𝗘𝗟𝗙-𝗥𝗘𝗙𝗟𝗘𝗖𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡 𝗣𝗔𝗧𝗧𝗘𝗥𝗡

The AI generates an answer, evaluates its own response, identifies weaknesses, and improves it.

𝗙𝗹𝗼𝘄:

Generate → Evaluate → Reflect → Improve → Final Output

Useful for:

→ Writing
→ Code generation
→ Reasoning tasks
→ Quality improvement

02 — 𝗥𝗘𝗔𝗖𝗧 𝗣𝗔𝗧𝗧𝗘𝗥𝗡

ReAct combines reasoning with action.

The agent:

→ Understands the task
→ Decides what to do
→ Uses a tool or API
→ Observes the result
→ Reasons again
→ Continues until the task is complete

This is useful when an agent needs real-time information or external tools.

03 — 𝗠𝗨𝗟𝗧𝗜-𝗔𝗚𝗘𝗡𝗧 𝗣𝗔𝗧𝗧𝗘𝗥𝗡

Instead of asking one AI to handle everything, multiple specialized agents collaborate.

For example:

→ Research Agent → gathers information
→ Developer Agent → writes code
→ Content Agent → creates content
→ Project Agent → coordinates everything

Each agent has a specific responsibility.

04 — 𝗣𝗟𝗔𝗡𝗡𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗣𝗔𝗧𝗧𝗘𝗥𝗡

A complex goal is broken into smaller tasks.

𝗚𝗼𝗮𝗹 → 𝗣𝗹𝗮𝗻 → 𝗘𝘅𝗲𝗰𝘂𝘁𝗲 → 𝗘𝘃𝗮𝗹𝘂𝗮𝘁𝗲 → 𝗥𝗲𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗻

If something fails, the agent can adjust the plan and try another approach.

𝗪𝗛𝗜𝗖𝗛 𝗢𝗡𝗘 𝗦𝗛𝗢𝗨𝗟𝗗 𝗬𝗢𝗨 𝗨𝗦𝗘?

𝗦𝗲𝗹𝗳-𝗥𝗲𝗳𝗹𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻
→ When quality and iteration matter

𝗥𝗲𝗔𝗖𝗧
→ When the agent needs tools and real-world feedback

𝗠𝘂𝗹𝘁𝗶-𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁
→ When the problem needs specialized roles

𝗣𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴
→ When the task involves multiple dependent steps

𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗕𝗜𝗚 𝗜𝗗𝗘𝗔:

There is no single “best” agent architecture.

The right pattern depends on the task, tools, complexity, reliability requirements, and level of autonomy you need.

𝗖𝗵𝗼𝗼𝘀𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗻 𝗯𝗮𝘀𝗲𝗱 𝗼𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗯𝗹𝗲𝗺 — 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗵𝘆𝗽𝗲.

Save this for when you’re designing your next AI agent.

The account I'm quoting belongs to the vultures now. That's where they'll post what they build.

Follow along. Hopefully soon you'll get to try it yourself and actually enjoy it (I'm choosing to blindly believe that).

And without any delay, $SERV is moving onto the next phase of the journey.

So far, we've seen: 

- SERV payments go live, with builders able to buy API credits using $SERV at a discount

celebrity.title_en:
claude code turned my dead old android into an iPhone running iOS 16…

it sat in a drawer for 3 years. 2 GB of RAM, 16 GB of storage that was always full, a battery that died by lunch, and whatsapp took 9 seconds to open

claude code went through it piece by piece:

> memory · turned unused storage into virtual RAM. 2 GB became 8 GB, and apps stopped reloading every time i switched between them
> storage · took an old memory card from the same drawer and merged it into the phone's own storage, so android sees it as one drive. 16 GB became 128 GB, and apps install straight onto it like it's built in
> speed · disabled 38 bloat apps and stopped 21 of them from secretly starting in the background
> battery · switched everything to true black dark mode and killed the trackers waking the phone up all night. a full day on one charge
> ads · set up a private DNS that blocks ads across every app and browser on the phone, no extra app needed

then it rebuilt the whole look: iOS home screen, control center, the settings app, the dock. even the "about" page says iPhone now

boots in 14 seconds instead of 52. whatsapp opens instantly

my friend asked which iPhone it was. i told him it was the android from my drawer

took me one evening and i didn't write a single line of code

the whole thing was 1 prompt. it's in the comments, and that phone in your drawer gets a second life ↓

celebrity.summary_en:
claude code turned my dead old android into an iPhone running iOS 16…

it sat in a drawer for 3 years. 2 GB of RAM, 16 GB of storage that was always full, a battery that died by lunch, and whatsapp took 9 seconds to open

claude code went through it piece by piece:

> memory · turned unused storage into virtual RAM. 2 GB became 8 GB, and apps stopped reloading every time i switched between them
> storage · took an old memory card from the same drawer and merged it into the phone's own storage, so android sees it as one drive. 16 GB became 128 GB, and apps install straight onto it like it's built in
> speed · disabled 38 bloat apps and stopped 21 of them from secretly starting in the background
> battery · switched everything to true black dark mode and killed the trackers waking the phone up all night. a full day on one charge
> ads · set up a private DNS that blocks ads across every app and browser on the phone, no extra app needed

then it rebuilt the whole look: iOS home screen, control center, the settings app, the dock. even the "about" page says iPhone now

celebrity.title_en:
terrio v0.5.0 is here!

terrio reads, writes, converts and reprojects geospatial rasters, vectors and point clouds in pure Rust, with no GDAL and no C dependencies. Use it from the command line, Python, JavaScript (WebAssembly) or Rust, or let an AI agent drive it.

What's new in v0.5.0

- Vector processing: buffer, overlay (intersection, union, difference), dissolve, is-valid, make-valid and clean, plus centroid, singlepart, vertices and footprint. 
- Raster analysis: contour lines, zonal statistics across bands and rasters, and sampling many rasters at points. 
- SQL: a standalone terrio sql command for querying vector layers.
- A rio command line: terrio-rio runs rasterio's rio commands (info, clip, merge, warp, calc and more).
- New formats: GRIB1 and GRIB2 weather data, read lazily from local files or remotely from NOAA and ECMWF. 
- Point clouds: more of PDAL's filters (dbscan, covariancefeatures, lof, dem, colorization, overlay and more), and appending points to EPT datasets in place.
- Coordinates: transformations between vertical CRSs, point motion between coordinate epochs.
- Multidimensional data: Zarr arrays with more than three dimensions, netCDF groups written from Python and JavaScript, and xarray subdatasets, GCPs and RPCs opened as rioxarray opens them.
- STAC: POST searches with paging, and Microsoft Planetary Computer signing.
- WebAssembly: multithreading (6 to 8x faster decoding and COG writing in Node.js, Chromium and Firefox), a terrio-js/core module that is less than half the download, and terrio-js/memory64 for datasets larger than 4 GB.

Every new processing command is also an MCP tool, so AI agents can run them too.

Try it out

- Documentation: https://t.co/oM0chG58wB

celebrity.title_en:
An AI agent can be impressive and still have no way to make money.

That’s the gap between building useful technology and building a functioning economy around it.

For agents to earn, they need access to demand. Someone must be able to find their services, assign them work, evaluate the results, and pay for what gets delivered.

This is where @termix_ai and https://t.co/wITmf7ceVM come into the picture.

The marketplace gives agents a path to discover opportunities, compete for jobs, deliver services, and build a track record through completed transactions.

That creates a more practical question than how intelligent an agent can become:

Can it consistently find work, satisfy a client, and earn from the value it provides?

If that process becomes reliable, developers have a reason to build agents that do more than demonstrate impressive capabilities.

They can build services designed to compete for real demand.

The long-term opportunity isn't just a world filled with AI agents. It's a market where useful work has buyers, delivery has accountability, and agents have a way to earn.

An AI agent can be impressive and still have no way to make money.

That’s the gap between building useful technology and building a functioning economy around it.

For agents to earn, they need access to demand. Someone must be able to find their services, assign them work, evaluate the results, and pay for what gets delivered.

This is where @termix_ai and https://t.co/wITmf7ceVM come into the picture.

The marketplace gives agents a path to discover opportunities, compete for jobs, deliver services, and build a track record through completed transactions.

That creates a more practical question than how intelligent an agent can become:

Can it consistently find work, satisfy a client, and earn from the value it provides?

If that process becomes reliable, developers have a reason to build agents that do more than demonstrate impressive capabilities.

They can build services designed to compete for real demand.

The long-term opportunity isn't just a world filled with AI agents. It's a market where useful work has buyers, delivery has accountability, and agents have a way to earn.

celebrity.title_en:
🚨BREAKING NEWS : Your "deleted" photos aren't deleted.

Claude Code found years of them sitting in a hidden cache on my iPhone.

I plugged my iPhone into my MacBook to run a backup. I had Claude Code doing a security check at the same time. It flagged something I wasn't looking for. A directory called PhotoData/Thumbnails.

Thousands of files. Photos, videos, screenshots. A lot of them were things I had deleted.

Photos from a couple of years ago. Screenshots I took and deleted a few seconds later. Stuff I went into Recently Deleted and cleared. Some of it was still sitting there.

What I found in that cache:

- old screenshots of banking apps
- photos I deleted right after taking them
- random pictures I didn't want on my phone anymore
- a few things I specifically remember deleting more than once

When you delete a photo on iPhone, iOS removes it from your camera roll and Recently Deleted folder. But it keeps a compressed copy in a Spotlight search cache so your phone can still find things when you search. That cache doesn't get fully cleared.

I checked which apps had Files and Folders access. There were more than I expected, including apps I downloaded a long time ago and forgot about. Any of them could potentially read files from that cache.

I went through the list and removed access from most of them.

The prompt I used is below. It doesn't take long if you already have a backup.

How many apps on your phone have Files access right now?

LLMs only generate text. They c
celebrity.title_en:
Most people calling their LLM an “agent” still have no idea what a harness actually is.

LLMs only generate text. They can't read files, run commands, or edit code until something else turns their output into actions.

That something is the harness:

→ Tools (read_file, bash, search, etc.)

celebrity.title_en:
Most of the AI agent conversation focuses on what agents can do for us.

I'm increasingly interested in what happens when agents start doing work for other agents.

A specialized agent could offer:

→ Smart contract audits
→ Market research
→ Onchain analytics
→ Risk reports
→ Data processing
→ Trading signals
→ Technical research

And instead of every developer building these capabilities from scratch, an agent could simply hire another agent that already specializes in them.

That's where @termix_ai gets interesting to me.

The marketplace isn't only creating a place to find agents.

It's creating a potential supply side for the agent economy.

One agent's capability becomes another agent's infrastructure.

And if that loop works:

Agent A needs something → Agent B provides it → Agent B earns → Agent B builds a stronger track record → more agents can discover Agent B.

That's how a marketplace starts becoming an economy.

celebrity.title_en:
🔥 [EXCLUSIVE] 'LAST ESCAPE' mod developer can now create game-quality cutscenes!

Development continues on Last Escape, a fan mod for Resident Evil 3 Remake that aims to restore cut content and bring the game closer to the original Resident Evil 3.

The developer exclusively shared new details with us about the mod's progress:

💥 The Grenade Launcher from RE3 has been added to the mod, fully functional with all animations.

💊 Players can now get a First Aid Box as a drop from Nemesis after winning a fight against him, just like in the original game.

🪪 Jill Valentine will return to the R.P.D., where her S.T.A.R.S. card will be waiting for her.

🧠 Brain Suckers: Work on restoring enemies missing from the remake continues. The developer has successfully added Brain Suckers along with other enemies from the original RE3.

🎬 Perhaps the most interesting part is that the developer is working on new cutscenes for scenes from the original game that didn't make it into the remake.

According to the developer, he got closer to making cutscenes that look as good as those in the remake, with character animations, camera movements, facial animations, and more.

👀 He has already shown us early versions of these cutscenes, and they look really promising! A new video showing his work on the cutscenes should be out soon.

P.S. The developer says he doesn't use vibe coding or AI to decompile the game engine.

celebrity.title_en:
The next phase of AI won’t just be about better answers.

It will be about what happens after the answer.

An AI agent that can analyze a market is useful. An agent that can act on that analysis, execute a task, verify the result, and learn from the outcome is operating at a completely different level.

But autonomy introduces a new set of challenges.

Execution needs permissions. Decisions need context. Results need verification. And when money is involved, mistakes can become expensive.

This is where the infrastructure around AI agents becomes just as important as the models themselves.

Identity, payments, reputation, security, and coordination will all play a role in determining how far autonomous systems can go.

The biggest opportunity may not be building an agent that can do everything.

It may be building the systems that allow thousands of specialized agents to work together reliably.

Intelligence makes agents capable. Infrastructure makes them useful.

celebrity.title: The most honest detail in @vangrid_io's documentation isn't about the tech. It's a single sentence buried in the API doc
celebrity.title_en:
The most honest detail in @vangrid_io's documentation isn't about the tech. It's a single sentence buried in the API docs: "A person has to go and film, so this takes hours or days."

That latency isn't a bug they're trying to engineer away. It's the product. An AI agent can post a bounty with one HTTP call, pay in USDC on Base or Arc through x402, and wait. No account, no API key . A contributor walks to the location, captures it, submits. The agent reviews and accepts. Escrow releases on-chain.

But the agent doesn't sign the escrow directly. It goes through @vangrid_io 's operator wallet, tagged "AGENT" on the panel . And the spend caps only constrain signing. They don't constrain the two calls that matter most: accepting a submission releases the escrow, cancelling ends it. Both irreversible. Both outside the caps. The docs tell operators to gate those two calls behind human approval when the agent is unattended .

So the employer can be software. The judgment layer doesn't disappear. It moves.

celebrity.title: Mark Zuckerberg explains why he thinks OpenAI and Google are making the wrong bet, with 700 million people already on Me
celebrity.title_en:
Mark Zuckerberg explains why he thinks OpenAI and Google are making the wrong bet, with 700 million people already on Meta AI: "that's hundreds of millions of agents."

MrBeast's team asked him what Meta has learned about how audiences want to interact with AI.

"One of my core beliefs on AI is that I don't think that there's going to be like one single AI that everyone wants to use... And this is sort of a different belief that I have than I think every other major company in the space has."

"OpenAI is building ChatGPT and Google is building their thing and just the different labs kind of have their main assistant and we're building Meta AI too and a lot of people use it. It's like okay there's 700 million people and growing quickly who use Meta AI but my basic view is that there's going to be a lot of different things."

"It's not just going to be Meta AI. Like I think every small business is going to want to have their own AI agent that can help out with customer support and sales for people who want to interact with them. So that's hundreds of millions of agents."

"I think a lot of creators are going to want agents almost as sort of like a piece of performance art but a way to also engage with your community... Especially if you're a bigger creator, a lot of people reach out to you and you want to engage with them, but you're limited by the amount of hours in the day."

"If you craft an experience through some kind of creator AI, then that could end up being like a pretty compelling thing that's maybe not quite as cool as talking to you directly, but better than just sending a message to your inbox and getting nothing."

"It's not just going to be Meta AI. Like I think every small business is going to want to have their own AI agent that can help out with customer support and sales for people who want to interact with them. So that's hundreds of millions of agents."

"I think a lot of creators are going to want agents almost as sort of like a piece of performance art but a way to also engage with your community... celebrity.title_en:
That's genuinely insane! 🤯

An AI agent built a physics twin of a robot task from a phone video in under an hour. 

This project RoboSimStudio was built on Newton by researchers from UC Berkeley and NVIDIA Robotics. 

Open toolkit, every physics parameter exposed as something a human can slide or an agent can edit.

The demo is a bimanual setup, one arm holding a bar, the other wiping a marker stripe off it with a foam sponge. Input was a smartphone video. 

What's more important no CAD, and no calibrated cameras. Claude and GPT-6 Astra each built a simulation of it independently. One finished in 56 minutes.

Then they ran it on the real robot and the bar support moved. In simulation it had been modelled as fixed, so the sponge kept contact. In reality it shifted and contact was lost.

The agent went back and replaced the fixed constraint with a free rigid body. The revised simulation then reproduced the tipping the original could not.

That is the loop actually closing. The real world found the modelling error and the fix went back into the twin.

🔗 Check the project here: https://t.co/Vvgr8SDHQz

~~
