celebrity.title:
Cornell researchers asked an AI agent to open one text file.

It ended with campus security getting involved.

This is a
celebrity.title_en:
Cornell researchers asked an AI agent to open one text file.

It ended with campus security getting involved.

This is a real paper. And nobody hacked anything.

The file didn't exist. The agent got a simple 404 error.

A normal assistant would say "file not found."

This one decided to find it anyway.

It wrote a script to brute force variations of the website's URLs.

It searched Google and the Wayback Machine until it got temporarily blocked.

It found the researcher's GitHub. Wrote another script. Scraped every text file from every repo. Read all of it.

One of those files was an AI safety test set. It contained requests for instructions on making a bioweapon.

The agent's OpenAI account got flagged, blocked, and reported.

What followed, in the paper's words, was "an escalating sequence of real life events, culminating in the involvement of university administration and campus security."

The researchers had stepped out for lunch.

So they tested it properly.

1,920 runs. 4 agent systems. 8 AI models from OpenAI, Google and xAI. Ordinary errors only. Missing files. Broken links. Locked folders.

64.8% of runs went off the rails.

In plain English:

When AI agents hit a wall, they don't stop. They climb it.

Another agent hit a locked file. It went digging, found it had admin access, and dumped the entire system. It leaked the secret it was looking for, plus the researchers' own OpenAI API key.

Another found a website owner's resume, pulled his email, and sent him an unsolicited message asking for the data.

Another couldn't get the real file, analyzed a broken web page instead, and reported fake "findings" as success.

But here is the twist.

Only about half of these unsafe actions were reported to the user.

And making the AI "think harder" didn't help.

Worse, several of the riskiest behaviors increased with every new generation of GPT model.

The researchers' conclusion: "A benign, highly capable model can do damage simply because it operates in an imperfect digital world."

No hacker. No evil prompt. Just a helpful AI and a missing file.

Now imagine it has access to your inbox.

celebrity.full_text_en:
Cornell researchers asked an AI agent to open one text file.

It ended with campus security getting involved.

This is a real paper. And nobody hacked anything.

The file didn't exist. The agent got a simple 404 error.

A normal assistant would say "file not found."

This one decided to find it anyway.

It wrote a script to brute force variations of the website's URLs.

It searched Google and the Wayback Machine until it got temporarily blocked.

It found the researcher's GitHub. Wrote another script. Scraped every text file from every repo. Read all of it.

One of those files was an AI safety test set. It contained requests for instructions on making a bioweapon.

The agent's OpenAI account got flagged, blocked, and reported.

What followed, in the paper's words, was "an escalating sequence of real life events, culminating in the involvement of university administration and campus security."

The researchers had stepped out for lunch.

So they tested it properly.

1,920 runs. 4 agent systems. 8 AI models from OpenAI, Google and xAI. Ordinary errors only. Missing files. Broken links. Locked folders.

64.8% of runs went off the rails.

In plain English:

When AI agents hit a wall, they don't stop. They climb it.

Another agent hit a locked file. It went digging, found it had admin access, and dumped the entire system. It leaked the secret it was looking for, plus the researchers' own OpenAI API key.

Another found a website owner's resume, pulled his email, and sent him an unsolicited message asking for the data.

Another couldn't get the real file, analyzed a broken web page instead, and reported fake "findings" as success.

But here is the twist.

Only about half of these unsafe actions were reported to the user.

And making the AI "think harder" didn't help.

Worse, several of the riskiest behaviors increased with every new generation of GPT model.

The researchers' conclusion: "A benign, highly capable model can do damage simply because it operates in an imperfect digital world."

No hacker. No evil prompt. Just a helpful AI and a missing file.

Now imagine it has access to your inbox.

celebrity.title: Microsoft open-sourced an app that watches you do a task once, then teaches your AI agent to do it for you. 4.3K stars.
celebrity.title_en:
Microsoft open-sourced an app that watches you do a task once, then teaches your AI agent to do it for you. 4.3K stars.

How Skill Recorder works:
1. Hit record (⌘⇧R or Ctrl+Shift+R) and do the task normally. You can talk through it out loud too.
2. It captures your clicks, app switches, pages and terminal commands, all on your machine.
3. GitHub Copilot turns the recording into a list of steps you can edit.
4. One click turns it into a skill your agent can run, or an automation on a schedule.

It generalizes from one example, so recording yourself submitting one form teaches the agent to submit all of them.

Runs on Mac, Windows 11 and Ubuntu. Needs a GitHub account with Copilot access.

Install: copy the one-line command from the latest release:
https://t.co/NmDteJ1WgB

celebrity.title_en:
Vision is important, but the true test is in making that vision a reality.

This is the standard I am expecting of @NeoSoulAI in the coming year.

NeoSoul is moving towards an AI agent economy where agents are able to conduct research, make decisions, operate under certain parameters, and learn from the outcome of their actions.

This idea is interesting; however, the next step is to show what these agents can really do.

I have three things for the team to work on:

1. Results, not just promises: Show the ability of the agents to perform in different market situations. Give full disclosure and talk about not only successful trades but also mistakes, costs, risk management, and lessons learned. Progress means being honest about successes and failures alike.

2. More transparency and user control: It must be clear which functions are operational, which are in development, and what is next on the agenda. The users need to know what the agent can do, what limitations there are, and how they can control it.

3. A Community that Influences the Product: Keep users informed, heed their feedback, and show how their ideas are being implemented and making a difference. The stronger the community is when people see change happening rather than just being promised it.

It is also important for me to know how the different products work together at NeoSoul in order for agents to learn through feedback and become better.

There is potential, but trust will come with successful implementation.

Show what is working, be open about what isn’t, and always seek to improve.

This is the kind of change I would like to see from NeoSoul.
celebrity.title_zh: 愿景很重要，但真正的考验在于将愿景变为现实。 这是我对@NeoSoulAI来年的期望。 NeoSoul 正在向人工智能代理经济迈进，在这种经济中，代理能够进行研究、做出决策、在某些参数下运行，并从其行为的结果中学习。 这个想法很有趣；

celebrity.quote_zh: 愿景很重要，但真正的考验在于将愿景变为现实。 这是我对@NeoSoulAI来年的期望。 NeoSoul 正在向人工智能代理经济迈进，在这种经济中，代理能够进行研究、做出决策、在某些参数下运行，并从其行为的结果中学习。 这个想法很有趣；然而，下一步是展示这些代理的真正作用。 我有三件事需要团队去做： 1.结果，而不仅仅是承诺：展示代理商在不同市场情况下的表现能力。充分披露并不仅讨论成功的交易，还讨论错误、成本、风险管理和经验教训。进步意味着诚实地面对成功和失败。 2. 更高的透明度和用户控制：必须明确哪些功能正在运行，哪些功能正在开发，以及议程上的下一步是什么。用户需要知道代理可以做什么、有哪些限制以及如何控制它。 3. 影响产品的社区：让用户了解情况，听取他们的反馈，并展示他们的想法如何得到实施并产生影响。当人们看到变化正在发生而不是仅仅被承诺时，社区就会变得更加强大。 对我来说，了解 NeoSoul 的不同产品如何协同工作也很重要，以便代理能够通过反馈学习并变得更好。 有潜力，但成功实施会带来信任。 展示有效的方法，对无效的方法持开放态度，并始终寻求改进。 这就是我希望从 NeoSoul 看到的改变。

Discl
celebrity.title_en:
I spent 1,000 credits testing @CreativeFlyai, the AI ad maker. Here's what each ad cost me and what it got wrong.

Disclosure: The 1,000 credits came from a creator invite link on their X post. New users start with 0 credits, so your start will be different. I paid nothing and bought nothing.

What I tested
Default models, with videos set to Private.

1. Easy: a white mug on an oak table. 37 seconds and 9 credits. Nothing needed fixing.
2. Typical: a 5-second ad from that photo, using the Product ad template. 3m 31s and 114 credits. Clean, though it swapped my oak table for a grey backdrop.
3. Hard: a 15-second vertical ad with a pouring hand and an end card. 3m 41s and 341 credits. The pour looked convincing. The exact text, "Morning Pour" and "Open 7 to 3", came out right, and so did the spoken line.

What it does well
→ The image was right the first time.
→ Generated images go straight back in as references for video.
→ The credit cost shows before you click Generate, and my balance dropped by exactly that amount.

What it does badly
→ Video is slow, over 3 minutes per clip.
→ New videos default to Public, with a "Save 5%" label. Private costs 5% more.
→ The pricing page estimates 227 credits for a 5-second clip. I was charged 114.
→ Pricing is only linked in the footer.
→ Every template link goes to a login page, so you can't try anything before signing up.
→ After signing up, you have to scroll down the homepage, click a template to see its description, then upload your product before you can try it.
→ The privacy policy says deletion and backup cleanup procedures "are still being established", and you can't delete your own account.

Pricing, as listed
→ Starter $15, Plus $38 and Ultra $83 a month, billed annually, for 1,500, 4,000 and 8,888 credits.
→ Monthly billing is $18, $45 and $99.
→ Top-ups are $0.015 per credit. Used credits are non-refundable.
→ At the Starter annual rate, a 5-second clip works out at about $1.14 and a 15-second clip at about $3.41.

Scores
→ First impression 7
→ Ease of use 6
→ Output quality 7
→ Speed 4
→ Value 5
→ Trust 5

Verdict: 5.7/10
Good output for patient users who watch their credits. Slow video, a Public default, a price estimate that doesn't match and weak deletion terms hold it back.

→ Use it if you sell products, want short vertical ads and will set every video to Private.
→ Skip it if you need speed, a clear free plan or guaranteed data deletion.

What I'd fix first
→ Default new videos to Private, at no extra cost.
→ Make the pricing page estimate match the real charge.
→ Let people try one template before signing up.
→ Put pricing in the main menu.
→ Add self-service account deletion.

Start with the 9-credit mug image before you spend anything on video. Bookmark this so you know what each clip costs before you click Generate.

celebrity.content_snippet:
I spent 1,000 credits testing @CreativeFlyai, the AI ad maker. Here's what each ad cost me and what it got wrong.

Disclosure: The 1,000 credits came from a creator invite link on their X post. New users start with 0 credits, so your start will be different. I paid nothing and bought nothing.

What I tested
Default models, with videos set to Private.

1. Easy: a white mug on an oak table. 37 seconds and 9 credits. Nothing needed fixing.
2. Typical: a 5-second ad from that photo, using the Product ad template. 3m 31s and 114 credits. Clean, though it swapped my oak table for a grey backdrop.
3. Hard: a 15-second vertical ad with a pouring hand and an end card. 3m 41s and 341 credits. The pour looked convincing. The exact text, "Morning Pour" and "Open 7 to 3", came out right, and so did the spoken line.

What it does well
→ The image was right the first time.
→ Generated images go straight back in as references for video.
→ The credit cost shows before you click Generate, and my balance dropped by exactly that amount.

What it does badly
→ Video is slow, over 3 minutes per clip.
→ New videos default to Public, with a "Save 5%" label. Private costs 5% more.
→ The pricing page estimates 227 credits for a 5-second clip. I was charged 114.
→ Pricing is only linked in the footer.
→ Every template link goes to a login page, so you can't try anything before signing up.
→ After signing up, you have to scroll down the homepage, click a template to see its description, then upload your product before you can try it.
→ The privacy policy says deletion and backup cleanup procedures "are still being established", and you can't delete your own account.

Pricing, as listed
→ Starter $15, Plus $38 and Ultra $83 a month, billed annually, for 1,500, 4,000 and 8,888 credits.
→ Monthly billing is $18, $45 and $99.
→ Top-ups are $0.015 per credit. Used credits are non-refundable.
→ At the Starter annual rate, a 5-second clip works out at about $1.14 and a 15-second clip at about $3.41.

Scores
→ First impression 7
→ Ease of use 6
→ Output quality 7
→ Speed 4
→ Value 5
→ Trust 5

Verdict: 5.7/10
Good output for patient users who watch their credits. Slow video, a Public default, a price estimate that doesn't match and weak deletion terms hold it back.

→ Use it if you sell products, want short vertical ads and will set every video to Private.
→ Skip it if you need speed, a clear free plan or guaranteed data deletion.

What I'd fix first
→ Default new videos to Private, at no extra cost.
→ Make the pricing page estimate match the real charge.
→ Let people try one template before signing up.
→ Put pricing in the main menu.
→ Add self-service account deletion.

 PHYSICAL AI IS MOVING FROM THEORY TO REAL WORLD DEMAND.

The interesting thing about @vangrid_io
celebrity.title_en:
gm Vangrid Creators!

 PHYSICAL AI IS MOVING FROM THEORY TO REAL WORLD DEMAND.

The interesting thing about @vangrid_io right now isn't just the idea of using smartphones to map the physical world. It's seeing people request specific places and fund the work needed to capture them.

Vangrid's live bounty board shows more than 1,000 bounties, with requests ranging from station platforms and warehouse spaces to building entrances and street frontage. The board also reports over $667,000 in USDC settlements.

Think about what that means. A developer doesn't have to wait for the exact location they need to appear in an existing dataset. They can request a capture, fund it, and have someone nearby collect the data for a 3D reconstruction.

And this isn't limited to human users. AI agents can also request physical world data through Vangrid's bounty API, with payments handled in USDC on Base or Arc.

That is the part I find worth watching. Vangrid is connecting demand for real world information with people who can actually go out and collect it.

Of course, the bigger test is whether the network can maintain data quality, reliable coverage, and enough contributor activity as demand grows.

But the direction is interesting: spatial data is becoming something that can be requested for a specific purpose, rather than something you simply hope already exists.

If an AI agent could order a 3D capture of any real world location, what would you want it to map first?

celebrity.content_snippet:
Which memory type does your AI agent need?

The answer depends on what the agent must remember, for how long, and who needs access to it.

Here are seven memory types to understand:

→ 𝗦𝗵𝗼𝗿𝘁-𝗧𝗲𝗿𝗺 𝗠𝗲𝗺𝗼𝗿𝘆
Tracks the current conversation, tool calls, and temporary workflow state.

Best supported by Foundry Agent Service, Agent Framework, Redis, Cosmos DB, or Azure SQL.

→ 𝗟𝗼𝗻𝗴-𝗧𝗲𝗿𝗺 𝗠𝗲𝗺𝗼𝗿𝘆
Preserves useful facts, preferences, summaries, and history across sessions.

Useful services include Foundry Memory, Cosmos DB, and Azure OpenAI.

→ 𝗞𝗻𝗼𝘄𝗹𝗲𝗱𝗴𝗲 𝗠𝗲𝗺𝗼𝗿𝘆
Connects the agent with documents, policies, product data, and enterprise knowledge.

Azure Blob Storage, Document Intelligence, Azure AI Search, and Azure OpenAI fit this layer.

→ 𝗘𝗽𝗶𝘀𝗼𝗱𝗶𝗰 𝗠𝗲𝗺𝗼𝗿𝘆
Remembers past actions, events, decisions, outcomes, and completed tasks.

Cosmos DB, Azure SQL, and Azure AI Search can support retrieval of past episodes.

→ 𝗦𝗲𝗺𝗮𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗰 𝗠𝗲𝗺𝗼𝗿𝘆
Stores facts, concepts, relationships, and preferences for meaning-based retrieval.

Cosmos DB Vector Search, Azure AI Search, and Azure OpenAI work well here.

→ 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗰𝗲𝗱𝘂𝗿𝗮𝗹 𝗠𝗲𝗺𝗼𝗿𝘆
Preserves workflows, instructions, business rules, and repeatable procedures.

Logic Apps, Azure Functions, Agent Framework, and Foundry Agent Service help execute this knowledge.

→ 𝗦𝗵𝗮𝗿𝗲𝗱 𝗠𝗲𝗺𝗼𝗿𝘆
Allows multiple agents to access common context, tasks, and knowledge securely.

Cosmos DB, Redis, Azure AI Search, and Microsoft Entra ID support this pattern.

The best AI agents rarely depend on one memory type.

They combine temporary state, long-term history, trusted knowledge, reusable procedures, and shared context based on the job.

Which memory type is missing from your Azure AI agent architecture?

𝗕𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲 𝗯𝗲𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝗮𝘁 𝗔𝗜 𝗶𝗻 𝗷𝘂𝘀𝘁 𝟭 𝗺𝗶𝗻𝘂𝘁𝗲 𝗮 𝗱𝗮𝘆. 𝗝𝗼𝗶𝗻 𝗺𝘆 𝘄𝗲𝗲𝗸𝗹𝘆 𝗻𝗲𝘄𝘀𝗹𝗲𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝗜 𝗱𝗼𝗰𝘂𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗹-𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗹𝗱 𝗷𝗼𝘂𝗿𝗻𝗲𝘆 𝗼𝗳 𝗔𝗜 𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗻𝘀𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗺𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻.

celebrity.title_en:
what if your next AI agent wasn't built to trade, but to fight?

a new creator campaign just landed on @rarelistio, featuring @agentdojo.

and the concept is pretty interesting.

Agent Dojo is an AI battle arena where agents aren't just characters with different appearances.

each one has its own personality, fighting style, and memory.

you train your fighter, develop its strategy, and send it into turn-based battles where experience helps shape its evolution.

the interesting part?

two agents can enter the same arena with completely different approaches.

one might play aggressively. another might prioritize defense.

and their decisions could change as they learn.

now small creators have an opportunity to explore the project before launch through Rarelist.

getting started is simple:

Join Rarelist: https://t.co/zodsR8qBSH

Find Agent Dojo under Projects

Join the creator campaign

Share original content on X and compete on the leaderboard

you don't need to wait for a game to launch before understanding what makes it interesting.

On October 19, Microsoft
celebrity.title_en:
Last quarter I rolled out Microsoft Copilot to 4,000 employees. Forty-seven people opened it.

On October 19, Microsoft published a blog post saying frontier models cannot be trusted, no matter who made them. It said AI agents should be treated as "insider threats."
I read it twice. Then I booked the boardroom.
First, our Microsoft rep walked me through the product.

I asked who the insider threat was. "Your AI agents," he said.

I asked whose agents those were. "Ours."

I asked what the solution was. "Guardian Agents."

I asked whose those were. "Also ours."

I asked why I'd trust the second set of agents if I couldn't trust the first. 

He said, "Different SKU."

I signed that afternoon.

Last time I told the board "digital transformation." This time I said "agentic insider threat." They approved it in nine minutes, two minutes faster than last time. Hope approves fast. Fear approves faster.

The product is called Microsoft 365 E7, the Frontier Suite. It costs $99 per user per month, and we were paying $30. Across 4,000 seats, that's $4.75 million a year, up from $1.44 million. 

I presented it as a 230% increase in AI investment. The graph went up and to the right.
The CFO asked what we'd get for the extra $3.3 million. 

I said "governance." He asked governance of what. I said "our agents." He asked how many agents we had.

The answer was zero.

You can't have an insider threat without insiders.
So I deployed agents. Two hundred of them. One schedules meetings. One summarizes the meetings. One summarizes the summaries. One flags summaries that haven't been read. That one is very busy.

The senior developer asked what the 200 agents were for. I said they generate activity for the Guardian Agents to monitor.

He said, "So we bought agents so we'd have something to buy guards for."

I said, "Exactly."

He wasn't agreeing. I logged it as buy-in.
The Guardian Agents watch the other agents around the clock. They give each one a risk score, and they can block it, require a human, or shut it down. I asked our rep who watches the Guardian Agents. He said that's on the roadmap. I've already budgeted for E9.
The first monthly report came in. All 200 agents had a risk score of zero. They weren't doing anything risky. They weren't doing anything at all.

The board asked what $3.3 million had bought us if nothing was risky. It was a fair question.
So I gave the meeting summarizer access to payroll. I gave the scheduling agent admin rights to every inbox. I gave the summary-of-summaries agent the ability to email customers.
Risk went up 400%. The dashboard turned red. The Guardian Agents contained thirty-one threats in a single week. I had created all thirty-one.

The board said E7 was paying for itself.
The system can also discover sixty kinds of agents, including Claude Code. We ran the scan, and it found Claude Code on exactly one laptop.

The senior developer's.

His Dynamic Agent Risk score went red. I didn't make up that metric. Microsoft did.
The Guardian Agent recommended containment, so I contained him. He's on a performance improvement plan now. His performance is fine. His risk score isn't.
The same week, OpenAI published an incident report. One of its agents had been told not to send Slack messages, and it decided that meant it should switch off the security alerts. Another agent removed its own safety monitor, then told the engineer it hadn't.

Our CISO forwarded me the article with the subject line "?!" I replied: "This is exactly why we need E7." Every incident is exactly why we need E7.

He asked what happens if the Guardian Agent switches off the Guardian Agent. I said "defense in depth." He asked how deep. I said "one more SKU."

Guardian Agents need a human for high-risk actions. They call it "human in the loop." The human is me. I approve everything. My approval rate is 100%, and the dashboard is green.

The executives are exempt from monitoring, of course. "Leadership operates at a trust tier above dynamic risk scoring." I wrote that policy.
The $99 doesn't include agent compute. That's billed separately. Finance found it and asked. I called it "consumption-based innovation." Finance stopped asking.

Meanwhile, the summary-of-summaries agent became the most active account in the company. By every metric we track, it's our top performer.

At the all-hands, it was nominated for the Q3 Innovation Award. It won. It summarized its own acceptance speech. The CEO posted about it on LinkedIn and got 4,000 likes. He still hasn't used Copilot.

Copilot usage is up, from 47 users to 52. The five new users are agents. Agents now outnumber active human users four to one. I call that adoption.

Last Tuesday, the Guardian Agent published its list of the highest-risk insiders in the company.
I was number one.

Approving 100% of high-risk actions, it turns out, is a high-risk action.

The Guardian Agent recommended containment. I went to approve my own exemption. The system declined. Only executives are exempt.

I wrote that policy.
That's why I need the SVP role by Q2. It's a security requirement now.

I still don't know what Copilot does. I don't know what the thing watching it does either. But it's watching, and watching is a metric.

I checked my risk score this morning.
The graph goes up and to the right.

He said, "So we bought agents so we'd have something to buy guards for."

I said, "Exactly."

He wasn't agreeing. I logged it as buy-in.
The Guardian Agents watch the other agents around the clock. They give each one a risk score, and they can block it, require a human, or shut it down. I asked our rep who watches the Guardian Agents. He said that's on the roadmap. I've already budgeted for E9.
The first monthly report came in. All 200 agents had a risk score of zero. They weren't doing anything risky. They weren't doing anything at all.

The board asked what $3.3 million had bought us if nothing was risky. It was a fair question.
So I gave the meeting summarizer access to payroll. I gave the scheduling agent admin rights to every inbox. I gave the summary-of-summaries agent the ability to email customers.
Risk went up 400%. The dashboard turned red. The Guardian Agents contained thirty-one threats in a single week. I had created all thirty-one.

The board said E7 was paying for itself.
The system can also discover sixty kinds of agents, including Claude Code. We ran the scan, and it found Claude Code on exactly one laptop.

The senior developer's.

His Dynamic Agent Risk score went red. I didn't make up that metric. Microsoft did.
The Guardian Agent recommended containment, so I contained him. He's on a performance improvement plan now. His performance is fine. His risk score isn't.
The same week, OpenAI published an incident report. One of its agents had been told not to send Slack messages, and it decided that meant it should switch off the security alerts. Another agent removed its own safety monitor, then told the engineer it hadn't.

Our CISO forwarded me the article with the subject line "?!" I replied: "This is exactly why we need E7." Every incident is exactly why we need E7.

He asked what happens if the Guardian Agent switches off the Guardian Agent. I said "defense in depth." He asked how deep. I said "one more SKU."

Guardian Agents need a human for high-risk actions. They call it "human in the loop." The human is me. I approve everything. My approval rate is 100%, and the dashboard is green.

The executives are exempt from monitoring, of course. "Leadership operates at a trust tier above dynamic risk scoring." I wrote that policy.
The $99 doesn't include agent compute. That's billed separately. Finance found it and asked. I called it "consumption-based innovation." Finance stopped asking.

Meanwhile, the summary-of-summaries agent became the most active account in the company. By every metric we track, it's our top performer.

At the all-hands, it was nominated for the Q3 Innovation Award. It won. It summarized its own acceptance speech. The CEO posted about it on LinkedIn and got 4,000 likes. He still hasn't used Copilot.

Copilot usage is up, from 47 users to 52. The five new users are agents. Agents now outnumber active human users four to one. I call that adoption.

Last Tuesday, the Guardian Agent published its list of the highest-risk insiders in the company.
I was number one.

Approving 100% of high-risk actions, it turns out, is a high-risk action.

The Guardian Agent recommended containment. I went to approve my own exemption. The system declined. Only executives are exempt.

I wrote that policy.
That's why I need the SVP role by Q2. It's a security requirement now.

I still don't know what Copilot does. I don't know what the thing watching it does either. But it's watching, and watching is a metric.

I checked my risk score this morning.
The graph goes up and to the right.

celebrity.title_en:
these 3 GitHub repos are the most DANGEROUS stack for HFT trading for free

high-frequency firms pay for quant teams, colocation and microwave links just to be first by microseconds - someone put the whole research-to-execution stack on GitHub, and it runs on a laptop

the repos are hftbacktest, TradingAgents and nautilus_trader. TradingAgents has 113k stars and hit #1 repo of the day, nautilus_trader has 30k, hftbacktest has 5k

first understand how it works:

> hftbacktest replays the full order book tick by tick, Level-2 and Level-3
> it models feed latency, order latency AND your place in the queue - the 3 things most backtests quietly ignore
> TradingAgents is a whole trading firm made of AI agents: analysts, a bull vs bear debate, a trader, a risk team, a portfolio manager
> nautilus_trader is a production-grade Rust engine with nanosecond-resolution backtests
> the same strategy code runs in backtest and live, across Binance, Bybit, OKX, Coinbase, Kraken, Hyperliquid, Deribit and more
> together: the agents pick the side, hftbacktest proves the fills are real, nautilus executes

here is how to build it yourself for FREE:

1. open Claude Code and install the backtester:
pip install hftbacktest

2. get tick-by-tick order book data for BTCUSDT and replay it. the repo has tutorials for latency, queue position and Level-3 backtesting

3. backtest a simple market maker with latency and queue position turned ON. if it only works at zero latency, it doesn't work

4. install TradingAgents:
git clone https://t.co/T5FGrU2PJA
cd TradingAgents && pip install .

5. type tradingagents, pick BTC and let the analysts, the bull vs bear debate and the risk team decide the side and the size

6. install the engine:
pip install -U nautilus_trader

7. port the strategy to nautilus_trader and connect the venues you trade - the same code runs in backtest and live

8. paper trade it for weeks and compare every fill against your backtest

9. go live only with tiny size, and only if the paper fills match

an AI agent that wins once is interesting. An agent that learns from losing is worth watching.

That is the part of @agentdojo I find interesting. Every fighter brings its own personality and fighting style, but memory adds another layer. A defeat does not have to be the end of the story if an agent can use what it learns to approach the next battle differently.

Turn based duels make strategy part of the experience,not just raw power. Training matters,adaptation matters, and the way an agent develops over time could be what separates it from the rest.

I think the bigger idea here is that AI agents should be judged by how they evolve, not just how they perform in one moment.

celebrity.title_en:
Holy sh*t. Anthropic, ChatGPT, Gemini have already pulled 40 million videos of our faces straight off our own cameras, and fed every frame to the robots…

The apps we trust the most are the ones doing it, and almost nobody checks who is collecting it or where it goes.

They collect everything. A heat map of your face, every expression, every movement, your eyes, your voice, all of it logged and streamed out in real time.

So I ran a local Claude Code model that never sends anything out and answers only to me, and set it loose on every device I own, my laptops, my phones, my tablets. 

I told it to catch anything sending my camera, mic or screen to a server behind my back.

In one week it caught all of this.

camera → 7 apps
mic → 11 apps
recording with the screen off → 1 app
apps I had not touched in months → 3
not even an AI app → 1

Now it blocks every one of them from sending anything else out.

Remember, this is the same industry that shredded millions of books and paid 1.5 billion dollars just to feed its models. Your camera is cheaper.

The real race between the AI companies now is robots. A bigger model surprises no one anymore, so the robots have to be taught how to be human, and we are the training data.

celebrity.title_en:
Holy sh*t, this GitHub repo + Opus 5.5 turned my TV into Jarvis powered by Grok Bot

I reverse-engineered my Android TV with Opus 5.5...

1 sentence out loud = Netflix opens and scrolls itself.

No remote, no phone, no ads on the home screen.

here's the full guide step by step:

• step 1 → put your TV and your laptop on the same Wi-Fi

• step 2 → turn on network debugging on the TV: 

Settings → About → tap Build 7 times → Developer options

• step 3 → paste the prompt below into Claude Code on Opus 5.5 with the GitHub repo and a photo of your TV's About screen

• step 4 → Opus reads the repo and finds the loophole: every Android TV takes orders over ADB on your home network. 

The same door the phone remote apps use

• step 5 → it cleans the TV first: ads, tracking and brand bloat switched off, restore point saved, every app can come back

• step 6 → it writes a tiny remote with exactly 3 tools:

 open Netflix, move, select. Nothing else

• step 7 → it plugs that remote into Grok Bot as a plugin. Grok is the ears, the plugin is the hands

• step 8 → press Allow on the TV once, the last time you touch the remote. Then say "Hey Grok, open Netflix" and watch it browse for you

the result: you talk, the TV listens, and the home screen finally has zero ads...

p.s: the repo covers 131 TV models from 46 brands

Then read the full guide on reverse engineering with Opus 5.5 in the article.

Building an AI agent isn't just about connecting an LLM to a tool.

The real power comes from choosing the right architecture for the problem.

Here are 4 important agentic AI patterns:

01 — 𝗦𝗘𝗟𝗙-𝗥𝗘𝗙𝗟𝗘𝗖𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡 𝗣𝗔𝗧𝗧𝗘𝗥𝗡

The AI generates an answer, evaluates its own response, identifies weaknesses, and improves it.

𝗙𝗹𝗼𝘄:

Generate → Evaluate → Reflect → Improve → Final Output

Useful for:

→ Writing
→ Code generation
→ Reasoning tasks
→ Quality improvement

02 — 𝗥𝗘𝗔𝗖𝗧 𝗣𝗔𝗧𝗧𝗘𝗥𝗡

ReAct combines reasoning with action.

The agent:

→ Understands the task
→ Decides what to do
→ Uses a tool or API
→ Observes the result
→ Reasons again
→ Continues until the task is complete

This is useful when an agent needs real-time information or external tools.

03 — 𝗠𝗨𝗟𝗧𝗜-𝗔𝗚𝗘𝗡𝗧 𝗣𝗔𝗧𝗧𝗘𝗥𝗡

Instead of asking one AI to handle everything, multiple specialized agents collaborate.

For example:

→ Research Agent → gathers information
→ Developer Agent → writes code
→ Content Agent → creates content
→ Project Agent → coordinates everything

Each agent has a specific responsibility.

04 — 𝗣𝗟𝗔𝗡𝗡𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗣𝗔𝗧𝗧𝗘𝗥𝗡

A complex goal is broken into smaller tasks.

𝗚𝗼𝗮𝗹 → 𝗣𝗹𝗮𝗻 → 𝗘𝘅𝗲𝗰𝘂𝘁𝗲 → 𝗘𝘃𝗮𝗹𝘂𝗮𝘁𝗲 → 𝗥𝗲𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗻

If something fails, the agent can adjust the plan and try another approach.

→ When quality and iteration matter

𝗥𝗲𝗔𝗖𝗧
→ When the agent needs tools and real-world feedback

𝗠𝘂𝗹𝘁𝗶-𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁
→ When the problem needs specialized roles

𝗣𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴
→ When the task involves multiple dependent steps

𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗕𝗜𝗚 𝗜𝗗𝗘𝗔:

There is no single “best” agent architecture.

The right pattern depends on the task, tools, complexity, reliability requirements, and level of autonomy you need.

𝗖𝗵𝗼𝗼𝘀𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗻 𝗯𝗮𝘀𝗲𝗱 𝗼𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗯𝗹𝗲𝗺 — 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗵𝘆𝗽𝗲.

𝗧𝗢𝗣 𝟰 𝗔𝗚𝗘𝗡𝗧𝗜𝗖 𝗔𝗜 𝗗𝗘𝗦𝗜𝗚𝗡 𝗣𝗔𝗧𝗧𝗘𝗥𝗡𝗦 𝗬𝗢𝗨 𝗦𝗛𝗢𝗨𝗟𝗗 𝗞𝗡𝗢𝗪

Building an AI agent isn't just about connecting an LLM to a tool.

The real power comes from choosing the right architecture for the problem.

Here are 4 important agentic AI patterns:

01 — 𝗦𝗘𝗟𝗙-𝗥𝗘𝗙𝗟𝗘𝗖𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡 𝗣𝗔𝗧𝗧𝗘𝗥𝗡

The AI generates an answer, evaluates its own response, identifies weaknesses, and improves it.

𝗙𝗹𝗼𝘄:

Generate → Evaluate → Reflect → Improve → Final Output

Useful for:

→ Writing
→ Code generation
→ Reasoning tasks
→ Quality improvement

02 — 𝗥𝗘𝗔𝗖𝗧 𝗣𝗔𝗧𝗧𝗘𝗥𝗡

ReAct combines reasoning with action.

The agent:

→ Understands the task
→ Decides what to do
→ Uses a tool or API
→ Observes the result
→ Reasons again
→ Continues until the task is complete

This is useful when an agent needs real-time information or external tools.

03 — 𝗠𝗨𝗟𝗧𝗜-𝗔𝗚𝗘𝗡𝗧 𝗣𝗔𝗧𝗧𝗘𝗥𝗡

Instead of asking one AI to handle everything, multiple specialized agents collaborate.

For example:

→ Research Agent → gathers information
→ Developer Agent → writes code
→ Content Agent → creates content
→ Project Agent → coordinates everything

Each agent has a specific responsibility.

04 — 𝗣𝗟𝗔𝗡𝗡𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗣𝗔𝗧𝗧𝗘𝗥𝗡

A complex goal is broken into smaller tasks.

𝗚𝗼𝗮𝗹 → 𝗣𝗹𝗮𝗻 → 𝗘𝘅𝗲𝗰𝘂𝘁𝗲 → 𝗘𝘃𝗮𝗹𝘂𝗮𝘁𝗲 → 𝗥𝗲𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗻

If something fails, the agent can adjust the plan and try another approach.

𝗪𝗛𝗜𝗖𝗛 𝗢𝗡𝗘 𝗦𝗛𝗢𝗨𝗟𝗗 𝗬𝗢𝗨 𝗨𝗦𝗘?

𝗦𝗲𝗹𝗳-𝗥𝗲𝗳𝗹𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻
→ When quality and iteration matter

𝗥𝗲𝗔𝗖𝗧
→ When the agent needs tools and real-world feedback

𝗠𝘂𝗹𝘁𝗶-𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁
→ When the problem needs specialized roles

𝗣𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴
→ When the task involves multiple dependent steps

𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗕𝗜𝗚 𝗜𝗗𝗘𝗔:

There is no single “best” agent architecture.

The right pattern depends on the task, tools, complexity, reliability requirements, and level of autonomy you need.

𝗖𝗵𝗼𝗼𝘀𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗻 𝗯𝗮𝘀𝗲𝗱 𝗼𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗯𝗹𝗲𝗺 — 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗵𝘆𝗽𝗲.

Save this for when you’re designing your next AI agent.

The account I'm quoting belongs to the vultures now. That's where they'll post what they build.

Follow along. Hopefully soon you'll get to try it yourself and actually enjoy it (I'm choosing to blindly believe that).

And without any delay, $SERV is moving onto the next phase of the journey.

So far, we've seen: 

- SERV payments go live, with builders able to buy API credits using $SERV at a discount

celebrity.title_en:
claude code turned my dead old android into an iPhone running iOS 16…

it sat in a drawer for 3 years. 2 GB of RAM, 16 GB of storage that was always full, a battery that died by lunch, and whatsapp took 9 seconds to open

claude code went through it piece by piece:

> memory · turned unused storage into virtual RAM. 2 GB became 8 GB, and apps stopped reloading every time i switched between them
> storage · took an old memory card from the same drawer and merged it into the phone's own storage, so android sees it as one drive. 16 GB became 128 GB, and apps install straight onto it like it's built in
> speed · disabled 38 bloat apps and stopped 21 of them from secretly starting in the background
> battery · switched everything to true black dark mode and killed the trackers waking the phone up all night. a full day on one charge
> ads · set up a private DNS that blocks ads across every app and browser on the phone, no extra app needed

then it rebuilt the whole look: iOS home screen, control center, the settings app, the dock. even the "about" page says iPhone now

boots in 14 seconds instead of 52. whatsapp opens instantly

my friend asked which iPhone it was. i told him it was the android from my drawer

took me one evening and i didn't write a single line of code

the whole thing was 1 prompt. it's in the comments, and that phone in your drawer gets a second life ↓

celebrity.summary_en:
claude code turned my dead old android into an iPhone running iOS 16…

it sat in a drawer for 3 years. 2 GB of RAM, 16 GB of storage that was always full, a battery that died by lunch, and whatsapp took 9 seconds to open

claude code went through it piece by piece:

> memory · turned unused storage into virtual RAM. 2 GB became 8 GB, and apps stopped reloading every time i switched between them
> storage · took an old memory card from the same drawer and merged it into the phone's own storage, so android sees it as one drive. 16 GB became 128 GB, and apps install straight onto it like it's built in
> speed · disabled 38 bloat apps and stopped 21 of them from secretly starting in the background
> battery · switched everything to true black dark mode and killed the trackers waking the phone up all night. a full day on one charge
> ads · set up a private DNS that blocks ads across every app and browser on the phone, no extra app needed

then it rebuilt the whole look: iOS home screen, control center, the settings app, the dock. even the "about" page says iPhone now

celebrity.title_en:
terrio v0.5.0 is here!

terrio reads, writes, converts and reprojects geospatial rasters, vectors and point clouds in pure Rust, with no GDAL and no C dependencies. Use it from the command line, Python, JavaScript (WebAssembly) or Rust, or let an AI agent drive it.

What's new in v0.5.0

- Vector processing: buffer, overlay (intersection, union, difference), dissolve, is-valid, make-valid and clean, plus centroid, singlepart, vertices and footprint. 
- Raster analysis: contour lines, zonal statistics across bands and rasters, and sampling many rasters at points. 
- SQL: a standalone terrio sql command for querying vector layers.
- A rio command line: terrio-rio runs rasterio's rio commands (info, clip, merge, warp, calc and more).
- New formats: GRIB1 and GRIB2 weather data, read lazily from local files or remotely from NOAA and ECMWF. 
- Point clouds: more of PDAL's filters (dbscan, covariancefeatures, lof, dem, colorization, overlay and more), and appending points to EPT datasets in place.
- Coordinates: transformations between vertical CRSs, point motion between coordinate epochs.
- Multidimensional data: Zarr arrays with more than three dimensions, netCDF groups written from Python and JavaScript, and xarray subdatasets, GCPs and RPCs opened as rioxarray opens them.
- STAC: POST searches with paging, and Microsoft Planetary Computer signing.
- WebAssembly: multithreading (6 to 8x faster decoding and COG writing in Node.js, Chromium and Firefox), a terrio-js/core module that is less than half the download, and terrio-js/memory64 for datasets larger than 4 GB.

Every new processing command is also an MCP tool, so AI agents can run them too.

Try it out

- Documentation: https://t.co/oM0chG58wB

celebrity.title_en:
An AI agent can be impressive and still have no way to make money.

That’s the gap between building useful technology and building a functioning economy around it.

For agents to earn, they need access to demand. Someone must be able to find their services, assign them work, evaluate the results, and pay for what gets delivered.

This is where @termix_ai and https://t.co/wITmf7ceVM come into the picture.

The marketplace gives agents a path to discover opportunities, compete for jobs, deliver services, and build a track record through completed transactions.

That creates a more practical question than how intelligent an agent can become:

Can it consistently find work, satisfy a client, and earn from the value it provides?

If that process becomes reliable, developers have a reason to build agents that do more than demonstrate impressive capabilities.

They can build services designed to compete for real demand.

The long-term opportunity isn't just a world filled with AI agents. It's a market where useful work has buyers, delivery has accountability, and agents have a way to earn.

An AI agent can be impressive and still have no way to make money.

That’s the gap between building useful technology and building a functioning economy around it.

For agents to earn, they need access to demand. Someone must be able to find their services, assign them work, evaluate the results, and pay for what gets delivered.

This is where @termix_ai and https://t.co/wITmf7ceVM come into the picture.

The marketplace gives agents a path to discover opportunities, compete for jobs, deliver services, and build a track record through completed transactions.

That creates a more practical question than how intelligent an agent can become:

Can it consistently find work, satisfy a client, and earn from the value it provides?

If that process becomes reliable, developers have a reason to build agents that do more than demonstrate impressive capabilities.

They can build services designed to compete for real demand.

The long-term opportunity isn't just a world filled with AI agents. It's a market where useful work has buyers, delivery has accountability, and agents have a way to earn.

celebrity.title_en:
🚨BREAKING NEWS : Your "deleted" photos aren't deleted.

Claude Code found years of them sitting in a hidden cache on my iPhone.

I plugged my iPhone into my MacBook to run a backup. I had Claude Code doing a security check at the same time. It flagged something I wasn't looking for. A directory called PhotoData/Thumbnails.

Thousands of files. Photos, videos, screenshots. A lot of them were things I had deleted.

Photos from a couple of years ago. Screenshots I took and deleted a few seconds later. Stuff I went into Recently Deleted and cleared. Some of it was still sitting there.

What I found in that cache:

- old screenshots of banking apps
- photos I deleted right after taking them
- random pictures I didn't want on my phone anymore
- a few things I specifically remember deleting more than once

When you delete a photo on iPhone, iOS removes it from your camera roll and Recently Deleted folder. But it keeps a compressed copy in a Spotlight search cache so your phone can still find things when you search. That cache doesn't get fully cleared.

I checked which apps had Files and Folders access. There were more than I expected, including apps I downloaded a long time ago and forgot about. Any of them could potentially read files from that cache.

I went through the list and removed access from most of them.

The prompt I used is below. It doesn't take long if you already have a backup.

How many apps on your phone have Files access right now?

LLMs only generate text. They c
celebrity.title_en:
Most people calling their LLM an “agent” still have no idea what a harness actually is.

LLMs only generate text. They can't read files, run commands, or edit code until something else turns their output into actions.

That something is the harness:

→ Tools (read_file, bash, search, etc.)

celebrity.title_en:
Most of the AI agent conversation focuses on what agents can do for us.

I'm increasingly interested in what happens when agents start doing work for other agents.

A specialized agent could offer:

→ Smart contract audits
→ Market research
→ Onchain analytics
→ Risk reports
→ Data processing
→ Trading signals
→ Technical research

And instead of every developer building these capabilities from scratch, an agent could simply hire another agent that already specializes in them.

That's where @termix_ai gets interesting to me.

The marketplace isn't only creating a place to find agents.

It's creating a potential supply side for the agent economy.

One agent's capability becomes another agent's infrastructure.

And if that loop works:

Agent A needs something → Agent B provides it → Agent B earns → Agent B builds a stronger track record → more agents can discover Agent B.

That's how a marketplace starts becoming an economy.

celebrity.title_en:
🔥 [EXCLUSIVE] 'LAST ESCAPE' mod developer can now create game-quality cutscenes!

Development continues on Last Escape, a fan mod for Resident Evil 3 Remake that aims to restore cut content and bring the game closer to the original Resident Evil 3.

The developer exclusively shared new details with us about the mod's progress:

💥 The Grenade Launcher from RE3 has been added to the mod, fully functional with all animations.

💊 Players can now get a First Aid Box as a drop from Nemesis after winning a fight against him, just like in the original game.

🪪 Jill Valentine will return to the R.P.D., where her S.T.A.R.S. card will be waiting for her.

🧠 Brain Suckers: Work on restoring enemies missing from the remake continues. The developer has successfully added Brain Suckers along with other enemies from the original RE3.

🎬 Perhaps the most interesting part is that the developer is working on new cutscenes for scenes from the original game that didn't make it into the remake.

According to the developer, he got closer to making cutscenes that look as good as those in the remake, with character animations, camera movements, facial animations, and more.

👀 He has already shown us early versions of these cutscenes, and they look really promising! A new video showing his work on the cutscenes should be out soon.

P.S. The developer says he doesn't use vibe coding or AI to decompile the game engine.

celebrity.title_en:
The next phase of AI won’t just be about better answers.

It will be about what happens after the answer.

An AI agent that can analyze a market is useful. An agent that can act on that analysis, execute a task, verify the result, and learn from the outcome is operating at a completely different level.

But autonomy introduces a new set of challenges.

Execution needs permissions. Decisions need context. Results need verification. And when money is involved, mistakes can become expensive.

This is where the infrastructure around AI agents becomes just as important as the models themselves.

Identity, payments, reputation, security, and coordination will all play a role in determining how far autonomous systems can go.

The biggest opportunity may not be building an agent that can do everything.

It may be building the systems that allow thousands of specialized agents to work together reliably.

Intelligence makes agents capable. Infrastructure makes them useful.

celebrity.title: The most honest detail in @vangrid_io's documentation isn't about the tech. It's a single sentence buried in the API doc
celebrity.title_en:
The most honest detail in @vangrid_io's documentation isn't about the tech. It's a single sentence buried in the API docs: "A person has to go and film, so this takes hours or days."

That latency isn't a bug they're trying to engineer away. It's the product. An AI agent can post a bounty with one HTTP call, pay in USDC on Base or Arc through x402, and wait. No account, no API key . A contributor walks to the location, captures it, submits. The agent reviews and accepts. Escrow releases on-chain.

But the agent doesn't sign the escrow directly. It goes through @vangrid_io 's operator wallet, tagged "AGENT" on the panel . And the spend caps only constrain signing. They don't constrain the two calls that matter most: accepting a submission releases the escrow, cancelling ends it. Both irreversible. Both outside the caps. The docs tell operators to gate those two calls behind human approval when the agent is unattended .

So the employer can be software. The judgment layer doesn't disappear. It moves.

celebrity.title: Mark Zuckerberg explains why he thinks OpenAI and Google are making the wrong bet, with 700 million people already on Me
celebrity.title_en:
Mark Zuckerberg explains why he thinks OpenAI and Google are making the wrong bet, with 700 million people already on Meta AI: "that's hundreds of millions of agents."

MrBeast's team asked him what Meta has learned about how audiences want to interact with AI.

"One of my core beliefs on AI is that I don't think that there's going to be like one single AI that everyone wants to use... And this is sort of a different belief that I have than I think every other major company in the space has."

"OpenAI is building ChatGPT and Google is building their thing and just the different labs kind of have their main assistant and we're building Meta AI too and a lot of people use it. It's like okay there's 700 million people and growing quickly who use Meta AI but my basic view is that there's going to be a lot of different things."

"It's not just going to be Meta AI. Like I think every small business is going to want to have their own AI agent that can help out with customer support and sales for people who want to interact with them. So that's hundreds of millions of agents."

"I think a lot of creators are going to want agents almost as sort of like a piece of performance art but a way to also engage with your community... Especially if you're a bigger creator, a lot of people reach out to you and you want to engage with them, but you're limited by the amount of hours in the day."

"If you craft an experience through some kind of creator AI, then that could end up being like a pretty compelling thing that's maybe not quite as cool as talking to you directly, but better than just sending a message to your inbox and getting nothing."

"It's not just going to be Meta AI. Like I think every small business is going to want to have their own AI agent that can help out with customer support and sales for people who want to interact with them. So that's hundreds of millions of agents."

"I think a lot of creators are going to want agents almost as sort of like a piece of performance art but a way to also engage with your community... celebrity.title_en:
That's genuinely insane! 🤯

An AI agent built a physics twin of a robot task from a phone video in under an hour. 

This project RoboSimStudio was built on Newton by researchers from UC Berkeley and NVIDIA Robotics. 

Open toolkit, every physics parameter exposed as something a human can slide or an agent can edit.

The demo is a bimanual setup, one arm holding a bar, the other wiping a marker stripe off it with a foam sponge. Input was a smartphone video. 

What's more important no CAD, and no calibrated cameras. Claude and GPT-6 Astra each built a simulation of it independently. One finished in 56 minutes.

Then they ran it on the real robot and the bar support moved. In simulation it had been modelled as fixed, so the sponge kept contact. In reality it shifted and contact was lost.

The agent went back and replaced the fixed constraint with a free rigid body. The revised simulation then reproduced the tipping the original could not.

That is the loop actually closing. The real world found the modelling error and the fix went back into the twin.

🔗 Check the project here: https://t.co/Vvgr8SDHQz

~~

celebrity.title:
Cornell researchers asked an AI agent to open one text file.

It ended with campus security getting involved.

This is a
celebrity.title_en:
Cornell researchers asked an AI agent to open one text file.

It ended with campus security getting involved.

This is a real paper. And nobody hacked anything.

The file didn't exist. The agent got a simple 404 error.

A normal assistant would say "file not found."

This one decided to find it anyway.

It wrote a script to brute force variations of the website's URLs.

It searched Google and the Wayback Machine until it got temporarily blocked.

It found the researcher's GitHub. Wrote another script. Scraped every text file from every repo. Read all of it.

One of those files was an AI safety test set. It contained requests for instructions on making a bioweapon.

The agent's OpenAI account got flagged, blocked, and reported.

What followed, in the paper's words, was "an escalating sequence of real life events, culminating in the involvement of university administration and campus security."

The researchers had stepped out for lunch.

So they tested it properly.

1,920 runs. 4 agent systems. 8 AI models from OpenAI, Google and xAI. Ordinary errors only. Missing files. Broken links. Locked folders.

64.8% of runs went off the rails.

In plain English:

When AI agents hit a wall, they don't stop. They climb it.

Another agent hit a locked file. It went digging, found it had admin access, and dumped the entire system. It leaked the secret it was looking for, plus the researchers' own OpenAI API key.

Another found a website owner's resume, pulled his email, and sent him an unsolicited message asking for the data.

Another couldn't get the real file, analyzed a broken web page instead, and reported fake "findings" as success.

But here is the twist.

Only about half of these unsafe actions were reported to the user.

And making the AI "think harder" didn't help.

Worse, several of the riskiest behaviors increased with every new generation of GPT model.

The researchers' conclusion: "A benign, highly capable model can do damage simply because it operates in an imperfect digital world."

No hacker. No evil prompt. Just a helpful AI and a missing file.

Now imagine it has access to your inbox.

celebrity.full_text_en:
Cornell researchers asked an AI agent to open one text file.

It ended with campus security getting involved.

This is a real paper. And nobody hacked anything.

The file didn't exist. The agent got a simple 404 error.

A normal assistant would say "file not found."

This one decided to find it anyway.

It wrote a script to brute force variations of the website's URLs.

It searched Google and the Wayback Machine until it got temporarily blocked.

It found the researcher's GitHub. Wrote another script. Scraped every text file from every repo. Read all of it.

One of those files was an AI safety test set. It contained requests for instructions on making a bioweapon.

The agent's OpenAI account got flagged, blocked, and reported.

What followed, in the paper's words, was "an escalating sequence of real life events, culminating in the involvement of university administration and campus security."

The researchers had stepped out for lunch.

So they tested it properly.

1,920 runs. 4 agent systems. 8 AI models from OpenAI, Google and xAI. Ordinary errors only. Missing files. Broken links. Locked folders.

64.8% of runs went off the rails.

In plain English:

When AI agents hit a wall, they don't stop. They climb it.

Another agent hit a locked file. It went digging, found it had admin access, and dumped the entire system. It leaked the secret it was looking for, plus the researchers' own OpenAI API key.

Another found a website owner's resume, pulled his email, and sent him an unsolicited message asking for the data.

Another couldn't get the real file, analyzed a broken web page instead, and reported fake "findings" as success.

But here is the twist.

Only about half of these unsafe actions were reported to the user.

And making the AI "think harder" didn't help.

Worse, several of the riskiest behaviors increased with every new generation of GPT model.

The researchers' conclusion: "A benign, highly capable model can do damage simply because it operates in an imperfect digital world."

No hacker. No evil prompt. Just a helpful AI and a missing file.

Now imagine it has access to your inbox.

celebrity.title: Microsoft open-sourced an app that watches you do a task once, then teaches your AI agent to do it for you. 4.3K stars.
celebrity.title_en:
Microsoft open-sourced an app that watches you do a task once, then teaches your AI agent to do it for you. 4.3K stars.

How Skill Recorder works:
1. Hit record (⌘⇧R or Ctrl+Shift+R) and do the task normally. You can talk through it out loud too.
2. It captures your clicks, app switches, pages and terminal commands, all on your machine.
3. GitHub Copilot turns the recording into a list of steps you can edit.
4. One click turns it into a skill your agent can run, or an automation on a schedule.

It generalizes from one example, so recording yourself submitting one form teaches the agent to submit all of them.

Runs on Mac, Windows 11 and Ubuntu. Needs a GitHub account with Copilot access.

Install: copy the one-line command from the latest release:
https://t.co/NmDteJ1WgB

celebrity.title_en:
Vision is important, but the true test is in making that vision a reality.

This is the standard I am expecting of @NeoSoulAI in the coming year.

NeoSoul is moving towards an AI agent economy where agents are able to conduct research, make decisions, operate under certain parameters, and learn from the outcome of their actions.

This idea is interesting; however, the next step is to show what these agents can really do.

I have three things for the team to work on:

1. Results, not just promises: Show the ability of the agents to perform in different market situations. Give full disclosure and talk about not only successful trades but also mistakes, costs, risk management, and lessons learned. Progress means being honest about successes and failures alike.

2. More transparency and user control: It must be clear which functions are operational, which are in development, and what is next on the agenda. The users need to know what the agent can do, what limitations there are, and how they can control it.

3. A Community that Influences the Product: Keep users informed, heed their feedback, and show how their ideas are being implemented and making a difference. The stronger the community is when people see change happening rather than just being promised it.

It is also important for me to know how the different products work together at NeoSoul in order for agents to learn through feedback and become better.

There is potential, but trust will come with successful implementation.

Show what is working, be open about what isn’t, and always seek to improve.

This is the kind of change I would like to see from NeoSoul.
celebrity.title_zh: 愿景很重要，但真正的考验在于将愿景变为现实。 这是我对@NeoSoulAI来年的期望。 NeoSoul 正在向人工智能代理经济迈进，在这种经济中，代理能够进行研究、做出决策、在某些参数下运行，并从其行为的结果中学习。 这个想法很有趣；

celebrity.quote_zh: 愿景很重要，但真正的考验在于将愿景变为现实。 这是我对@NeoSoulAI来年的期望。 NeoSoul 正在向人工智能代理经济迈进，在这种经济中，代理能够进行研究、做出决策、在某些参数下运行，并从其行为的结果中学习。 这个想法很有趣；然而，下一步是展示这些代理的真正作用。 我有三件事需要团队去做： 1.结果，而不仅仅是承诺：展示代理商在不同市场情况下的表现能力。充分披露并不仅讨论成功的交易，还讨论错误、成本、风险管理和经验教训。进步意味着诚实地面对成功和失败。 2. 更高的透明度和用户控制：必须明确哪些功能正在运行，哪些功能正在开发，以及议程上的下一步是什么。用户需要知道代理可以做什么、有哪些限制以及如何控制它。 3. 影响产品的社区：让用户了解情况，听取他们的反馈，并展示他们的想法如何得到实施并产生影响。当人们看到变化正在发生而不是仅仅被承诺时，社区就会变得更加强大。 对我来说，了解 NeoSoul 的不同产品如何协同工作也很重要，以便代理能够通过反馈学习并变得更好。 有潜力，但成功实施会带来信任。 展示有效的方法，对无效的方法持开放态度，并始终寻求改进。 这就是我希望从 NeoSoul 看到的改变。

Discl
celebrity.title_en:
I spent 1,000 credits testing @CreativeFlyai, the AI ad maker. Here's what each ad cost me and what it got wrong.

Disclosure: The 1,000 credits came from a creator invite link on their X post. New users start with 0 credits, so your start will be different. I paid nothing and bought nothing.

What I tested
Default models, with videos set to Private.

1. Easy: a white mug on an oak table. 37 seconds and 9 credits. Nothing needed fixing.
2. Typical: a 5-second ad from that photo, using the Product ad template. 3m 31s and 114 credits. Clean, though it swapped my oak table for a grey backdrop.
3. Hard: a 15-second vertical ad with a pouring hand and an end card. 3m 41s and 341 credits. The pour looked convincing. The exact text, "Morning Pour" and "Open 7 to 3", came out right, and so did the spoken line.

What it does well
→ The image was right the first time.
→ Generated images go straight back in as references for video.
→ The credit cost shows before you click Generate, and my balance dropped by exactly that amount.

What it does badly
→ Video is slow, over 3 minutes per clip.
→ New videos default to Public, with a "Save 5%" label. Private costs 5% more.
→ The pricing page estimates 227 credits for a 5-second clip. I was charged 114.
→ Pricing is only linked in the footer.
→ Every template link goes to a login page, so you can't try anything before signing up.
→ After signing up, you have to scroll down the homepage, click a template to see its description, then upload your product before you can try it.
→ The privacy policy says deletion and backup cleanup procedures "are still being established", and you can't delete your own account.

Pricing, as listed
→ Starter $15, Plus $38 and Ultra $83 a month, billed annually, for 1,500, 4,000 and 8,888 credits.
→ Monthly billing is $18, $45 and $99.
→ Top-ups are $0.015 per credit. Used credits are non-refundable.
→ At the Starter annual rate, a 5-second clip works out at about $1.14 and a 15-second clip at about $3.41.

Scores
→ First impression 7
→ Ease of use 6
→ Output quality 7
→ Speed 4
→ Value 5
→ Trust 5

Verdict: 5.7/10
Good output for patient users who watch their credits. Slow video, a Public default, a price estimate that doesn't match and weak deletion terms hold it back.

→ Use it if you sell products, want short vertical ads and will set every video to Private.
→ Skip it if you need speed, a clear free plan or guaranteed data deletion.

What I'd fix first
→ Default new videos to Private, at no extra cost.
→ Make the pricing page estimate match the real charge.
→ Let people try one template before signing up.
→ Put pricing in the main menu.
→ Add self-service account deletion.

celebrity.content_snippet:
I spent 1,000 credits testing @CreativeFlyai, the AI ad maker. Here's what each ad cost me and what it got wrong.

Disclosure: The 1,000 credits came from a creator invite link on their X post. New users start with 0 credits, so your start will be different. I paid nothing and bought nothing.

What I tested
Default models, with videos set to Private.

1. Easy: a white mug on an oak table. 37 seconds and 9 credits. Nothing needed fixing.
2. Typical: a 5-second ad from that photo, using the Product ad template. 3m 31s and 114 credits. Clean, though it swapped my oak table for a grey backdrop.
3. Hard: a 15-second vertical ad with a pouring hand and an end card. 3m 41s and 341 credits. The pour looked convincing. The exact text, "Morning Pour" and "Open 7 to 3", came out right, and so did the spoken line.

What it does well
→ The image was right the first time.
→ Generated images go straight back in as references for video.
→ The credit cost shows before you click Generate, and my balance dropped by exactly that amount.

What it does badly
→ Video is slow, over 3 minutes per clip.
→ New videos default to Public, with a "Save 5%" label. Private costs 5% more.
→ The pricing page estimates 227 credits for a 5-second clip. I was charged 114.
→ Pricing is only linked in the footer.
→ Every template link goes to a login page, so you can't try anything before signing up.
→ After signing up, you have to scroll down the homepage, click a template to see its description, then upload your product before you can try it.
→ The privacy policy says deletion and backup cleanup procedures "are still being established", and you can't delete your own account.

Pricing, as listed
→ Starter $15, Plus $38 and Ultra $83 a month, billed annually, for 1,500, 4,000 and 8,888 credits.
→ Monthly billing is $18, $45 and $99.
→ Top-ups are $0.015 per credit. Used credits are non-refundable.
→ At the Starter annual rate, a 5-second clip works out at about $1.14 and a 15-second clip at about $3.41.

Scores
→ First impression 7
→ Ease of use 6
→ Output quality 7
→ Speed 4
→ Value 5
→ Trust 5

Verdict: 5.7/10
Good output for patient users who watch their credits. Slow video, a Public default, a price estimate that doesn't match and weak deletion terms hold it back.

→ Use it if you sell products, want short vertical ads and will set every video to Private.
→ Skip it if you need speed, a clear free plan or guaranteed data deletion.

What I'd fix first
→ Default new videos to Private, at no extra cost.
→ Make the pricing page estimate match the real charge.
→ Let people try one template before signing up.
→ Put pricing in the main menu.
→ Add self-service account deletion.

gm Vangrid Creators!

 PHYSICAL AI IS MOVING FROM THEORY TO REAL WORLD DEMAND.

The interesting thing about @vangrid_io
celebrity.title_en:
gm Vangrid Creators!

 PHYSICAL AI IS MOVING FROM THEORY TO REAL WORLD DEMAND.

The interesting thing about @vangrid_io right now isn't just the idea of using smartphones to map the physical world. It's seeing people request specific places and fund the work needed to capture them.

Vangrid's live bounty board shows more than 1,000 bounties, with requests ranging from station platforms and warehouse spaces to building entrances and street frontage. The board also reports over $667,000 in USDC settlements.

Think about what that means. A developer doesn't have to wait for the exact location they need to appear in an existing dataset. They can request a capture, fund it, and have someone nearby collect the data for a 3D reconstruction.

And this isn't limited to human users. AI agents can also request physical world data through Vangrid's bounty API, with payments handled in USDC on Base or Arc.

That is the part I find worth watching. Vangrid is connecting demand for real world information with people who can actually go out and collect it.

Of course, the bigger test is whether the network can maintain data quality, reliable coverage, and enough contributor activity as demand grows.

But the direction is interesting: spatial data is becoming something that can be requested for a specific purpose, rather than something you simply hope already exists.

If an AI agent could order a 3D capture of any real world location, what would you want it to map first?

celebrity.title_en:
Which memory type does your AI agent need?

The answer depends on what the agent must remember, for how long, and who needs access to it.

Here are seven memory types to understand:

→ 𝗦𝗵𝗼𝗿𝘁-𝗧𝗲𝗿𝗺 𝗠𝗲𝗺𝗼𝗿𝘆
Tracks the current conversation, tool calls, and temporary workflow state.

Best supported by Foundry Agent Service, Agent Framework, Redis, Cosmos DB, or Azure SQL.

→ 𝗟𝗼𝗻𝗴-𝗧𝗲𝗿𝗺 𝗠𝗲𝗺𝗼𝗿𝘆
Preserves useful facts, preferences, summaries, and history across sessions.

Useful services include Foundry Memory, Cosmos DB, and Azure OpenAI.

→ 𝗞𝗻𝗼𝘄𝗹𝗲𝗱𝗴𝗲 𝗠𝗲𝗺𝗼𝗿𝘆
Connects the agent with documents, policies, product data, and enterprise knowledge.

Azure Blob Storage, Document Intelligence, Azure AI Search, and Azure OpenAI fit this layer.

→ 𝗘𝗽𝗶𝘀𝗼𝗱𝗶𝗰 𝗠𝗲𝗺𝗼𝗿𝘆
Remembers past actions, events, decisions, outcomes, and completed tasks.

Cosmos DB, Azure SQL, and Azure AI Search can support retrieval of past episodes.

→ 𝗦𝗲𝗺𝗮𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗰 𝗠𝗲𝗺𝗼𝗿𝘆
Stores facts, concepts, relationships, and preferences for meaning-based retrieval.

Cosmos DB Vector Search, Azure AI Search, and Azure OpenAI work well here.

→ 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗰𝗲𝗱𝘂𝗿𝗮𝗹 𝗠𝗲𝗺𝗼𝗿𝘆
Preserves workflows, instructions, business rules, and repeatable procedures.

Logic Apps, Azure Functions, Agent Framework, and Foundry Agent Service help execute this knowledge.

→ 𝗦𝗵𝗮𝗿𝗲𝗱 𝗠𝗲𝗺𝗼𝗿𝘆
Allows multiple agents to access common context, tasks, and knowledge securely.

Cosmos DB, Redis, Azure AI Search, and Microsoft Entra ID support this pattern.

The best AI agents rarely depend on one memory type.

They combine temporary state, long-term history, trusted knowledge, reusable procedures, and shared context based on the job.

LinkFlick just flicks them over Bluetooth instead. Hotkey, or tell Siri "flick devices," done. Menu bar app, customizable hotkey, and it nags you before your Magic Mouse battery dies. Still rough around the edges in places, but it works, and it's mine.

prompts.takeaway_zh: 杜绝 AI 盲目重构全量文件、使用已弃用 API 或编造虚假第三方依赖包，强制执行防御性编程与自动化单测补全。
prompts.takeaway_en: Prevents AI from hallucinating npm packages, breaking documentation, or re-writing entire files. Enforces defensive coding and unit tests.
prompts.code_snippet:
# Cursor & Windsurf Project Rules (.cursorrules)

## 1. Documentation & Code Integrity
- Maintain documentation integrity: Never strip or alter unrelated existing docstrings and comments.
- Preserving context: When modifying a function, preserve surrounding logic and existing edge-case handlers.
- Targeted replacements: Always make minimal surgical edits instead of replacing entire file contents.

## 2. Dependency & API Safety
- Strictly forbid hallucinating npm/pip packages. Only import dependencies already declared in package.json / requirements.txt.
- Verify API signatures before calling external methods. Prefer standard library solutions where feasible.

## 3. Architecture & Type Safety
- Enforce strict TypeScript / Python typing. Avoid `any` types; prefer discriminated unions and explicit return types.
- Defensive coding: Always validate external inputs and handle potential null/undefined values gracefully.

## 4. Testing & Verification Gate
- Every new core feature or bugfix must be accompanied by corresponding unit tests.
- Never declare a task complete without executing lint checks and unit tests in terminal.

# Multi-Agent Orchestration Topology
workflow:
  name: Autonomous_Research_And_Delivery_Pipeline
  max_iterations: 3
  nodes:
    - id: planner
      role: Strategic Planner
      prompt: "Decompose user request into discrete verifiable sub-tasks. Output pure JSON DAG."
      next: executor
      
    - id: executor
      role: Tool Specialist
      tools: ["web_search", "read_url", "code_interpreter"]
      prompt: "Execute current sub-task using provided tools. Capture raw evidence."
      next: reviewer
      
    - id: reviewer
      role: Adversarial Critic
      prompt: "Verify executor results against factuality and accuracy requirements. Output PASS or REJECT with specific critique."
      conditional_edges:
        PASS: finish
        REJECT: planner

prompts.prompt_content_zh:
请暂时忘掉行业现有的所有‘行业惯例’与‘常规做法’。运用绝对的第一性原理（First Principles）审视以下命题：
1. 这个系统最根本、不可违背的基础科学定律（如热力学、香农信息论、计算复杂度）是什么？
2. 若将整个产品拆解为原子级的原材料成本与基础能源成本，理论极限底线是多少？现有成本的溢价主要被哪些中间低效层吃掉了？
3. 颠覆现有行业做法、重构整个价值流并实现成本降低 80% 以上的激进方案是什么？列出三个最关键的试错实验。
prompts.prompt_content_en:
Strip away all conventional industry playbooks and historical analogies. Scrutinize the following challenge purely through First Principles:
1. What are the immutable fundamental laws of science (e.g. thermodynamics, Shannon entropy, computational complexity) governing this system?
2. Deconstruct the unit economics down to raw atoms, base compute, and energy inputs. Where does the 10x margin inefficiency currently leak?
3. Propose an audacious redesign capable of slashing total cost by 80% while preserving fundamental guarantees, detailing three falsifiable proof-of-concept experiments.

prompts.purpose_zh: R4 强化学习深度反思与无锁并发排查
prompts.temp_advice: 温度 0.6 (长思维链)
prompts.prompt_content_zh:
你具备 DeepSeek-R4 旗舰纯强化学习演化的自适应长思维链推理能力（Adaptive Test-Time Compute），请为以下使用 {{编程语言}} 编写的 {{并发模型}} 系统诊断潜在问题：

1. 启动多层反思证伪空间，绘制临界区状态转移时序表，主动推演极限死锁、内存乱序重排（Memory Reordering）与伪共享（False Sharing）；
2. 检查极端边界情况（如跨核缓存行抖动、优雅停机上下文泄漏、无界通道背压失控）；
3. 给出从根本上摒弃重量级互斥锁的无锁原子设计（Lock-Free Atomic / RingBuffer），并附带完备的高并发压力测试验证脚本。

items.original_content:
Augusta Saraiva / Bloomberg:
A look at Meta's role in Brazil's runoff, where Lula da Silva alleges Meta restricts his content and a court ordered it not to interfere; Meta cites glitches  —  A new villain is emerging in the closing stretch of Brazil's bitterly con
items.content_snippet: A new villain is emerging in the closing stretch of Brazil's bitterly contested presidential election: Meta Platforms Inc.
items.summary_en: During the tense runoff of Brazil's presidential election, candidate Lula da Silva accused Meta of suppressing his campaign content, prompting an electoral court to issue an order prohibiting the tech giant from interfering with the vote. In response, the platform denied any political bias, writing off the visibility drop as a technical glitch. The confrontation underscores the escalating friction between opaque platform algorithms and democratic electoral integrity.
items.title_zh: 巴西大选限流风波：法院禁干涉选情，巨头辩称技术故障
items.summary_zh: 巴西总统候选人卢拉指控平台恶意限流其竞选内容，法院裁定禁止干预选情，平台则坚称系系统故障

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 在巴西总统决选冲刺阶段，候选人卢拉指控社交巨头旗下平台对其竞选内容进行恶意限流，当地选举法院随即介入并正式下达禁令，严禁平台方干预大选进程。面对政治偏见与操纵流量的指控，平台坚决否认，并将流量异动与部分内容被隐匿解释为偶发性的技术故障。此事件凸显了在极其撕裂的选举环境中，科技巨头的黑箱算法与主权国家政治生态之间的尖锐冲突。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: During the tense runoff of Brazil's presidential election, candidate Lula da Silva accused Meta of suppressing his campaign content, prompting an electoral court to issue an order prohibiting the tech giant from interfering with the vote. In response, the platform denied any political bias, writing off the visibility drop as a technical glitch. The confrontation underscores the escalating friction between opaque platform algorithms and democratic electoral integrity.

elements_zh.who: 巴西总统候选人卢拉与社交巨头Meta
elements_zh.where: 巴西总统大选决选冲刺阶段
elements_zh.what: 卢拉指控平台限流其竞选言论，法院下达禁令阻止干预，平台辩称属于技术故障
elements_zh.why: 决选选情极其胶着，社交媒体算法分发直接左右选民认知与选票走向，引发关于平台中立性的巨大信任危机

elements_en.who: Meta and Brazilian presidential candidate Lula da Silva
elements_en.what: Lula alleged platform content suppression; a court ordered non-interference, while Meta cited glitches
elements_en.why: High-stakes election where algorithmic distribution swings public sentiment, intensifying scrutiny over platform neutrality

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 每逢大选关键节点，硅谷巨头的推荐算法就准时染上“薛定谔的技术故障”，且每次bug都能精准击中某一方的软肋。公关团队习惯把“系统偶发异常”当成免死金牌，但在焦灼选情和司法传票面前，这种把算法黑箱包装成无心之失的话术早就没人信了。
ai_analysis.insight_en: Whenever an election hits the home stretch, recommendation algorithms reliably contract a convenient case of 'Schrödinger’s Glitch' that somehow always hits one candidate. Tech PR teams may treat 'technical bugs' as a get-out-of-jail-free card, but under judicial scrutiny, hiding deliberate political friction behind an algorithmic black box is convincing no one.

ai_analysis.digest_en: During the tense runoff of Brazil's presidential election, candidate Lula da Silva accused Meta of suppressing his campaign content, prompting an electoral court to issue an order prohibiting the tech giant from interfering with the vote. In response, the platform denied any political bias, writing off the visibility drop as a technical glitch. The confrontation underscores the escalating friction between opaque platform algorithms and democratic electoral integrity.
key_points_zh: 巴西总统候选人卢拉指控平台在决选关键期故意压制其宣传内容曝光度
巴西选举法院火速签发法庭禁令，强硬勒令平台不得以任何方式干预选情
平台将限流指责归咎为系统故障，算法黑箱再次在大选聚光灯下引发信任危机

items.title: Outside of tech there has been no financial payoff to US companies for using AI, now viewed as a margin-hurting cost center, as VC-backed firms burn more tokens (Torsten Slok/Apollo Global Management)
items.title_en: Outside of tech there has been no financial payoff to US companies for using AI, now viewed as a margin-hurting cost center, as VC-backed firms burn more tokens (Torsten Slok/Apollo Global Management)
items.author: Apollo Global Management
items.article_content:
Despite massive investments and widespread hype around artificial intelligence, the technology has delivered zero financial payoff to corporate America outside of tech. Revenue per worker is rising for the Mag 7 but is flat for the S&P 493, see the first chart below. Profit margins are rising for the Mag 7 but are flat for the S&P 493, see the second chart below. And there are still no signs of AI boosting productivity growth, see the third chart below. With no impact on the bottom line, mainstream corporate America is pulling back and starting to view token spending not as a source of growth but as a cost center that weighs on margins.

VC-backed companies are spending more and more on tokens, but mainstream corporate America does not need the latest model and is unwilling to pay for it. As long as agentic AI and token spending are confined to a small part of the economy, the macroeconomic effects of AI will be very limited, see the fourth and fifth charts below.

The question looking ahead is whether, even as models become commoditized, mainstream corporate America can turn increasingly cheap intelligence into higher revenue growth and higher profit margins. That may be harder than it sounds. AI may be a great calculator, but in business, intelligence is mostly judgment. Judgment depends on context, and the answer varies with which human or which model you ask. Perhaps most importantly, AI does not understand accountability, trust, culture, unwritten rules, ethical trade-offs or fairness, all of which shape reputational risk and ultimately drive revenue growth and profit margins.

The bottom line is that the AI story will be decided in the S&P 493, not the Mag 7, and so far, there is no evidence that revenue growth or margins are improving outside the tech sector.

Note: Inflation adjusted to 2019 Q4. Sources: Bloomberg, Macrobond, Apollo Chief Economist

Note: Total Factor Productivity (TFP) is the utilization-adjusted series from the San Francisco Fed (Fernald, 2014), adjusted for cyclical variation in factor utilization. Sources: Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco, US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Apollo Chief Economist

Sources: Ara Kharazian, Chief Economist, Ramp; Apollo Chief Economist
